Collections — Array, Map, Set & Friends

Which container, what each operation costs, and the traps that differ from Swift.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.6
  • node >=22.18
  • any ES2023+ engine; the examples run on Node.js

Sources: Keyed collections — MDN JavaScript Guide · Indexed collections — MDN JavaScript Guide

Pick the container

The need decides the type. Plain objects are records, not dictionaries.

NeedUseWhy
Ordered list, index accessT[] / readonly T[]contiguous in practice; readonly removes the mutating methods from the type
Key → value, any key typeMap<K, V>keeps insertion order, no prototype keys, size is O(1)
Fixed record shapeobject / interfaceknown keys checked by the compiler; not a dictionary
Membership, dedupeSet<T>O(1) has; compares objects by identity
Numbers in bulkFloat64Array, Int32Array…fixed length, unboxed, no holes
Cache keyed by an objectWeakMap<object, V>entries vanish with their key; not iterable
FIFO queuearray + head index, or a ring buffershift() re-indexes the whole array: O(n)

What operations cost

The language specification does not mandate complexities; these are what V8, SpiderMonkey and JavaScriptCore deliver.

OperationArrayMap / Set
read by index / keyO(1)O(1) average
push / pop / set / addO(1) amortisedO(1) average
shift / unshift / splice in the middleO(n)—
includes / indexOf / hasO(n)O(1) average
sort / toSortedO(n log n), stable since ES2019sort [...map] then rebuild
deleteleaves a hole — use spliceO(1) average

Map for dictionaries, objects for records

A plain object inherits keys like __proto__; a Map has none and keeps insertion order.

const counts = new Map<string, number>();
for (const word of "the cat and the hat".split(" ")) {
  counts.set(word, (counts.get(word) ?? 0) + 1);
}
console.log([...counts]);                    // insertion order
console.log(counts.get("the"), counts.has("dog"));

const record: Record<string, number> = {};
record["__proto__"] = 1;                     // hits the inherited __proto__ setter: no key is added
console.log(Object.keys(record).length);
Result
[ [ 'the', 2 ], [ 'cat', 1 ], [ 'and', 1 ], [ 'hat', 1 ] ]
2 false
0
Setup
  1. Node.js 22.18 or later (it runs .mts files directly by stripping the types)
  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts
  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

Ran with Node 24.16.0, TypeScript 5.9.3 on 2026-11-11: the output matched the result shown.

Set algebra, and identity

The ES2025 set methods return new sets. Two equal-looking objects are two members.

const a = new Set([1, 2, 3]);
const b = new Set([2, 3, 4]);
console.log([...a.union(b)], [...a.intersection(b)], [...a.difference(b)]);
console.log(a.isSubsetOf(new Set([1, 2, 3, 4])));

const points = new Set([{ x: 1 }, { x: 1 }]);   // compared by reference, not by value
console.log(points.size);
Result
[ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] [ 2, 3 ] [ 1 ]
true
2

The default sort compares strings

Always pass a comparator for numbers. toSorted copies; sort mutates in place.

const nums = [10, 9, 1, 100];
console.log(nums.toSorted());                // [1, 10, 100, 9]: compared as text
console.log(nums.toSorted((a, b) => a - b));
console.log(nums);                           // unchanged
Result
[ 1, 10, 100, 9 ]
[ 1, 9, 10, 100 ]
[ 10, 9, 1, 100 ]

Read-only arrays and typed arrays

readonly T[] is a compile-time promise; a typed array is a runtime container of fixed length.

function total(xs: readonly number[]): number {
  // xs.push(1);   // error TS2339: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly number[]'
  return xs.reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0);
}

const samples = new Float64Array([0.5, 1.5, 2]);
console.log(total([1, 2, 3]), total(Array.from(samples)), samples.length);
Result
6 4 3

Pitfalls

Where code that reads like Swift behaves differently.

  • queue.shift() in a loop is O(n²) overall — keep a head index or use a ring buffer.
  • delete xs[i] leaves a hole (length unchanged); splice(i, 1) removes.
  • [1, 2] === [1, 2] is false: arrays and objects compare by reference, also as Set/Map keys.
  • JSON.stringify(new Map()) is {} — serialise [...map] or Object.fromEntries(map).
  • Use Map for anything keyed at runtime, Set for membership, and readonly in signatures.
  • Arrays have no value semantics: const ys = xs aliases. Copy with [...xs] or structuredClone(xs).

Transform and fold

Chains read top to bottom; each step allocates a new array.

const orders = [
  { id: 1, customer: "ana", total: 30 },
  { id: 2, customer: "bo", total: 12 },
  { id: 3, customer: "ana", total: 8 },
];
const big = orders.filter((o) => o.total >= 10).map((o) => o.id);
const revenue = orders.reduce((sum, o) => sum + o.total, 0);
console.log(big, revenue);
Result
[ 1, 2 ] 50

Group and index

Object.groupBy returns a null-prototype object whose values may be undefined to the type checker.

const people = [
  { name: "Ana", team: "web" },
  { name: "Bo", team: "data" },
  { name: "Cy", team: "web" },
];
const byTeam = Object.groupBy(people, (p) => p.team);
console.log(Object.keys(byTeam), byTeam.web?.map((p) => p.name));

const byName = new Map(people.map((p) => [p.name, p]));
console.log(byName.get("Bo")?.team);
Result
[ 'web', 'data' ] [ 'Ana', 'Cy' ]
data

Search and test

find returns undefined on a miss, findIndex returns -1.

const xs = [3, 8, 12, 5, 20];
console.log(xs.find((x) => x > 10), xs.findLast((x) => x > 10), xs.findIndex((x) => x > 100));
console.log(xs.some((x) => x % 2 === 0), xs.every((x) => x > 0), xs.includes(5));

true true true

Sort by several keys

The sort is stable; chain keys with ||, and use localeCompare for text.

type Player = { name: string; score: number };
const players: Player[] = [
  { name: "cy", score: 7 },
  { name: "ana", score: 9 },
  { name: "bo", score: 7 },
];
const ranked = players.toSorted((a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.name.localeCompare(b.name));
console.log(ranked.map((p) => `${p.name}:${p.score}`).join(" "));
Result
ana:9 bo:7 cy:7

Chunk, window and dedupe

Not built in — two small generic helpers cover both.

function chunk<T>(xs: readonly T[], size: number): T[][] {
  return Array.from({ length: Math.ceil(xs.length / size) }, (_, i) => xs.slice(i * size, i * size + size));
}
function windows<T>(xs: readonly T[], size: number): T[][] {
  return xs.slice(0, Math.max(0, xs.length - size + 1)).map((_, i) => xs.slice(i, i + size));
}

console.log(chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2));
console.log(windows([1, 2, 3, 4], 3));
console.log([...new Set(["b", "a", "b", "c", "a"])]);   // first occurrence wins
Result
[ [ 1, 2 ], [ 3, 4 ], [ 5 ] ]
[ [ 1, 2, 3 ], [ 2, 3, 4 ] ]
[ 'b', 'a', 'c' ]

Copy or mutate

The ES2023 copying methods leave the source alone; splice and sort do not.

const xs = [3, 1, 2];
const ys = xs.toSorted().toReversed().with(0, 99);
console.log(xs, ys);
xs.splice(1, 1);                             // removes 1 element at index 1, in place
console.log(xs);
Result
[ 3, 1, 2 ] [ 99, 2, 1 ]
[ 3, 2 ]

Lazy pipelines with iterator helpers

Iterator helpers pull one value at a time, so an infinite generator is fine.

function* naturals() {
  let n = 1;
  while (true) yield n++;
}
const firstOddSquares = naturals()
  .map((n) => n * n)
  .filter((n) => n % 2 === 1)
  .take(3)
  .toArray();
console.log(firstOddSquares);
Result
[ 1, 9, 25 ]

Strings — Standard Operations

UTF-16 underneath, graphemes on screen — search, split, slice, compare, fold, build, format and match text correctly.

  • node
  • browser

I want to…

The standard method for each everyday job, and the trap that comes with it.

I want to…UseWatch out
know if text contains a wordincludes, startsWith, endsWithcase- and accent-sensitive: fold or collate first
find where it isindexOf, lastIndexOf, search(regex)-1 when absent, and 0 is falsy — compare with -1
split into fieldssplit(";"), split(",", limit)"".split(";") is [""], not []
split into what a reader seesIntl.Segmenter (grapheme, word, sentence)split("") breaks emoji; split(" ") fails on Japanese or Thai
joinparts.join(", "); Intl.ListFormat for prose"a, b, and c" is English only — format lists per locale
trimtrim, trimStart, trimEndstrips every Unicode space, including the no-break space
replace every matchreplaceAll("-", " "), or replace(/-/g, fn)replace("-", " ") replaces the first only; $& and $1 are special in the replacement
pad or repeatpadStart(5, "0"), padEnd, repeatcounts UTF-16 units, so emoji misalign columns
take a pieceslice(start, end), at(-1)indexes are UTF-16 units: an emoji can be cut in half
sort for peoplenew Intl.Collator(locale).compare< and sort() compare code units: "Zoe" < "adam"
ignore case when comparinga collator with sensitivity: "base" or "accent"toLowerCase() misses ß vs SS and the Turkish dotless i
count characters[...segmenter.segment(s)].length.length counts UTF-16 code units

Code units, code points, graphemes, bytes — and slicing safely

Reach for graphemes whenever a person will see the result (length limits, truncation, cursors); for storage and wire limits, count UTF-8 bytes.

const graphemes = new Intl.Segmenter("en", { granularity: "grapheme" });
const chars = (text: string) => Array.from(graphemes.segment(text), (s) => s.segment);
const utf8 = new TextEncoder();
const labels = ["units", "points", "graphemes", "bytes"];

const samples = {
  plain: "Ada",
  family: "\u{1F469}\u200D\u{1F469}\u200D\u{1F467}", // 👩‍👩‍👧: three emoji glued by ZERO WIDTH JOINER
  composed: "Zo\u00EB",                             // Zoë, ë as one code point
  decomposed: "Zoe\u0308",                          // Zoë, e + COMBINING DIAERESIS
  flag: "\u{1F1E8}\u{1F1F4}",                       // 🇨🇴: two regional-indicator letters
};
for (const [name, text] of Object.entries(samples)) {
  // .length, [i] and slice() count UTF-16 units; the string iterator yields code points;
  // a VARCHAR(n) in bytes, a header or a payload limit counts UTF-8 bytes
  const counts = [text.length, [...text].length, chars(text).length, utf8.encode(text).length];
  console.log(name.padEnd(10), labels.map((label, i) => `${label} ${counts[i]}`).join("  "));
}

function truncate(text: string, max: number): string {
  const all = chars(text);
  return all.length <= max ? text : `${all.slice(0, max - 1).join("")}…`;
}

const status = "Shipped \u{1F680} today";                // "Shipped 🚀 today"
const naive = status.slice(0, 9);                     // ends on half of 🚀
console.log(JSON.stringify(naive), naive.isWellFormed());
console.log(truncate(status, 10));
// at(-1) is half a flag; the last grapheme is the whole flag
console.log(JSON.stringify(samples.flag.at(-1)), chars(samples.flag).at(-1) === samples.flag);
Result
plain      units 3  points 3  graphemes 3  bytes 3
family     units 8  points 5  graphemes 1  bytes 18
composed   units 3  points 3  graphemes 3  bytes 4
decomposed units 4  points 4  graphemes 3  bytes 5
flag       units 4  points 2  graphemes 1  bytes 8
"Shipped \ud83d" false
Shipped 🚀…
"\uddf4" true

Search, split, trim, replace, pad

Parsing a pasted contact list: trim first, split with a known separator, default every destructured field.

const pasted = [
  "  Lovelace, Ada ; ADA@Example.com ; admin|editor ",
  "# exported 2026-03-08",
  "Hopper, Grace;grace@navy.example;",
  "",
];

for (const [index, raw] of pasted.entries()) {
  const line = raw.trim();
  if (line === "" || line.startsWith("#")) continue;

  const [name = "", email = "", roles = ""] = line.split(";").map((field) => field.trim());
  const [family = "", given = ""] = name.split(",", 2).map((part) => part.trim());
  const at = email.indexOf("@");
  const domain = at === -1 ? "(no email)" : email.slice(at + 1).toLowerCase();
  const roleList = roles === "" ? [] : roles.split("|");

  const id = `C-${String(index + 1).padStart(4, "0")}`;
  const columns = [id, `${given} ${family}`.padEnd(14), domain.padEnd(14), roleList.join(", ") || "-"];
  console.log(columns.join(" | "));
}

console.log("2026-03-08".replaceAll("-", "/"), "2026-03-08".replace("-", "/"));
console.log(JSON.stringify("".split(";")), "admin|".split("|").length);
// lowercasing is fine for ASCII identifiers; for names and prose, see "Compare and sort by locale"
console.log("Ada Lovelace".includes("love"), "Ada Lovelace".toLowerCase().includes("love"));
Result
C-0001 | Ada Lovelace   | example.com    | admin, editor
C-0003 | Grace Hopper   | navy.example   | -
2026/03/08 2026/03-08
[""] 2
false true

Compare and sort by locale

Sort anything a person reads with an Intl.Collator built once; sort() alone orders by UTF-16 code unit.

const contacts = ["zoe", "Émile", "adam", "Zoë", "Ärzte GmbH", "Oskar", "Øster"];

console.log([...contacts].sort().join(", "));       // code units: uppercase first, accents last

const english = new Intl.Collator("en");
const swedish = new Intl.Collator("sv");            // å, ä, ö are letters after z
console.log([...contacts].sort(english.compare).join(", "));
console.log([...contacts].sort(swedish.compare).join(", "));

// numeric: true sorts digits by value — file names, versions, room numbers
const natural = new Intl.Collator("en", { numeric: true });
console.log(["Room 10", "Room 9", "Room 1"].sort(natural.compare).join(", "));

// sorting records: one collator, reused by every comparison
type Contact = { name: string; city: string };
const people: Contact[] = [
  { name: "Émile", city: "Lyon" },
  { name: "adam", city: "Lyon" },
  { name: "Beatriz", city: "Bogotá" },
];
people.sort((a, b) => english.compare(a.city, b.city) || english.compare(a.name, b.name));
console.log(people.map((p) => `${p.city}/${p.name}`).join(", "));

const base = new Intl.Collator("en", { sensitivity: "base" });     // ignores case and accents
const accent = new Intl.Collator("en", { sensitivity: "accent" }); // ignores case only
console.log(base.compare("Zoë", "zoe"), accent.compare("Zoë", "zoe"));
Result
Oskar, Zoë, adam, zoe, Ärzte GmbH, Émile, Øster
adam, Ärzte GmbH, Émile, Oskar, Øster, zoe, Zoë
adam, Émile, Oskar, zoe, Zoë, Ärzte GmbH, Øster
Room 1, Room 9, Room 10
Bogotá/Beatriz, Lyon/adam, Lyon/Émile
0 1

Case folding and normalization

Normalize before you store or compare user input; compare case-insensitively with a collator, not with lowercase copies.

console.log("straße".toUpperCase());                          // case mapping can change the length
console.log("TITLE".toLowerCase(), "TITLE".toLocaleLowerCase("tr"));
console.log("İstanbul".toLowerCase().length);                 // 9: İ lowercases to i + U+0307

// case-insensitive equality: lowercase copies miss ß = SS, a base-sensitivity collator does not
const sameIgnoringCase = new Intl.Collator("de", { sensitivity: "base" });
console.log("STRASSE".toLowerCase() === "straße".toLowerCase());
console.log(sameIgnoringCase.compare("STRASSE", "straße") === 0);

// the same visible name in two encodings: NFC (one code point) vs NFD (letter + mark)
const typedOnMac: string = "Zoe\u0308";
const storedInDb: string = "Zo\u00EB";
console.log(typedOnMac === storedInDb, typedOnMac.normalize("NFC") === storedInDb);

// NFKC also folds compatibility forms (ligatures, full-width): for keys, never for display
console.log("ﬁle Ｎｏ１".normalize("NFKC"));

// a Latin-script search key: decompose, drop only the combining accents (U+0300–U+036F).
// \p{Diacritic} would be wrong: it also deletes Japanese ー and voicing marks, and ASCII ^ and `
const latinKey = (text: string) =>
  text.normalize("NFD").replace(/[\u0300-\u036f]/g, "").normalize("NFC").toLowerCase();
console.log(latinKey("Crème Brûlée"), latinKey("Zoë") === latinKey("ZOE"));
console.log(latinKey("コーヒー"), latinKey("がっこう"), latinKey("C^2"));   // kana and ASCII survive intact
// Latin text only: Cyrillic й and Greek ά decompose into this range too, and would lose their marks.
// letters without a decomposition (đ, ø, ł, ß) stay as they are: "Đà Nẵng" keys to "đa nang", not "da nang".
// A base-sensitivity collator matches them: new Intl.Collator(locale, { sensitivity: "base" })

Building strings and formatting values

+= is not slow in modern engines — the win is readability: template literals, map + join, and a number formatter instead of hand-made money.

Concatenation
type Line = { item: string; qty: number; unitPrice: number };
const order: Line[] = [
  { item: "Espresso", qty: 2, unitPrice: 3.5 },
  { item: "Croissant", qty: 1, unitPrice: 3.25 },
];

let receipt = "";
let total = 0;
for (let i = 0; i < order.length; i++) {
  const line = order[i]!;
  const amount = line.qty * line.unitPrice;
  total += amount;
  receipt += line.qty + " x " + line.item.padEnd(10) + ("$" + amount.toFixed(2)).padStart(8) + "\n";
}
receipt += "Total".padEnd(14) + ("$" + total.toFixed(2)).padStart(8);
console.log(receipt);
Template literals, join, Intl
type Line = { item: string; qty: number; unitPrice: number };
const order: Line[] = [
  { item: "Espresso", qty: 2, unitPrice: 3.5 },
  { item: "Croissant", qty: 1, unitPrice: 3.25 },
];

const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" });
const money = (amount: number) => usd.format(amount).padStart(8);
const total = order.reduce((sum, line) => sum + line.qty * line.unitPrice, 0);

const receipt = [
  ...order.map(({ item, qty, unitPrice }) => `${qty} x ${item.padEnd(10)}${money(qty * unitPrice)}`),
  `${"Total".padEnd(14)}${money(total)}`,
].join("\n");
console.log(receipt);
Result
2 x Espresso     $7.00
1 x Croissant    $3.25
Total           $10.25

Tagged templates

A tag sees the literal parts and the values separately — so it can escape, parameterize or reject the values.

type Query = { text: string; values: unknown[] };

// the literal parts are code you wrote; every ${value} becomes a $n placeholder, never SQL
function sql(strings: TemplateStringsArray, ...values: unknown[]): Query {
  const text = strings.reduce((query, part, i) => `${query}$${i}${part}`);
  return { text, values };
}

const email = "ada@example.com' OR '1'='1";
const query = sql`SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = ${email} AND active = ${true}`;
console.log(query.text);
console.log(query.values);

// safe for element text and QUOTED attribute values only: it does not make href="${url}"
// (javascript: URLs), unquoted attributes, <script> or <style> safe. Validate URLs, and
// prefer the framework's escaping or textContent.
const escapes: Record<string, string> = {
  "&": "&amp;", "<": "&lt;", ">": "&gt;", '"': "&quot;", "'": "&#39;",
};
const escape = (value: unknown) => String(value).replace(/[&<>"']/g, (c) => escapes[c]!);
function html(strings: TemplateStringsArray, ...values: unknown[]): string {
  return strings.reduce((out, part, i) => out + escape(values[i - 1]) + part);
}
console.log(html`<li title="${'Ada "the first"'}">${"<b>Ada</b>"}</li>`);

// String.raw is the built-in tag: backslashes stay as typed
console.log(String.raw`C:\new\table`, String.raw`\d+`.length);
Result
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE email = $1 AND active = $2
[ "ada@example.com' OR '1'='1", true ]
<li title="Ada &quot;the first&quot;">&lt;b&gt;Ada&lt;/b&gt;</li>
C:\new\table 3

Regular expressions: named groups, matchAll, sticky

Name your groups, iterate with matchAll, and use the sticky flag y for tokenizers that must not skip input.

const log = `2026-03-08 14:30 ERROR order=A-1042 user=ada
2026-03-08 14:31 INFO order=A-1043 user=grace
2026-03-08 14:35 ERROR order=A-1044 user=zoë`;

// m: ^ and $ per line; u: \p{L} matches any letter, so "zoë" is one user name
const entry =
  /^(?<date>[\d-]+) (?<time>[\d:]+) (?<level>[A-Z]+) order=(?<order>[A-Z]-\d+) user=(?<user>\p{L}+)$/gmu;
for (const { groups } of log.matchAll(entry)) {
  if (groups?.level === "ERROR") console.log(groups.order, groups.user);
}
console.log("2026-03-08".replace(/(?<y>\d{4})-(?<m>\d{2})-(?<d>\d{2})/, "$<d>/$<m>/$<y>"));

// y (sticky): each match must start exactly at lastIndex, so nothing is silently skipped
function tokenize(source: string): string[] {
  const token = /\s*(?:(?<number>\d+(?:\.\d+)?)|(?<op>[-+*\/()]))/y;
  const end = source.trimEnd().length;            // trailing spaces are not an error
  const tokens: string[] = [];
  while (token.lastIndex < end) {
    const at = token.lastIndex;
    const match = token.exec(source);
    if (!match) {
      const rest = source.slice(at);
      const column = at + rest.length - rest.trimStart().length;   // where the bad token starts
      throw new SyntaxError(`unexpected "${rest.trim()}" at ${column}`);
    }
    tokens.push(match.groups?.number ?? match.groups?.op ?? "");
  }
  return tokens;
}
console.log(tokenize("(12.5 + 3) * 2 ").join(" "));
try {
  tokenize("2 + two");
} catch (e) {
  console.log((e as Error).message);
}
Result
A-1042 ada
A-1044 zoë
08/03/2026
( 12.5 + 3 ) * 2
unexpected "two" at 4

The u and v flags: letters, emoji and set operations

Without u, a regex sees UTF-16 units; v (ES2024) adds string properties such as whole emoji sequences, and set subtraction and intersection.

const reply = "Done \u{1F680}\u{1F469}\u200D\u{1F4BB}!";       // "Done 🚀👩‍💻!"

// no flag: "." is one UTF-16 unit, so a single emoji is not "one character"
console.log(/^.$/.test("\u{1F680}"), /^.$/u.test("\u{1F680}"));

// u: \p{…} Unicode properties. \p{Emoji_Presentation} still splits a ZWJ sequence apart
console.log(reply.match(/\p{Emoji_Presentation}/gu)?.length);

// v: \p{RGI_Emoji} matches whole sequences — 🚀 and 👩‍💻 are two emoji, not three.
// A literal /…/v needs "target": "ES2024" in tsconfig; RegExp(…, "v") type-checks at any target.
const emoji = new RegExp(String.raw`\p{RGI_Emoji}`, "gv");
console.log(reply.match(emoji)?.length);

// v: set subtraction — letters that are not plain ASCII, e.g. to flag names for review
const nonAsciiLetter = new RegExp(String.raw`[\p{L}--[a-zA-Z]]`, "gv");
console.log("Señor Ñandú".match(nonAsciiLetter));

// v: intersection — Greek letters only, from a mixed product code
console.log("SKU-αβ12-Ω".match(new RegExp(String.raw`[\p{Script=Greek}&&\p{L}]`, "gv"))?.join(""));

Catastrophic backtracking

A nested quantifier that can split the same text many ways turns one bad input into seconds of CPU — rewrite it so each character has one path, accepting exactly the same inputs.

Nested quantifier
// (\w+\s?)* can divide "aaaa…" into words in 2^n ways: on "a".repeat(28) + "!"
// a backtracking engine tries them all — over a second — before answering false
const tagList = /^(\w+\s?)*$/;

for (const input of ["vip beta", "vip beta ", "vip\tbeta", "", "vip  beta", "vip beta!"]) {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(input), tagList.test(input));
}
One path per character, same language
// words separated by exactly one whitespace, optional trailing one, or nothing at all:
// the separator is mandatory between words, so there is one way to match any text
const tagList = /^(?:\w+(?:\s\w+)*\s?)?$/;

for (const input of ["vip beta", "vip beta ", "vip\tbeta", "", "vip  beta", "vip beta!"]) {
  console.log(JSON.stringify(input), tagList.test(input));
}
Result
"vip beta" true
"vip beta " true
"vip\tbeta" true
"" true
"vip  beta" false
"vip beta!" false

Sources: Regular expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) — OWASP

Pitfalls worth saying out loud

Most string bugs are Unicode bugs that ASCII test data never finds.

  • Test with real text: Zoë in both NFC and NFD, 👩‍👩‍👧, 🇨🇴, straße, İstanbul, Arabic and Japanese.
  • Normalize at the boundary (normalize("NFC") on input), compare with Intl.Collator, count with Intl.Segmenter, limit storage by UTF-8 bytes.
  • Create Intl.Collator and Intl.Segmenter once and reuse them — for large sorts MDN recommends a collator over localeCompare.
  • .length as a user-facing limit, slice for truncation, split("") to reverse — all three cut emoji and accents apart.
  • toLowerCase() for case-insensitive keys: misses ß/SS, and toLocaleLowerCase() without a locale follows the machine (I → ı in Turkish).
  • Stripping \p{Diacritic} to make search keys: it also deletes Japanese ー and voicing marks. Strip only U+0300–U+036F, or use a collator.
  • Regexes on untrusted input with nested quantifiers like (a+)+ or (\w+\s?)* — a ReDoS. Cap the input length too.
  • replace with a string pattern replaces once; replaceAll with a regex requires the g flag or it throws.
  • Strings are immutable: every method returns a new string; s[0] = "x" is a type error, and a TypeError in strict-mode JavaScript.

Serialization — JSON, Validation & Binary

JSON with a schema as the single source of types: key renaming, optional and unknown fields, dates and bigint, unions, codecs, structuredClone and a fixed binary layout.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • zod >=4.1
  • any ES2023 engine; the examples run on Node.js

Sources: JSON — MDN · Zod documentation · structuredClone() — MDN · DataView — MDN

The Codable idea in TypeScript

JSON in JavaScript is untyped data: types are erased at run time, so the schema — not the type — is what checks the wire.

You needSwiftTypeScript
A typed modelstruct Order: Codableconst Order = z.object({…}); type Order = z.infer<typeof Order>
DecodeJSONDecoder().decode(Order.self, from: data)Order.parse(JSON.parse(text)) — or safeParse to get a result instead of a throw
EncodeJSONEncoder().encode(order)JSON.stringify(order) (or Schema.encode when a codec changes the shape)
Renamed keysCodingKeys, .convertFromSnakeCaseA key mapper before parsing, or .transform for odd names
Missing / nullOptional, decodeIfPresent.optional() (may be absent), .nullable() (may be null), .default(v)
Dates and custom typesdateDecodingStrategy, init(from:)z.codec(wire, domain, { decode, encode }); replacer/reviver/toJSON without a schema
Enums with payloadsenum with associated valuesz.discriminatedUnion("type", […]) → a TS discriminated union
BinaryData, PropertyListEncoder, swift-protobufTextEncoder, DataView; Protocol Buffers (@bufbuild/protobuf) or MessagePack

`as` is not validation: parse and safeParse

JSON.parse returns any and as Order checks nothing, so let a schema check the data and give you the type — safeParse where bad input is expected (forms, webhooks), parse where it would be a bug.

import { z } from "zod";

const Order = z.object({
  id: z.string(),
  total: z.number().nonnegative(),
  status: z.enum(["open", "paid", "shipped"]),
  items: z.array(z.object({ sku: z.string(), quantity: z.int().positive() })),
});
type Order = z.infer<typeof Order>;                // one source of truth: the type follows the schema

const wire = `{"id":"o-1","total":"42.50","status":"refunded","items":[{"sku":"MUG","quantity":2}]}`;

const trusted = JSON.parse(wire) as Order;         // compiles, and is a lie
console.log("typed as number, actually:", typeof trusted.total);

const result = Order.safeParse(JSON.parse(wire));
if (!result.success) {
  for (const issue of result.error.issues) {
    console.log(`${issue.path.join(".")}: ${issue.message}`);
  }
}

const order: Order = Order.parse(JSON.parse(`{"id":"o-1","total":42.5,"status":"paid","items":[]}`));
console.log(order.status, order.total.toFixed(2));
console.log(JSON.stringify(order));
Result
typed as number, actually: string
total: Invalid input: expected number, received string
status: Invalid option: expected one of "open"|"paid"|"shipped"
paid 42.50
{"id":"o-1","total":42.5,"status":"paid","items":[]}

snake_case on the wire, camelCase in the code

Rename every key at the boundary with one mapper (like .convertFromSnakeCase), and use .transform for the odd legacy names a rule cannot derive.

import { z } from "zod";

const toCamel = (key: string) => key.replace(/_([a-z0-9])/g, (_, c: string) => c.toUpperCase());
const toSnake = (key: string) => key.replace(/[A-Z]/g, (c) => `_${c.toLowerCase()}`);

function mapKeys(value: unknown, rename: (key: string) => string): unknown {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) return value.map((item) => mapKeys(item, rename));
  if (value === null || typeof value !== "object") return value;
  return Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(value).map(([k, v]) => [rename(k), mapKeys(v, rename)]));
}

const Customer = z.object({
  customerId: z.string(),
  firstName: z.string(),
  shippingAddress: z.object({ postalCode: z.string(), countryCode: z.string().length(2) }),
});

const wire = `{"customer_id":"c-7","first_name":"Ana",
  "shipping_address":{"postal_code":"10115","country_code":"DE"}}`;
const customer = Customer.parse(mapKeys(JSON.parse(wire), toCamel));
console.log(customer.firstName, customer.shippingAddress.postalCode);
console.log(JSON.stringify(mapKeys({ ...customer, firstName: "Ana María" }, toSnake)));

// A legacy endpoint whose names no rule derives: map them explicitly, like CodingKeys.
const LegacyOrder = z
  .object({ ORDER_NO: z.string(), "e-mail": z.email() })
  .transform((w) => ({ orderNumber: w.ORDER_NO, email: w["e-mail"] }));
console.log(LegacyOrder.parse({ ORDER_NO: "100234", "e-mail": "ana@example.com" }));

Missing, null, defaults — and unknown keys

Say for every field whether it may be absent, may be null, or gets a default; and choose what happens to keys you did not declare: dropped (default), refused, or kept.

import { z } from "zod";

const Preferences = z.object({
  newsletter: z.boolean().default(false),          // absent → false
  nickname: z.string().optional(),                 // may be absent; never null
  deliveryNote: z.string().nullable(),             // must be present; may be null
  locale: z.string().catch("en"),                  // anything invalid → "en" (lenient, for cosmetic fields)
});

console.log(Preferences.parse({ deliveryNote: null, locale: 42 }));
console.log("missing:", Preferences.safeParse({ newsletter: true }).error?.issues[0]?.path);
console.log("stringify:", JSON.stringify({ nickname: undefined, deliveryNote: null }));   // undefined dropped

const LineItem = z.object({ sku: z.string(), quantity: z.number() });
const wire = { sku: "MUG", quantity: 2, giftWrap: true };   // a field added by a newer backend
console.log("strip  :", LineItem.parse(wire));     // reading: tolerate what you do not know
console.log("loose  :", LineItem.loose().parse(wire));     // proxies: pass it through untouched
console.log("strict :", LineItem.strict().safeParse(wire).error?.issues[0]?.code);   // writes: refuse it
Result
{ newsletter: false, deliveryNote: null, locale: 'en' }
missing: [ 'deliveryNote' ]
stringify: {"deliveryNote":null}
strip  : { sku: 'MUG', quantity: 2 }
loose  : { sku: 'MUG', quantity: 2, giftWrap: true }
strict : unrecognized_keys

Dates, bigint, Map and Set without a schema

JSON has no dates, bigints, maps or sets — Date becomes a string through its toJSON, BigInt throws, Map and Set silently become {} — so a replacer and a matching reviver carry them across.

class Money {
  cents: bigint;

  constructor(cents: bigint) {
    this.cents = cents;
  }

  toJSON() {
    return { $cents: String(this.cents) };            // JSON.stringify calls this
  }
}

const order = {
  placedAt: new Date("2026-11-16T09:30:00Z"),
  total: new Money(4250n),
  tags: new Set(["gift", "express"]),
  stockBySku: new Map([["MUG", 3]]),
};

console.log("naive:", JSON.stringify({ tags: order.tags, stockBySku: order.stockBySku }));
try {
  JSON.stringify({ cents: 4250n });
} catch (e) {
  console.log("bigint:", (e as Error).message);
}

function replacer(_key: string, value: unknown): unknown {
  if (value instanceof Set) return { $set: [...value] };
  if (value instanceof Map) return { $map: [...value] };
  return value;                                       // Dates arrive here already turned into strings
}

function reviver(key: string, value: unknown): unknown {
  if (key === "placedAt" && typeof value === "string") return new Date(value);   // by key, not by look
  if (typeof value !== "object" || value === null) return value;
  if ("$set" in value) return new Set(value.$set as unknown[]);
  if ("$map" in value) return new Map(value.$map as [unknown, unknown][]);
  if ("$cents" in value) return new Money(BigInt(String(value.$cents)));
  return value;
}

const text = JSON.stringify(order, replacer);
console.log(text);
const back = JSON.parse(text, reviver) as typeof order;
console.log(back.placedAt.getUTCHours(), back.total.cents + 1n);
console.log(back.tags.has("express"), back.stockBySku.get("MUG"));
Result
naive: {"tags":{},"stockBySku":{}}
bigint: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt
{"placedAt":"2026-11-16T09:30:00.000Z","total":{"$cents":"4250"},"tags":{"$set":["gift","express"]},"stockBySku":{"$map":[["MUG",3]]}}
9 4251n
true 3

Discriminated unions for polymorphic payloads

A type field picks the variant, the decoded value narrows in a switch, and the compiler flags any variant you forget, so decide up front whether an unknown variant is an error or a placeholder.

import { z } from "zod";

const PaymentMethod = z.discriminatedUnion("type", [
  z.object({ type: z.literal("card"), brand: z.enum(["visa", "mastercard"]), last4: z.string().length(4) }),
  z.object({ type: z.literal("paypal"), email: z.email() }),
  z.object({ type: z.literal("bank_transfer"), iban: z.string().min(15) }),
]);
type PaymentMethod = z.infer<typeof PaymentMethod>;

function describe(method: PaymentMethod): string {
  switch (method.type) {
    case "card": return `${method.brand} ending ${method.last4}`;
    case "paypal": return `PayPal (${method.email})`;
    case "bank_transfer": return `transfer from …${method.iban.slice(-4)}`;
    default: {
      const unhandled: never = method;             // a new variant fails to compile here
      return unhandled;
    }
  }
}

const wire = `[
  {"type":"card","brand":"visa","last4":"4242"},
  {"type":"paypal","email":"ana@example.com"},
  {"type":"bank_transfer","iban":"DE89370400440532013000"},
  {"type":"crypto","wallet":"0xabc"}
]`;
for (const raw of JSON.parse(wire) as unknown[]) {
  const parsed = PaymentMethod.safeParse(raw);
  console.log(parsed.success ? describe(parsed.data) : `rejected: ${parsed.error.issues[0]?.message}`);
}

transfer from …3000

A custom codec pair

When the wire shape and the domain shape differ (ISO strings ↔ Date, decimal strings ↔ integer cents), declare both directions once with z.codec; decode reads, encode writes, and parse decodes untrusted input.

import { z } from "zod";

const isoDateTime = z.codec(z.iso.datetime(), z.date(), {
  decode: (iso) => new Date(iso),
  encode: (date) => date.toISOString(),
});

const decimalCents = z.codec(z.string().regex(/^\d+\.\d{2}$/), z.bigint(), {
  decode: (text) => BigInt(text.replace(".", "")),   // "42.50" → 4250n: no floating-point money
  encode: (cents) => `${cents / 100n}.${String(cents % 100n).padStart(2, "0")}`,
});

const Invoice = z.object({ id: z.string(), issuedAt: isoDateTime, total: decimalCents });

const wire = `{"id":"inv-9","issuedAt":"2026-11-16T09:30:00.000Z","total":"42.50"}`;
const invoice = Invoice.parse(JSON.parse(wire));   // parse = validate and decode untrusted input
console.log(invoice.issuedAt.getUTCDate(), invoice.total);

const corrected = { ...invoice, total: invoice.total + 1999n };
console.log(JSON.stringify(Invoice.encode(corrected)));

const bad = Invoice.safeParse({ id: "inv-10", issuedAt: "16/11/2026", total: "42.5" });

structuredClone versus a JSON round trip

To copy data (undo stacks, optimistic updates, worker messages) use structuredClone, which keeps dates, maps, sets, bigints and cycles where a JSON round trip does not, though neither keeps class prototypes or functions.

const draft = {
  placedAt: new Date("2026-11-16T09:30:00Z"),
  tags: new Set(["gift"]),
  items: [{ sku: "MUG", quantity: 2 }],
};

const viaJson = JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(draft));
const viaClone = structuredClone(draft);
console.log("JSON :", typeof viaJson.placedAt, JSON.stringify(viaJson.tags));
console.log("clone:", viaClone.placedAt instanceof Date, viaClone.tags.has("gift"),
  viaClone.items !== draft.items);

type Category = { name: string; parent?: Category; children: Category[] };

const root: Category = { name: "Kitchen", children: [] };
root.children.push({ name: "Mugs", parent: root, children: [] });
const tree = structuredClone(root);
console.log("cycle kept:", tree.children[0]!.parent === tree);
try {
  JSON.stringify(root);
} catch (e) {
  console.log("JSON on a cycle:", (e as Error).name);
}

class Cart {
  items: string[] = [];

  count() {
    return this.items.length;
  }
}

console.log("prototype kept:", structuredClone(new Cart()) instanceof Cart);
try {
  structuredClone({ onChange: () => {} });
} catch (e) {
  console.log("functions:", (e as DOMException).name);
}

clone: true true true
cycle kept: true
JSON on a cycle: TypeError

Binary: write a fixed layout with DataView and TextEncoder

Write a compact packet (a WebSocket feed, a BLE device, a file header) field by field at fixed offsets with explicit endianness and money as integer cents, and prefer a schema-first format such as Protocol Buffers or MessagePack for messages that evolve between services.

const STATUS = ["open", "paid", "shipped"] as const;

type OrderEvent = {
  orderNumber: number;
  status: (typeof STATUS)[number];
  itemCount: number;
  totalCents: number;                                // money as integer cents, never a float
  customer: string;
};

// 0 version u8 | 1 status u8 | 2 itemCount u16 | 4 orderNumber u32 | 8 totalCents u32 | 12 nameLength u8
const HEADER = 13;                                   // the UTF-8 name follows at byte 13

function encodeEvent(event: OrderEvent): Uint8Array {
  const name = new TextEncoder().encode(event.customer);           // UTF-8: "Zoë" is 4 bytes, not 3
  if (name.length > 255) throw new RangeError("customer name too long for a u8 length");
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(HEADER + name.length);
  const view = new DataView(bytes.buffer);
  view.setUint8(0, 1);                                              // format version, for the next change
  view.setUint8(1, STATUS.indexOf(event.status));
  view.setUint16(2, event.itemCount, true);                         // true = little-endian, always explicit
  view.setUint32(4, event.orderNumber, true);
  view.setUint32(8, event.totalCents, true);
  view.setUint8(12, name.length);
  bytes.set(name, HEADER);
  return bytes;
}

const event: OrderEvent = {
  orderNumber: 100234, status: "paid", itemCount: 3, totalCents: 4250, customer: "Zoë",
};
const packet = encodeEvent(event);
const jsonBytes = new TextEncoder().encode(JSON.stringify(event)).length;
console.log(`${packet.length} bytes, against ${jsonBytes} as JSON`);
console.log([...packet].map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, "0")).join(" "));
Result
17 bytes, against 88 as JSON
01 01 03 00 8a 87 01 00 9a 10 00 00 04 5a 6f c3 ab

Binary: read it back defensively

Decode through a DataView over the array's own slice, and check the length, the version and every enum value before trusting a field, so a cut-off or newer packet fails loudly instead of decoding garbage.

const STATUS = ["open", "paid", "shipped"] as const;

type OrderEvent = {
  orderNumber: number;
  status: (typeof STATUS)[number];
  itemCount: number;
  totalCents: number;
  customer: string;
};

const HEADER = 13;                                   // the layout written by the previous card

function decodeEvent(bytes: Uint8Array): OrderEvent {
  const view = new DataView(bytes.buffer, bytes.byteOffset, bytes.byteLength);   // the array may be a slice
  const complete = bytes.length >= HEADER && bytes.length === HEADER + view.getUint8(12);
  if (!complete) throw new RangeError("truncated packet");         // fail loudly, never decode half a name
  if (view.getUint8(0) !== 1) throw new Error(`unsupported version ${view.getUint8(0)}`);
  const status = STATUS[view.getUint8(1)];
  if (!status) throw new Error(`unknown status ${view.getUint8(1)}`);
  return {
    orderNumber: view.getUint32(4, true),
    status,
    itemCount: view.getUint16(2, true),
    totalCents: view.getUint32(8, true),
    customer: new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true }).decode(bytes.subarray(HEADER)),   // bad UTF-8 throws
  };
}

// As received from the order feed's WebSocket
const packet = Uint8Array.of(0x01, 0x01, 0x03, 0x00, 0x8a, 0x87, 0x01, 0x00, 0x9a, 0x10, 0x00, 0x00,
  0x04, 0x5a, 0x6f, 0xc3, 0xab);
console.log(decodeEvent(packet));

const damaged = { "cut off": packet.subarray(0, 15), "from v2": Uint8Array.of(2, ...packet.subarray(1)) };
for (const [label, bytes] of Object.entries(damaged)) {
  try {
    decodeEvent(bytes);
  } catch (e) {
    console.log(`${label}:`, (e as Error).message);
  }
}
Result
{
  orderNumber: 100234,
  status: 'paid',
  itemCount: 3,
  totalCents: 4250,
  customer: 'Zoë'
}
cut off: truncated packet
from v2: unsupported version 2

Pitfalls worth saying out loud

Where JSON quietly loses or invents data.

  • JSON.parse(text) as T on anything from the network, storage or postMessage. Parse unknown with a schema.
  • Money as a float (0.1 + 0.2). Send integer minor units or a decimal string, decode to bigint or a decimal type.
  • IDs above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 − 1) sent as JSON numbers: JSON.parse rounds them. Send them as strings.
  • Dates on the wire as ISO 8601 with an offset (2026-11-16T09:30:00Z); never new Date("16/11/2026"), which parses differently per engine.
  • Tolerant readers, strict writers: strip unknown keys when reading, refuse them when accepting writes.
  • A blanket key mapper also renames keys that are data (a map keyed by SKU or locale); exempt those fields or map explicitly.
  • JSON.stringify drops undefined and functions, turns NaN/Infinity into null, and emits integer-like keys first (ascending), then the rest in insertion order — so { sku: 1, 10: 2, 2: 3 } comes out as {"2":3,"10":2,"sku":1}. Do not hash its output across implementations.

Async/Await, Promises & Cancellation

One thread, one event loop — sequential vs concurrent awaits, combinators, AbortSignal, async iteration.

Sequential vs concurrent

A promise starts when it is created; await only waits. Start both, then await both.

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
async function load(name: string, ms: number): Promise<string> {
  await sleep(ms);
  return name;
}

let start = performance.now();
const a = await load("user", 100);           // total = a + b (about 200 ms)
const b = await load("posts", 100);
const sequential = performance.now() - start;

start = performance.now();
const [c, d] = await Promise.all([load("user", 100), load("posts", 100)]);   // total = max(a, b) (about 100 ms)
const concurrent = performance.now() - start;
console.log(a, b, "|", c, d);
console.log("concurrent took well under the sequential time:", concurrent < sequential * 0.75);
Result
user posts | user posts
concurrent took well under the sequential time: true

all, allSettled, any

all fails fast on the first rejection; allSettled never rejects; any takes the first success.

const ok = (v: number) => Promise.resolve(v);
const fail = (why: string) => Promise.reject(new Error(why));

const settled = await Promise.allSettled([ok(1), fail("boom"), ok(3)]);
console.log(settled.map((r) => (r.status === "fulfilled" ? r.value : r.reason.message)));

try {
  await Promise.all([ok(1), fail("first failure wins")]);
} catch (e) {
  console.log((e as Error).message);
}
console.log(await Promise.any([fail("a"), ok(2), ok(3)]));

Cancellation with AbortSignal

Promises cannot be cancelled; work is. Pass a signal down, honour it at every await, and detach the listener when the wait ends normally.

function delay(ms: number, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<void> {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    if (signal?.aborted) return reject(signal.reason);
    const onAbort = () => {
      clearTimeout(timer);
      reject(signal!.reason);
    };
    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      signal?.removeEventListener("abort", onAbort);   // no listener left behind per tick
      resolve();
    }, ms);
    signal?.addEventListener("abort", onAbort, { once: true });
  });
}

async function poll(signal: AbortSignal, onTick: (i: number) => void) {
  for (let i = 1; ; i++) {
    await delay(50, signal);                 // each await is a cancellation point
    console.log("tick", i);
    onTick(i);
  }
}

const controller = new AbortController();
try {
  await poll(controller.signal, (i) => {
    if (i === 2) controller.abort();          // e.g. the user left the screen
  });
} catch (e) {
  console.log((e as DOMException).name);     // AbortSignal.timeout(ms) rejects the same way, as TimeoutError
}
Result
tick 1
tick 2
AbortError

Async iteration

An async generator is a pull-based stream; break calls its return(), so no further page is fetched.

async function* pages(total: number, size: number) {
  for (let offset = 0; offset < total; offset += size) {
    await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 10));        // stand-in for a fetch
    yield Array.from({ length: Math.min(size, total - offset) }, (_, i) => offset + i);
  }
}

let seen = 0;
for await (const page of pages(7, 3)) {
  seen += page.length;
  console.log(page);
  if (seen >= 6) break;
}
Result
[ 0, 1, 2 ]
[ 3, 4, 5 ]

The forEach trap

forEach ignores the promises its callback returns; for…of awaits each in turn.

  await sleep(ms);
  log.push(`forEach ${ms}`);
});
log.push("after forEach");

for (const ms of [30, 10]) {
  await sleep(ms);
  log.push(`for-of ${ms}`);
}
log.push("after for-of");

Swift concurrency → TypeScript

The same ideas on a single-threaded event loop.

SwiftTypeScriptDifference

withThrowingTaskGroupPromise.all(items.map(work))no automatic cancellation of siblings

Rules

What reviewers flag first.

  • A floating promise (no await, no return, no .catch) loses its errors — Node then exits on the unhandled rejection.
  • Independent work: Promise.all. Partial failure acceptable: Promise.allSettled.
  • Accept an AbortSignal in every long-running function and pass it to fetch, timers and streams.
  • AbortSignal.timeout(ms) and AbortSignal.any([a, b]) compose deadlines without timers of your own.
  • CPU-bound work blocks everything: move it to a Worker (browser) or worker_threads (Node).

The built-ins' costs, then the patterns that solve most problems — with no standard heap or deque.

Built-in costs

Engine behaviour, not a specification guarantee — measure when it matters.

NeedBuilt-inCostInstead
stackpush / popO(1) amortised—
queuepush / shiftO(n) per shiftarray + head index
priority queuenone—a binary heap (below): O(log n)
membershipincludesO(n)Set#has: O(1) average
sorttoSorted (TimSort in V8)O(n log n), stable—

Two pointers

On sorted input, move the pointer that brings the sum closer. O(n), O(1) space.

function pairWithSum(sorted: readonly number[], target: number): [number, number] | null {
  let lo = 0;
  let hi = sorted.length - 1;
  while (lo < hi) {
    const sum = sorted[lo]! + sorted[hi]!;
    if (sum === target) return [lo, hi];
    if (sum < target) lo++;
    else hi--;
  }
  return null;
}
console.log(pairWithSum([1, 3, 4, 6, 9], 10), pairWithSum([1, 2], 7));

Sliding window

Longest substring without repeats — grow the right edge, jump the left past the last repeat. O(n).

function longestUnique(s: string): number {
  const lastSeen = new Map<string, number>();
  let start = 0;
  let best = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
    const prev = lastSeen.get(s[i]!);
    if (prev !== undefined && prev >= start) start = prev + 1;
    lastSeen.set(s[i]!, i);
    best = Math.max(best, i - start + 1);
  }
  return best;
}
console.log(longestUnique("abcabcbb"), longestUnique("pwwkew"));
Result
3 3

Binary search — lower bound

The first index whose value is not less than the target. Plain division keeps the midpoint exact — >>> 1 would wrap past 2^31 elements.

function lowerBound(xs: readonly number[], target: number): number {
  let lo = 0;
  let hi = xs.length;                        // the answer lies in [lo, hi]
  while (lo < hi) {
    const mid = Math.floor((lo + hi) / 2);   // exact up to 2^53
    if (xs[mid]! < target) lo = mid + 1;
    else hi = mid;
  }
  return lo;
}
const xs = [1, 3, 3, 5, 8];
console.log(lowerBound(xs, 3), lowerBound(xs, 4), lowerBound(xs, 9));
Result
1 3 5

Heap — top k

Keep a min-heap of size k; its root is the smallest of the k largest. O(n log k).

class MinHeap {
  private items: number[] = [];
  get size() { return this.items.length; }
  push(x: number) {
    const a = this.items;
    a.push(x);
    for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; ) {
      const p = (i - 1) >> 1;
      if (a[p]! <= a[i]!) break;
      [a[p], a[i]] = [a[i]!, a[p]!];
      i = p;
    }
  }
  pop(): number | undefined {
    const a = this.items;
    const top = a[0];
    const last = a.pop();
    if (a.length && last !== undefined) {
      a[0] = last;
      for (let i = 0; ; ) {
        const l = 2 * i + 1;
        const r = l + 1;
        let m = i;
        if (l < a.length && a[l]! < a[m]!) m = l;
        if (r < a.length && a[r]! < a[m]!) m = r;
        if (m === i) break;
        [a[m], a[i]] = [a[i]!, a[m]!];
        i = m;
      }
    }
    return top;
  }
}

function topK(xs: readonly number[], k: number): number[] {
  const heap = new MinHeap();
  for (const x of xs) {
    heap.push(x);
    if (heap.size > k) heap.pop();
  }
  const out: number[] = [];
  while (heap.size) out.push(heap.pop()!);
  return out.reverse();
}
console.log(topK([5, 1, 9, 3, 7, 9, 2], 3));

[ 9, 9, 7 ]

Breadth-first search on a grid

BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. Dequeue by index — shift() would make it O(n²).

function shortestPath(grid: string[], from: [number, number], to: [number, number]): number {
  const rows = grid.length;
  const cols = grid[0]!.length;
  const dist = new Map<string, number>([[from.join(","), 0]]);
  const queue: [number, number][] = [from];
  for (let head = 0; head < queue.length; head++) {
    const [r, c] = queue[head]!;
    const here = dist.get(`${r},${c}`)!;
    if (r === to[0] && c === to[1]) return here;
    for (const [dr, dc] of [[1, 0], [-1, 0], [0, 1], [0, -1]] as const) {
      const nr = r + dr;
      const nc = c + dc;
      const key = `${nr},${nc}`;
      if (nr < 0 || nc < 0 || nr >= rows || nc >= cols || grid[nr]![nc] === "#" || dist.has(key)) continue;
      dist.set(key, here + 1);
      queue.push([nr, nc]);
    }
  }
  return -1;
}
const maze = ["..#.", ".##.", "...."];
console.log(shortestPath(maze, [0, 0], [0, 3]));
Result
7

Hash map: counting, grouping, memory of the past

Two-sum on unsorted input, anagram groups, the first unique character — the default first idea: O(n) hash operations for O(n) memory (anagram keys add a per-word sort).

// Two-sum, unsorted: remember every value already passed, and where.
function twoSum(nums: readonly number[], target: number): [number, number] | null {
  const seen = new Map<number, number>();              // value -> index
  for (const [i, n] of nums.entries()) {
    const j = seen.get(target - n);
    if (j !== undefined) return [j, i];
    seen.set(n, i);
  }
  return null;
}

// Group anagrams: words with the same sorted letters share a key.
function groupAnagrams(words: readonly string[]): string[][] {
  return [...Map.groupBy(words, (w) => [...w].sort().join("")).values()];
}

// First non-repeating character: count in one pass, find in a second.
function firstUnique(text: string): string | undefined {
  const counts = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const ch of text) counts.set(ch, (counts.get(ch) ?? 0) + 1);
  return [...text].find((ch) => counts.get(ch) === 1);
}

console.log(firstUnique("swiss"));

Prefix sums & difference arrays

Many range-sum queries, "how many runs sum to k", or many range increments — O(n) preparation, then O(1) each.

// Daily sales: answer "total from day l to day r" any number of times.
const sales = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6];
const prefix = [0];                                  // prefix[i] = sum of the first i days
for (const s of sales) prefix.push(prefix.at(-1)! + s);
const rangeSum = (l: number, r: number) => prefix[r + 1]! - prefix[l]!;

// How many contiguous runs sum to exactly k? A prefix seen k earlier closes one. O(n)
function runsSummingTo(nums: readonly number[], k: number): number {
  const seen = new Map<number, number>([[0, 1]]);    // prefix value -> how many times
  let running = 0;
  let total = 0;
  for (const n of nums) {
    running += n;
    total += seen.get(running - k) ?? 0;
    seen.set(running, (seen.get(running) ?? 0) + 1);
  }
  return total;
}

// Difference array: "add v to every day in [l, r]" costs O(1); one running sum applies them all.
function applyRangeAdds(days: number, updates: readonly (readonly [number, number, number])[]): number[] {
  const diff = new Array<number>(days + 1).fill(0);
  for (const [l, r, v] of updates) {
    diff[l] = diff[l]! + v;
    diff[r + 1] = diff[r + 1]! - v;
  }
  const totals: number[] = [];
  let running = 0;
  for (const d of diff.slice(0, days)) {
    running += d;
    totals.push(running);
  }
  return totals;
}

console.log(rangeSum(2, 5), runsSummingTo([1, 2, 3, -3, 3], 3));
console.log(applyRangeAdds(6, [[0, 2, 5], [1, 4, 1], [3, 5, 2]]));

[ 5, 6, 6, 3, 3, 2 ]

Sort then sweep: intervals

Merge a calendar's busy blocks and count the rooms it needs — sorting first turns both into one linear pass, O(n log n) in all.

type Meeting = { start: number; end: number };        // hours, 13.5 = 13:30

function mergeBusy(meetings: readonly Meeting[]): Meeting[] {
  const merged: Meeting[] = [];
  for (const m of meetings.toSorted((a, b) => a.start - b.start)) {
    const last = merged.at(-1);
    if (last && m.start <= last.end) last.end = Math.max(last.end, m.end);   // overlap: extend
    else merged.push({ ...m });
  }
  return merged;
}

// Rooms needed = the most meetings in progress at once. Sweep: +1 at a start, -1 at an end.
function roomsNeeded(meetings: readonly Meeting[]): number {
  const events = meetings
    .flatMap((m) => [[m.start, 1], [m.end, -1]] as const)
    .toSorted((a, b) => a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1]);   // on a tie the end frees the room first
  let current = 0;
  let most = 0;
  for (const [, delta] of events) {
    current += delta;
    most = Math.max(most, current);
  }
  return most;
}

const day: Meeting[] = [
  { start: 9, end: 10 }, { start: 13, end: 15 }, { start: 9.5, end: 11 },
  { start: 11, end: 12 }, { start: 14, end: 16 },
];
console.log(mergeBusy(day));
console.log(roomsNeeded(day));

Stack & monotonic stack

Bracket matching, and "how many days until a warmer one" — a stack of still-unanswered indices makes it O(n).

const opener = new Map([[")", "("], ["]", "["], ["}", "{"]]);

function isBalanced(source: string): boolean {
  const stack: string[] = [];
  for (const ch of source) {
    const open = opener.get(ch);
    if (open !== undefined) {
      if (stack.pop() !== open) return false;
    } else if ("([{".includes(ch)) {
      stack.push(ch);
    }
  }
  return stack.length === 0;
}

// Each index waits on the stack (temperatures decreasing) until a warmer day pops it.
function daysUntilWarmer(temps: readonly number[]): number[] {
  const wait = new Array<number>(temps.length).fill(0);
  const stack: number[] = [];
  for (const [today, t] of temps.entries()) {
    while (stack.length && temps[stack.at(-1)!]! < t) {
      const day = stack.pop()!;
      wait[day] = today - day;                       // today answers that day
    }
    stack.push(today);
  }
  return wait;                                       // 0: no warmer day ever came
}

console.log(isBalanced("save(order[0], { draft: true })"), isBalanced("(]"));
console.log(daysUntilWarmer([73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]).join(" "));

Fast & slow pointers (linked lists)

Does a playlist's "next" chain loop forever, where is its middle — O(n) time, O(1) memory.

type Track = { title: string; next: Track | null };

function playlist(titles: readonly string[]): Track | null {
  let head: Track | null = null;
  for (const title of titles.toReversed()) head = { title, next: head };
  return head;
}

// Floyd: the fast pointer can only meet the slow one again if the chain loops.
function loops(head: Track | null): boolean {
  let slow = head;
  let fast = head;
  while (fast?.next) {
    slow = slow!.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
    if (slow === fast) return true;                 // the same node, not an equal title
  }
  return false;
}

// When fast reaches the end, slow has gone half as far.
function middle(head: Track | null): string | undefined {
  let slow = head;
  let fast = head;
  while (fast?.next) {
    slow = slow!.next;
    fast = fast.next.next;
  }
  return slow?.title;
}

const mix = playlist(["Intro", "Verse", "Bridge", "Chorus", "Outro"]);
console.log(loops(mix), middle(mix));
mix!.next!.next!.next!.next!.next = mix!.next;      // Outro -> Verse: an endless loop
console.log(loops(mix));
Result
false Bridge
true

Trees: DFS and BFS

Recursion goes deep (in-order lists a search tree sorted); a level-by-level queue goes wide.

type TreeNode = { value: number; left?: TreeNode; right?: TreeNode };

// Recursion depth = tree height; V8 overflows near 10k frames: unbalanced trees need an explicit stack.
function inorder(node: TreeNode | undefined, out: number[] = []): number[] {
  if (!node) return out;
  inorder(node.left, out);
  out.push(node.value);
  inorder(node.right, out);
  return out;
}

// Level order: the whole current level becomes the next level's parents.
function levels(root: TreeNode | undefined): number[][] {
  const result: number[][] = [];
  let level = root ? [root] : [];
  while (level.length) {
    result.push(level.map((n) => n.value));
    level = level.flatMap((n) => [n.left, n.right]).filter((c): c is TreeNode => c !== undefined);
  }
  return result;
}

// Validate a search tree by passing the allowed range down: a parent check alone misses grandchildren.
function isSearchTree(node: TreeNode | undefined, lo = -Infinity, hi = Infinity): boolean {
  if (!node) return true;
  return lo < node.value && node.value < hi
    && isSearchTree(node.left, lo, node.value) && isSearchTree(node.right, node.value, hi);
}

const prices: TreeNode = {
  value: 8,
  left: { value: 3, left: { value: 1 }, right: { value: 6 } },
  right: { value: 10, right: { value: 14 } },
};
const broken: TreeNode = { value: 8, left: { value: 3, right: { value: 9 } } };   // 9 is left of 8
console.log(inorder(prices), levels(prices));
console.log(isSearchTree(prices), isSearchTree(broken));

Graphs: BFS and DFS

Fewest flights between two airports (BFS), everywhere reachable from one (DFS) — adjacency list plus a visited set, O(V + E).

const routes = new Map<string, string[]>([
  ["BOS", ["JFK", "ORD"]], ["JFK", ["LHR", "MIA"]], ["ORD", ["DEN"]],
  ["DEN", ["SFO"]], ["LHR", ["SFO"]], ["SFO", []], ["MIA", []], ["HNL", ["SFO"]],
]);

// BFS visits in order of distance, so the first time it reaches `to` is the shortest.
function fewestFlights(from: string, to: string): number {
  const hops = new Map([[from, 0]]);
  const queue = [from];
  for (let head = 0; head < queue.length; head++) {     // a head index: shift() is O(n)
    const here = queue[head]!;
    if (here === to) return hops.get(here)!;
    for (const next of routes.get(here) ?? []) {
      if (hops.has(next)) continue;
      hops.set(next, hops.get(here)! + 1);
      queue.push(next);
    }
  }
  return -1;
}

// DFS with an explicit stack: no recursion depth limit on a big graph.
function reachable(from: string): Set<string> {
  const seen = new Set<string>();
  const stack = [from];
  while (stack.length) {
    const here = stack.pop()!;
    if (seen.has(here)) continue;
    seen.add(here);
    for (const next of routes.get(here) ?? []) if (!seen.has(next)) stack.push(next);   // no ...spread: hubs
  }
  return seen;
}

Graphs: topological sort

A build order for packages that depend on each other — Kahn's algorithm, O(V + E), which also detects a dependency cycle.

// dependents: package -> the packages that need it built first.
function buildOrder(dependents: Map<string, string[]>): string[] | null {
  const waitingOn = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const [pkg, users] of dependents) {
    waitingOn.set(pkg, waitingOn.get(pkg) ?? 0);
    for (const u of users) waitingOn.set(u, (waitingOn.get(u) ?? 0) + 1);
  }
  const order = [...waitingOn.keys()].filter((p) => waitingOn.get(p) === 0);
  for (let head = 0; head < order.length; head++) {      // the order doubles as the queue
    for (const u of dependents.get(order[head]!) ?? []) {
      waitingOn.set(u, waitingOn.get(u)! - 1);
      if (waitingOn.get(u) === 0) order.push(u);
    }
  }
  return order.length === waitingOn.size ? order : null;   // leftovers are on a cycle or wait on one
}

const monorepo = new Map([
  ["utils", ["api-client", "ui"]],
  ["api-client", ["web", "cli"]],
  ["ui", ["web"]],
]);
console.log(buildOrder(monorepo));
monorepo.set("web", ["utils"]);                           // utils now needs web: a cycle
console.log(buildOrder(monorepo));
// Weighted edges? Dijkstra is BFS with a min-heap keyed by distance (see the heap card).

Backtracking

Every way to pay an exact amount, every order to visit stops — choose, explore, un-choose and prune early, in exponential time by nature.

// Every combination of coin values (each reusable) that pays exactly `total`.
function waysToPay(coins: readonly number[], total: number): number[][] {
  const sorted = coins.filter((c) => c > 0).toSorted((a, b) => a - b);   // a 0 coin would recurse forever
  const found: number[][] = [];
  const picked: number[] = [];
  const explore = (start: number, remaining: number): void => {
    if (remaining === 0) found.push([...picked]);
    for (let i = start; i < sorted.length; i++) {
      const coin = sorted[i]!;
      if (coin > remaining) break;          // prune: sorted, so every later coin is too big too
      picked.push(coin);                    // choose
      explore(i, remaining - coin);         // explore (i, not i + 1: a coin may repeat)
      picked.pop();                         // un-choose
    }
  };
  explore(0, total);
  return found;
}

// Every order to visit the stops: n! of them.
function routes(stops: readonly string[]): string[][] {
  const found: string[][] = [];
  const path: string[] = [];
  const used = new Set<number>();
  const explore = (): void => {
    if (path.length === stops.length) found.push([...path]);
    for (const [i, stop] of stops.entries()) {
      if (used.has(i)) continue;
      used.add(i);                          // choose
      path.push(stop);
      explore();
      path.pop();                           // un-choose
      used.delete(i);
    }
  };
  explore();
  return found;
}

Dynamic programming

Fewest coins for an amount (where greedy is wrong) and edit distance for "did you mean" — overlapping subproblems filled in a table.

// 1-D: best[a] = fewest coins that make a; build up from 0.
function fewestCoins(coins: readonly number[], amount: number): number {
  const best = new Array<number>(amount + 1).fill(Infinity);
  best[0] = 0;
  for (let a = 1; a <= amount; a++) {
    for (const coin of coins) {
      if (coin <= a) best[a] = Math.min(best[a]!, best[a - coin]! + 1);
    }
  }
  return Number.isFinite(best[amount]) ? best[amount]! : -1;
}

// 2-D, two rows at a time: prev[j] = edits turning a's first i-1 letters into b's first j.
function editDistance(a: string, b: string): number {
  let prev = Array.from({ length: b.length + 1 }, (_, j) => j);   // from "": insert j letters
  for (let i = 1; i <= a.length; i++) {
    const curr = [i];                                              // to "": delete i letters
    for (let j = 1; j <= b.length; j++) {
      curr[j] = a[i - 1] === b[j - 1]
        ? prev[j - 1]!                                             // letters match: free
        : 1 + Math.min(prev[j]!, curr[j - 1]!, prev[j - 1]!);     // delete, insert, substitute
    }
    prev = curr;
  }
  return prev[b.length]!;
}

// Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1; the table finds 3 + 3.

console.log(editDistance("recieve", "receive"), editDistance("kitten", "sitting"));

Union-Find (disjoint set)

How many separate networks do these cables make, and which cable is redundant — near O(1) per operation.

class UnionFind {
  private parent: number[];
  private rank: number[];
  components: number;

  constructor(size: number) {
    this.parent = Array.from({ length: size }, (_, i) => i);
    this.rank = new Array<number>(size).fill(0);
    this.components = size;
  }

  find(x: number): number {
    const p = this.parent[x]!;
    if (p !== x) this.parent[x] = this.find(p);            // path compression
    return this.parent[x]!;
  }

  /** false when a and b were already connected: the edge closes a loop. */
  union(a: number, b: number): boolean {
    let ra = this.find(a);
    let rb = this.find(b);
    if (ra === rb) return false;
    if (this.rank[ra]! < this.rank[rb]!) [ra, rb] = [rb, ra];
    this.parent[rb] = ra;                                  // the shorter tree goes under
    if (this.rank[ra] === this.rank[rb]) this.rank[ra] = this.rank[ra]! + 1;
    this.components--;
    return true;
  }
}

const servers = new UnionFind(6);
const cables = [[0, 1], [1, 2], [3, 4], [2, 0]] as const;
const redundant = cables.filter(([a, b]) => !servers.union(a, b));
console.log(servers.components, redundant);

Trie (prefix tree)

Autocomplete for a search box — a prefix lookup costs its own length, however many words are stored.

class TrieNode {
  children = new Map<string, TrieNode>();
  isWord = false;
}

class Trie {
  private root = new TrieNode();

  insert(word: string): void {
    let node = this.root;
    for (const ch of word) {
      let next = node.children.get(ch);
      if (!next) {
        next = new TrieNode();
        node.children.set(ch, next);
      }
      node = next;
    }
    node.isWord = true;
  }

  /** Up to `limit` stored words that start with `prefix`. */
  complete(prefix: string, limit = 5): string[] {
    let node: TrieNode | undefined = this.root;
    for (const ch of prefix) node = node?.children.get(ch);
    const found: string[] = [];
    const walk = (n: TrieNode, word: string): void => {
      if (found.length === limit) return;
      if (n.isWord) found.push(word);
      for (const [ch, child] of n.children) walk(child, word + ch);   // Map keeps insertion order
    };
    if (node) walk(node, prefix);
    return found;
  }
}

const cities = new Trie();
for (const c of ["paris", "parma", "porto", "park city", "prague"]) cities.insert(c);
console.log(cities.complete("par"), cities.complete("po"), cities.complete("x"));

Bit manipulation & cyclic sort

The lone unpaired id, permission flags, the smallest missing ticket number — tricks that turn O(n) memory into O(1), on 32-bit operators unless you use bigint.

// Bitwise operators truncate numbers to 32-bit signed integers: every trick here needs bigint past that.
// The lone unpaired order id: x ^ x = 0, so the pairs cancel.
const lone = [4, 1, 2, 1, 2].reduce((acc, id) => acc ^ id, 0);
const loneBig = [3_000_000_000n, 7n, 7n].reduce((acc, id) => acc ^ id);   // number ^ gives -1294967296

// Flags: up to 32 per number (test with !== 0, never > 0: bit 31 is the sign). 1 << 32 wraps to 1.
const READ = 1 << 0;
const WRITE = 1 << 1;
const ADMIN = 1 << 2;
let perms = READ | WRITE | ADMIN;
perms &= ~ADMIN;                                   // revoke one flag
const has = (flag: number) => (perms & flag) !== 0;

// Popcount. On a `number`, `&` sees only the low 32 bits — hence bigint.
function bitCount(x: bigint): number {
  if (x < 0n) throw new RangeError("popcount of a negative bigint is unbounded");   // two's complement
  let n = 0;
  while (x !== 0n) {
    x &= x - 1n;                                   // clears the lowest set bit
    n++;
  }
  return n;
}

// Cyclic sort: put each value v in 1..n at index v - 1; the first misfit is the gap.
function firstMissingTicket(input: readonly number[]): number {
  const a = [...input];
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; ) {
    const target = a[i]! - 1;
    if (target >= 0 && target < a.length && a[target] !== a[i]) [a[i], a[target]] = [a[target]!, a[i]!];
    else i++;
  }
  const gap = a.findIndex((v, i) => v !== i + 1);
  return gap === -1 ? a.length + 1 : gap + 1;
}

console.log(lone, loneBig, has(WRITE), has(ADMIN), bitCount(0b1011_0110n), bitCount(2n ** 40n + 3n));
console.log(firstMissingTicket([3, 4, -1, 1]), firstMissingTicket([1, 2, 3]));

Working a problem out loud

The habits that matter more than the language.

  • State the brute force and its cost first, then the bottleneck the better pattern removes.
  • Name the edge cases before coding: empty input, one element, duplicates, negative numbers, NaN.
  • Comparing with sort() without a comparator, or summing money in floating point.
  • Say the complexity of the built-ins you lean on (includes is O(n), shift is O(n)).

Streaming & Time-Series Patterns

Unbounded data, bounded memory: windows, sketches, rate limits and backpressure — over async iterables and Node streams.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.4
  • node >=22.18
  • an engine with Array.fromAsync (Baseline 2024); the examples run on Node.js

Sources: for await...of — MDN · Stream — Node.js · Backpressuring in streams — Node.js

The constraints that define the field

Every card below is an answer to one of these.

  • You see each item once, in order, and cannot keep them all — so answers are incremental, approximate, or over a window.
  • Bounded memory is the whole game: O(1) or O(window) per stream, never O(stream).
  • Time is two things: event time (when it happened) and processing time (when you saw it). They diverge; a watermark says how late you still accept data.
  • Exact vs approximate: a sketch trades a percent of accuracy for orders of magnitude of memory. State the error bound out loud.
  • In TypeScript a stream is an AsyncIterable (pull: the consumer sets the pace), a Node or web stream (push, held back by a highWaterMark), or an RxJS Observable (push with no backpressure: you choose a buffering operator).
  • Inject the clock and the random source. Date.now() and Math.random() inside the algorithm make it untestable and unreplayable.

Windowing a stream

Almost every streaming requirement is one of these windows plus a lateness policy.

WindowShapeAnswersGroup by
Tumblingfixed size, no overlap: [0, 60s), [60s, 120s)orders per minute, a billing periodt - t % size
Hoppingfixed size advancing by a smaller hop; an event is in size / hop windowsa 5-minute error rate refreshed every 10 severy hop start in (t - size, t]
Sessionper key, closed by a gap of inactivitya user's visit, a burst of typingkey, extended while the next event is within the gap
Count (sliding)the last n eventsthe average of the last 100 requestsposition: a ring buffer
Late eventsits window has already closed: window end ≤ watermark (highest event time − allowed lateness)what happens to a delayed uploaddrop and count, hold longer, or reopen the window and re-emit

Ring buffer — a fixed-size sliding window

A moving average of the last k request latencies in O(1) per event and O(k) memory — and, when full, the drop-oldest queue for a source you cannot pause.

class RingBuffer<T> {
  private readonly slots: (T | undefined)[];
  private next = 0;                                  // where the next item goes
  size = 0;

  constructor(capacity: number) {
    this.slots = new Array<T | undefined>(capacity);
  }

  /** Adds an item; once full, returns the oldest one it pushed out. */
  push(item: T): T | undefined {
    const evicted = this.size === this.slots.length ? this.slots[this.next] : undefined;
    this.slots[this.next] = item;
    this.next = (this.next + 1) % this.slots.length;
    this.size = Math.min(this.size + 1, this.slots.length);
    return evicted;
  }

  /** Oldest first. */
  toArray(): T[] {
    const start = (this.next - this.size + this.slots.length) % this.slots.length;
    return Array.from({ length: this.size }, (_, i) => this.slots[(start + i) % this.slots.length]!);
  }
}

// Rolling sum: add the newcomer, subtract the evicted — never re-sum the window.
const window = new RingBuffer<number>(3);
let sum = 0;
const averages: number[] = [];
for (const latencyMs of [120, 80, 100, 400, 90, 110]) {
  sum += latencyMs - (window.push(latencyMs) ?? 0);
  averages.push(Math.round(sum / window.size));
}
console.log(averages.join(" "), "| window:", window.toArray());
// With floats the running sum drifts slowly: recompute it from the window every few thousand events.
Result
120 100 100 193 197 200 | window: [ 400, 90, 110 ]

Tumbling windows with a watermark

Revenue per minute by event time: a window closes once the watermark passes its end, so a delayed order still counts — up to the allowed lateness.

type Order = { at: number; cents: number };            // at: event time in ms
type Window = { start: number; orders: number; cents: number };

function tumblingWindows(sizeMs: number, latenessMs: number) {
  const open = new Map<number, Window>();               // window start -> running totals
  let watermark = -Infinity;                            // highest event time seen − allowed lateness
  let late = 0;

  const close = (due: (end: number) => boolean): Window[] => {
    const closed = [...open.values()].filter((w) => due(w.start + sizeMs)).sort((a, b) => a.start - b.start);
    for (const w of closed) open.delete(w.start);
    return closed;
  };

  return {
    /** Adds an order; returns the windows the advancing watermark closed, oldest first. */
    add(order: Order): Window[] {
      const start = order.at - (order.at % sizeMs);
      if (start + sizeMs <= watermark) {                // its window is already final: count, don't reopen
        late++;
        return [];
      }
      const w = open.get(start) ?? { start, orders: 0, cents: 0 };
      open.set(start, { start, orders: w.orders + 1, cents: w.cents + order.cents });
      watermark = Math.max(watermark, order.at - latenessMs);
      return close((end) => end <= watermark);
    },
    flush: () => close(() => true),                     // end of stream: everything still open is final
    late: () => late,
  };
}

const perMinute = tumblingWindows(60_000, 10_000);      // 1-minute windows, 10 s allowed lateness

const show = (w: Window) => `[${w.start / 1000}s, +60s) count ${w.orders}, $${(w.cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;
const arrivals = [[5, 1200], [20, 800], [58, 450], [62, 2000], [50, 300], [75, 990], [130, 1500], [55, 700]];
for (const [second, cents] of arrivals as [number, number][]) {
  for (const w of perMinute.add({ at: second * 1000, cents })) console.log(`after ${second}s:`, show(w));
}

for (const w of perMinute.flush()) console.log("at the end:", show(w));
console.log("late orders dropped:", perMinute.late());

Running statistics — Welford & EMA

Mean, standard deviation, a z-score for anomaly alerts and a smoothed level, in O(1) memory and without losing precision.

// Welford's online algorithm: numerically stable where "sum of squares" is not.
class RunningStats {
  count = 0;
  mean = 0;
  private m2 = 0;                                       // sum of squared distances from the mean

  add(x: number): void {
    this.count++;
    const delta = x - this.mean;
    this.mean += delta / this.count;
    this.m2 += delta * (x - this.mean);
  }

  get variance(): number {
    return this.count > 1 ? this.m2 / (this.count - 1) : 0;
  }
}

// Exponential moving average: no window and no history, one multiply per event.
function ema(period: number): (x: number) => number {
  const alpha = 2 / (period + 1);
  let level: number | undefined;
  return (x) => {
    level = level === undefined ? x : alpha * x + (1 - alpha) * level;
    return level;
  };
}

const stats = new RunningStats();
const smooth = ema(4);
for (const ms of [102, 98, 110, 95, 105, 99, 101, 104]) {
  stats.add(ms);
  smooth(ms);
}
const sd = Math.sqrt(stats.variance);
console.log(stats.mean.toFixed(2), sd.toFixed(2), "| z of 160 ms:", ((160 - stats.mean) / sd).toFixed(1));
console.log("smoothed level after a spike:", smooth(300).toFixed(1));

// Large offsets (nanosecond timestamps, meter readings): the naive formula cancels itself out.
const readings = [4, 7, 13, 16].map((x) => 1e9 + x);
const sum = readings.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0);
const naive = (readings.reduce((s, x) => s + x * x, 0) - sum ** 2 / readings.length) / (readings.length - 1);
const welford = new RunningStats();
readings.forEach((x) => welford.add(x));
console.log("variance — naive:", naive, "| Welford:", welford.variance);

Reservoir sampling

A uniform sample of k requests to keep for an audit, from a stream of unknown length, in O(k) memory and with an injected random source so a test can replay it.

type Random = () => number;                             // uniform in [0, 1)

function reservoir<T>(capacity: number, random: Random = Math.random) {
  const sample: T[] = [];
  let seen = 0;
  return {
    sample,
    add(item: T): void {
      seen++;
      if (sample.length < capacity) {
        sample.push(item);
        return;
      }
      const j = Math.floor(random() * seen);            // kept with probability k / seen
      if (j < capacity) sample[j] = item;
    },
  };
}

// mulberry32: a tiny seeded generator. Repeatable, fast — and never for security.
function seeded(seed: number): Random {
  return () => {
    seed = (seed + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0;
    let t = Math.imul(seed ^ (seed >>> 15), 1 | seed);
    t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t;
    return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4_294_967_296;
  };
}

const audit = reservoir<string>(4, seeded(42));
for (let i = 1; i <= 100_000; i++) audit.add(`req-${i}`);
console.log(audit.sample);

// Uniform? Each of 10 items should land in a 3-item sample 30% of the time.
const random = seeded(7);
const hits = new Array<number>(10).fill(0);
for (let trial = 0; trial < 20_000; trial++) {
  const r = reservoir<number>(3, random);
  for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) r.add(i);
  for (const i of r.sample) hits[i] = hits[i]! + 1;
}
console.log(hits.map((h) => `${Math.round((h / 20_000) * 100)}%`).join(" "));
