Count-Min Sketch — approximate frequencies

Requests per endpoint over millions of distinct keys in a fixed few kilobytes — it may overcount, but never undercounts.

// FNV-1a plus a murmur finaliser: fast, deterministic, well spread (not cryptographic).
function hash(key: string, seed: number): number {
  let h = 0x811c9dc5 ^ seed;
  for (let i = 0; i < key.length; i++) h = Math.imul(h ^ key.charCodeAt(i), 0x01000193);
  h = Math.imul(h ^ (h >>> 16), 0x85ebca6b);
  h = Math.imul(h ^ (h >>> 13), 0xc2b2ae35);
  return (h ^ (h >>> 16)) >>> 0;
}

class CountMinSketch {
  private readonly rows: Uint32Array[];                // wraps past 4.29 billion: Float64Array if unbounded
  private readonly width: number;

  // width ≈ e / ε, depth ≈ ln(1 / δ): 2048 × 5 overcounts by ≤ 0.13% of the total, 99% of the time.
  constructor(width = 2048, depth = 5) {
    this.width = width;
    this.rows = Array.from({ length: depth }, () => new Uint32Array(width));
  }

  add(key: string, count = 1): void {
    for (const [seed, row] of this.rows.entries()) row[hash(key, seed) % this.width]! += count;
  }

  /** Each row overcounts by its collisions, so the smallest row is the best guess. */
  estimate(key: string): number {
    return Math.min(...this.rows.map((row, seed) => row[hash(key, seed) % this.width]!));
  }
}

const sketch = new CountMinSketch(256, 4);              // 4 KB, deliberately small to show collisions
const truth = new Map<string, number>();
for (let i = 0; i < 60_000; i++) {
  const endpoint = i % 3 === 0 ? "/v1/charges" : i % 5 === 0 ? "/v1/refunds" : `/v1/customers/${i % 5_000}`;
  sketch.add(endpoint);
  truth.set(endpoint, (truth.get(endpoint) ?? 0) + 1);
}
for (const key of ["/v1/charges", "/v1/refunds", "/v1/customers/42"]) {
  console.log(key, "true", truth.get(key), "estimate", sketch.estimate(key));
}
console.log(truth.size, "distinct keys counted in", 256 * 4 * 4, "bytes");

Bloom filter — approximate membership

"Have I already synced this event?" without keeping every id: "definitely not" or "probably yes", in about 10 bits per key at 1%.

function hash(key: string, seed: number): number {      // FNV-1a + murmur finaliser, as for Count-Min
  let h = 0x811c9dc5 ^ seed;
  for (let i = 0; i < key.length; i++) h = Math.imul(h ^ key.charCodeAt(i), 0x01000193);
  h = Math.imul(h ^ (h >>> 16), 0x85ebca6b);
  h = Math.imul(h ^ (h >>> 13), 0xc2b2ae35);
  return (h ^ (h >>> 16)) >>> 0;
}

class BloomFilter {
  readonly bitCount: number;
  readonly hashCount: number;
  private readonly bits: Uint32Array;

  constructor(expected: number, falsePositiveRate = 0.01) {
    // m = -n·ln(p) / (ln 2)²  and  k = (m / n)·ln 2
    this.bitCount = Math.ceil((-expected * Math.log(falsePositiveRate)) / Math.LN2 ** 2);
    this.hashCount = Math.max(1, Math.round((this.bitCount / expected) * Math.LN2));
    this.bits = new Uint32Array(Math.ceil(this.bitCount / 32));
  }

  // Double hashing: k positions from two hashes, h1 + i·h2.
  private positions(key: string): number[] {
    const h1 = hash(key, 1);
    const h2 = (hash(key, 2) | 1) >>> 0;                // odd, read back as unsigned
    return Array.from({ length: this.hashCount }, (_, i) => (h1 + i * h2) % this.bitCount);
  }

  add(key: string): void {
    for (const p of this.positions(key)) this.bits[p >>> 5]! |= 1 << (p & 31);
  }

  /** false: definitely never added. true: probably added. */
  mayContain(key: string): boolean {
    return this.positions(key).every((p) => (this.bits[p >>> 5]! & (1 << (p & 31))) !== 0);
  }
}

const ids = (prefix: string) => Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, i) => `${prefix}${i}`);
const synced = new BloomFilter(10_000, 0.01);
for (const id of ids("evt_")) synced.add(id);
const missed = ids("evt_").filter((id) => !synced.mayContain(id)).length;
const falseHits = ids("evt_new_").filter((id) => synced.mayContain(id)).length;
console.log(Math.ceil(synced.bitCount / 8), "bytes,", synced.hashCount, "hashes");
console.log("false negatives:", missed, "| false positives:", `${(falseHits / 100).toFixed(2)}%`);

Heavy hitters — Misra–Gries

The accounts placing most orders, tracked with k counters for any number of accounts — anything above n/(k+1) occurrences is guaranteed to survive.

class HeavyHitters<K> {
  private readonly counters = new Map<K, number>();
  private readonly capacity: number;

  constructor(capacity: number) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
  }

  add(key: K): void {
    const count = this.counters.get(key);
    if (count !== undefined) {
      this.counters.set(key, count + 1);
    } else if (this.counters.size < this.capacity) {
      this.counters.set(key, 1);
    } else {
      // No room: every counter loses one, and those that reach zero leave.
      for (const [k, n] of this.counters) {
        if (n === 1) this.counters.delete(k);
        else this.counters.set(k, n - 1);
      }
    }
  }

  /** Candidates with lower-bound counts (low by at most n/(k+1)); a second pass gives exact ones. */
  top(n: number): [K, number][] {
    return [...this.counters].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, n);
  }
}

const accountOf = (i: number) =>
  i % 5 === 0 ? "acme" : i % 7 === 0 ? "globex" : i % 11 === 0 ? "initech" : `cust-${i % 4_000}`;
const orders = Array.from({ length: 30_000 }, (_, i) => accountOf(i));
const hitters = new HeavyHitters<string>(20);           // guaranteed: anyone above 30,000 / 21 ≈ 1,429
for (const account of orders) hitters.add(account);
const exact = (account: string) => orders.filter((a) => a === account).length;
for (const [account, atLeast] of hitters.top(3)) {
  console.log(account, "at least", atLeast, "exactly", exact(account));
}

Streaming quantiles

p50/p95/p99 latency without storing the requests: log-sized buckets (the DDSketch idea) keep every estimate within 1% of a real value.

class QuantileSketch {
  readonly buckets = new Map<number, number>();         // bucket index -> count
  private readonly gamma: number;
  private count = 0;

  constructor(relativeAccuracy = 0.01) {
    this.gamma = (1 + relativeAccuracy) / (1 - relativeAccuracy);
  }

  /** Positive values only. Bucket i holds (gamma^(i-1), gamma^i]. */
  add(value: number): void {
    const i = Math.ceil(Math.log(value) / Math.log(this.gamma));
    this.buckets.set(i, (this.buckets.get(i) ?? 0) + 1);
    this.count++;
  }

  quantile(q: number): number {
    const rank = q * (this.count - 1);
    let seen = 0;
    for (const i of [...this.buckets.keys()].sort((a, b) => a - b)) {
      seen += this.buckets.get(i)!;
      if (seen > rank) return (2 * this.gamma ** i) / (this.gamma + 1); // ±1% of every value in it
    }
    return Number.NaN;
  }
}

// 100,000 latencies: mostly 20–150 ms, 2% slow outliers. Park–Miller is seeded, so the run repeats.
let seed = 3;
function random(): number {
  seed = (seed * 48_271) % 2_147_483_647;
  return seed / 2_147_483_647;
}
const latency = () => (20 - Math.log(1 - random()) * 30) * (random() < 0.02 ? 15 : 1);
const latencies = Array.from({ length: 100_000 }, latency);

const sketch = new QuantileSketch(0.01);
for (const ms of latencies) sketch.add(ms);
const sorted = latencies.toSorted((a, b) => a - b);    // the exact answer, for comparison only
for (const q of [0.5, 0.95, 0.99]) {
  const exact = sorted[Math.floor(q * (sorted.length - 1))]!;
  console.log(`p${q * 100}`, "exact", exact.toFixed(1), "sketch", sketch.quantile(q).toFixed(1));
}
console.log(sketch.buckets.size, "buckets for", latencies.length, "values");

Rate limiting — token bucket vs sliding window

The same requests under two policies and an injected clock: a token bucket lets a burst through and then a steady rate, while a sliding window log allows at most n in any window.

type Clock = () => number;   // milliseconds; in production performance.now — monotonic, unlike Date.now
type Limiter = () => boolean;                           // true: let this request through

// Token bucket: `capacity` is the burst you tolerate, `perSecond` the sustained rate.
function tokenBucket(capacity: number, perSecond: number, clock: Clock): Limiter {
  let tokens = capacity;
  let last = clock();
  return () => {
    const now = clock();
    tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + ((now - last) / 1000) * perSecond);
    last = now;
    if (tokens < 1) return false;
    tokens -= 1;
    return true;
  };
}

// Sliding window log: never more than `limit` in any `windowMs`; memory grows with the limit.
function slidingWindow(limit: number, windowMs: number, clock: Clock): Limiter {
  const hits: number[] = [];                            // at most `limit` timestamps, oldest first
  return () => {
    const now = clock();
    // shift() is fine for small limits; keep a ring buffer of `limit` timestamps for large ones.
    while (hits.length && hits[0]! <= now - windowMs) hits.shift();
    if (hits.length >= limit) return false;
    hits.push(now);
    return true;
  };
}

let now = 0;
const clock: Clock = () => now;
const bucket = tokenBucket(3, 2, clock);                // bursts of 3, then 2 per second
const window = slidingWindow(3, 1_000, clock);          // at most 3 in any 1 second
const verdict = (ok: boolean) => (ok ? "allow" : "deny ");
for (const t of [0, 0, 0, 0, 300, 600, 1_000, 1_000, 1_001, 2_500]) {
  now = t;
  console.log(`${`${t} ms`.padEnd(8)} bucket ${verdict(bucket())}  window ${verdict(window())}`);
}
// Leaky bucket: a queue drained at a fixed rate — smooth output; requests wait instead of failing.

Live debounce, cancellable

Search-as-you-type on live input: a timer-based debounce with an injected scheduler, cancellable so a search box that unmounts never fires a stale query.

import { mock } from "node:test";

type Timers = { setTimeout(run: () => void, ms: number): unknown; clearTimeout(id: unknown): void };

// Run once the input has been quiet for quietMs; the scheduler is injected so a test can drive it.
function debounce<A>(run: (arg: A) => void, quietMs: number, timers: Timers = globalThis) {
  let pending: unknown;
  return {
    call(arg: A): void {
      timers.clearTimeout(pending);                     // each keystroke restarts the quiet period
      pending = timers.setTimeout(() => run(arg), quietMs);
    },
    cancel(): void {
      timers.clearTimeout(pending);                     // nothing fires later, no timer holds Node open
    },
  };
}

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] });           // a test's clock; production keeps real timers
const searched: string[] = [];
const search = debounce((query: string) => searched.push(query), 300);

search.call("s");
search.call("sw");
mock.timers.tick(400);                                  // quiet for 300 ms: one search, for "sw"
console.log("after the pause:", searched);

search.call("swift");
search.cancel();                                        // the search box unmounts with a search pending
mock.timers.tick(1_000);
console.log("after cancel:", searched);
mock.timers.reset();
// Throttle, sample and audit on live input, and their RxJS forms: see the Timing Operators sheet.
Result
after the pause: [ 'sw' ]
after cancel: [ 'sw' ]

Debounce, throttle & sample over recorded events

Debounce, throttle and sample over recorded, timestamped events — replayed logs and tests — where each operator works on event time and acts only as the next event arrives.

// Recorded events (replayed logs, tests): each operator works on event time and acts only when
// the next event arrives — for live input, use timers as in the live debounce card.
type Timed<T> = { at: number; value: T };                // at: event time in ms
type Events<T> = Iterable<Timed<T>> | AsyncIterable<Timed<T>>;

// Debounce: keep a value only if nothing newer came within quietMs.
async function* debounce<T>(events: Events<T>, quietMs: number) {
  let pending: Timed<T> | undefined;
  for await (const e of events) {
    if (pending && e.at - pending.at >= quietMs) yield pending;
    pending = e;
  }
  if (pending) yield pending;                            // the recording ended: nothing newer can come
}

// Throttle: the first value, then nothing for ms.
async function* throttle<T>(events: Events<T>, ms: number) {
  let openAt = -Infinity;
  for await (const e of events) {
    if (e.at < openAt) continue;
    openAt = e.at + ms;
    yield e;
  }
}

// Sample: the latest value at each tick. Like RxJS sampleTime, a value pending at the end is dropped.
async function* sample<T>(events: Events<T>, ms: number) {
  let latest: Timed<T> | undefined;
  let tick = ms;
  for await (const e of events) {
    if (e.at >= tick && latest) yield { at: tick, value: latest.value };   // at the first tick passed
    while (e.at >= tick) tick += ms;
    latest = e;
  }
}

const typed = [[0, "s"], [90, "sw"], [170, "swi"], [600, "swif"], [680, "swift"], [1300, "swift u"]] as const;
const keystrokes = typed.map(([at, value]) => ({ at, value }));
const show = async (events: AsyncIterable<Timed<string>>) =>
  (await Array.fromAsync(events)).map((e) => `${e.at}:${e.value}`).join("  ");

console.log("debounce 300 |", await show(debounce(keystrokes, 300)));
console.log("throttle 500 |", await show(throttle(keystrokes, 500)));
console.log("sample   500 |", await show(sample(keystrokes, 500)));
Result

Backpressure & buffering policy

When production outruns consumption, either slow the producer — pull, or honour highWaterMark — or decide explicitly what to drop.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { Writable } from "node:stream";
import { finished } from "node:stream/promises";

// Pull: an async generator runs only when the consumer asks for the next value.
async function* sensorReadings(): AsyncGenerator<number> {
  for (let n = 1; n <= 3; n++) {
    console.log(`produce ${n}`);
    yield n;
  }
}
for await (const n of sensorReadings()) console.log(`consume ${n}`);   // strictly alternating: no queue grows

// Push with a limit: write() returns false once highWaterMark items wait; resume on "drain".
const uploaded: number[] = [];
const slowUpload = new Writable({
  objectMode: true,
  highWaterMark: 2,
  write(batch: number, _encoding, done) {
    setTimeout(() => {
      uploaded.push(batch);
      done();
    }, 5);
  },
});
const accepted: boolean[] = [];
for (let batch = 1; batch <= 6; batch++) {
  const ok = slowUpload.write(batch);
  accepted.push(ok);
  if (!ok) await once(slowUpload, "drain");          // the producer waits instead of piling up
}
slowUpload.end();
await finished(slowUpload);
console.log(accepted.join(" "), "| uploaded:", uploaded.join(" "));

// A source you cannot pause (a WebSocket, a sensor) needs a stated policy:
//   keep the newest n  -> a ring buffer (telemetry, prices: only recent values matter)
//   keep the oldest n  -> reject new arrivals when full (a job queue answering "try later")
//   coalesce           -> keep only the latest value per key (see batching)
// events.on(emitter, "data") and an unbounded array queue every event until consumed.
Result
produce 1
consume 1
produce 2
consume 2
produce 3
consume 3
true false true false true false | uploaded: 1 2 3 4 5 6

Batching, chunking and coalescing

Amortise per-item cost: upload analytics in batches by size or age, split a bulk call at the API's limit, and send only the latest update per key.

type Timed<T> = { at: number; value: T };

// Flush when `size` items wait or the oldest has waited maxWaitMs, whichever comes first.
async function* batched<T>(source: AsyncIterable<Timed<T>>, size: number, maxWaitMs: number) {
  let batch: Timed<T>[] = [];
  const flush = () => {
    const values = batch.map((e) => e.value);
    batch = [];
    return values;
  };
  for await (const event of source) {
    if (batch.length && event.at - batch[0]!.at >= maxWaitMs) yield flush();
    batch.push(event);
    if (batch.length === size) yield flush();
  }
  if (batch.length) yield flush();                    // never lose the tail
}
// (Live, a timer also flushes an aged batch when no next event arrives to trigger it.)

async function* clicks(): AsyncGenerator<Timed<string>> {
  for (const at of [0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 900, 2_500, 2_600]) yield { at, value: `click@${at}` };
}
for await (const batch of batched(clicks(), 4, 1_000)) console.log("upload", batch);

// Chunk: the bulk endpoint takes at most 3 ids per call.
function chunk<T>(items: readonly T[], n: number): T[][] {
  return Array.from({ length: Math.ceil(items.length / n) }, (_, i) => items.slice(i * n, i * n + n));
}
console.log(chunk(["a1", "a2", "a3", "a4", "a5", "a6", "a7"], 3));

// Coalesce: of many cart updates per SKU, only the last one matters.
const updates = [
  { sku: "mug", qty: 1 }, { sku: "tee", qty: 2 }, { sku: "mug", qty: 3 }, { sku: "mug", qty: 2 },
];
console.log([...new Map(updates.map((u) => [u.sku, u])).values()]);

Deduplication with a TTL

Webhooks and queues deliver at least once, so drop an event id seen within the last few minutes, in bounded memory.

type Clock = () => number;

// A Map keeps insertion order, so it is also a queue by age: evict from the front.
class RecentIds {
  private readonly seenAt = new Map<string, number>();
  private readonly ttlMs: number;
  private readonly capacity: number;
  private readonly clock: Clock;

  constructor(ttlMs: number, capacity: number, clock: Clock) {
    this.ttlMs = ttlMs;
    this.capacity = capacity;
    this.clock = clock;
  }

  /** true the first time an id is seen within the TTL. Past `capacity` ids per TTL the oldest are
   *  forgotten early and their redeliveries run again: size capacity to peak rate × TTL. */
  firstTime(id: string): boolean {
    const now = this.clock();
    for (const [old, at] of this.seenAt) {             // oldest first: stop at the first fresh one
      if (now - at < this.ttlMs) break;
      this.seenAt.delete(old);
    }
    if (this.seenAt.has(id)) return false;
    this.seenAt.set(id, now);
    if (this.seenAt.size > this.capacity) this.seenAt.delete(this.seenAt.keys().next().value!);
    return true;
  }
}

let now = 0;
const recent = new RecentIds(5_000, 1_000, () => now);
const deliveries = [
  [0, "evt_1"], [100, "evt_2"], [200, "evt_1"], [4_900, "evt_2"], [6_000, "evt_1"],
] as const;
for (const [at, id] of deliveries) {
  now = at;
  console.log(at, id, recent.firstTime(id) ? "process" : "duplicate");
}
// Millions of ids? Use a Bloom filter per time slice and accept ~1% false duplicates.
Result

100 evt_2 process
200 evt_1 duplicate
4900 evt_2 duplicate
6000 evt_1 process

Merging ordered streams & change detection

Combine per-device readings into one time-ordered stream — closing every input if the consumer stops early — then alert on a threshold without flapping.

type Reading = { at: number; device: string; cpu: number };

// k-way merge: each input is sorted by event time, so the smallest head is next overall.
async function* mergeByTime(streams: AsyncIterable<Reading>[]): AsyncGenerator<Reading> {
  const inputs = streams.map((s) => s[Symbol.asyncIterator]());
  const next = async (i: number) => {
    const r = await inputs[i]!.next();
    return r.done ? undefined : r.value;              // a generator's return value is not a reading
  };
  try {
    const heads = await Promise.all(inputs.map((_, i) => next(i)));
    for (;;) {
      let min = -1;
      for (const [i, h] of heads.entries()) {
        if (h && (min === -1 || h.at < heads[min]!.at)) min = i;
      }
      if (min === -1) return;
      yield heads[min]!;
      heads[min] = await next(min);                   // a silent input stalls the merge: order costs latency
    }
  } finally {
    await Promise.all(inputs.map((it) => it.return?.()));   // break/throw downstream closes every input
  }
}

async function* device(name: string, samples: [number, number][]): AsyncGenerator<Reading> {
  try {
    for (const [at, cpu] of samples) yield { at, device: name, cpu };
  } finally {
    console.log(`${name} closed`);                    // where a socket or file handle is released
  }
}

const alerting = new Set<string>();   // hysteresis per device: alert above 80, clear only below 60
const web1 = device("web-1", [[0, 50], [20, 81], [40, 79], [60, 55], [80, 90]]);
const web2 = device("web-2", [[10, 70], [30, 82], [50, 78], [70, 50]]);

for await (const r of mergeByTime([web1, web2])) {
  const was = alerting.has(r.device);
  if (!was && r.cpu > 80) alerting.add(r.device);
  if (was && r.cpu < 60) alerting.delete(r.device);
  if (was !== alerting.has(r.device)) console.log(`${r.at}s ${was ? "clear" : "ALERT"} ${r.device}`);
  if (r.at >= 60) break;                              // stop early: both inputs must still be closed
}
Result
20s ALERT web-1
30s ALERT web-2
60s clear web-1
web-1 closed
web-2 closed

QuestionStructureMemoryError

Have I seen X before?Bloom filter~10 bits per key at 1%false positives only
What are the top k keys?Misra–Gries / Space-SavingO(k)may miss keys at or under n/(k+1); counts low by at most n/(k+1)
What is the p95 latency?DDSketch / t-digest / reservoirO(buckets) or O(sample)±1% relative (DDSketch)
A uniform sample of k itemsReservoir samplingO(k)exact and unbiased
A rolling averageRing buffer or EMAO(k) or O(1)exact / smoothed

Streaming pitfalls

The bugs that only appear at production volume.

  • Unbounded buffers: an array used as a queue, events.on over a fast emitter, an RxJS buffer with no limit. Every hot source needs a stated policy.
  • Recomputing the whole window per event — O(n·k) instead of O(n). Slide: add the newcomer, subtract the evicted.
  • queue.shift() on a long array is O(n): use a head index or a ring buffer.
  • Using processing time when the business asks about event time. Network and device delays reorder everything.
  • Assuming exactly-once delivery. Design for at-least-once and make the consumer idempotent.
  • Summing squares for variance — it cancels to nonsense at large offsets. Use Welford.
  • Counting past 2^53 in a number, past 2^32 in a Uint32Array, or hashing with bitwise operators and forgetting they are 32-bit: >>> 0 to read unsigned, bigint for more.
  • A merge or operator that stops early without calling return() on its inputs leaks their sockets and file handles.
  • Decide the lateness policy explicitly: drop, hold until a watermark passes, or reopen the window and re-emit.
  • Instrument the stream itself: input rate, drop count, queue depth, end-to-end lag.

node:test basics

Running the file runs its tests; any failure makes the process exit 1.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { test } from "node:test";

function slugify(title: string): string {
  return title.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/g, "-").replace(/^-|-$/g, "");
}

test("joins words with single hyphens", () => {
  assert.equal(slugify("  Hello, World!  "), "hello-world");
});

test("deep equality compares structure", () => {
  assert.deepEqual([slugify("A b"), slugify("--x--")], ["a-b", "x"]);
});
Result

Both tests pass — ✔ joins words with single hyphens, ✔ deep equality compares structure, then tests 2, pass 2, fail 0 — and the process exits 0 (the timings vary).

Design for testability — inject the clock

Code that reads time through a parameter can be tested without sleeping.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { test } from "node:test";

type Clock = () => number;

function makeSession(clock: Clock, ttlMs: number) {
  const started = clock();
  return { expired: () => clock() - started >= ttlMs };
}

test("expires after its time to live", () => {
  let now = 1_000;
  const session = makeSession(() => now, 500);
  assert.equal(session.expired(), false);
  now += 500;                                // the test owns time
  assert.equal(session.expired(), true);
});
Result

✔ expires after its time to live, pass 1, exit status 0.

Spies and fake timers

mock.timers replaces setTimeout, so a 300 ms debounce is tested in microseconds.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { mock, test } from "node:test";

function debounce<A extends unknown[]>(fn: (...args: A) => void, ms: number) {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  return (...args: A) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms);
  };
}

test("debounce calls once, with the last arguments", () => {
  mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] });
  const save = mock.fn((_text: string) => {});
  const onInput = debounce(save, 300);
  onInput("h");
  onInput("he");
  onInput("hey");
  mock.timers.tick(299);
  assert.equal(save.mock.callCount(), 0);
  mock.timers.tick(1);
  assert.deepEqual(save.mock.calls.map((c) => c.arguments), [["hey"]]);
  mock.timers.reset();
});
Result

✔ debounce calls once, with the last arguments, pass 1, exit status 0.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";

  if (!Number.isInteger(n) || n < 1 || n > 65535) throw new RangeError(`not a port: ${text}`);
  return n;
}

test("accepts a port and rejects text", async () => {
  assert.equal(await parsePort("8080"), 8080);
  await assert.rejects(parsePort("http"), { name: "RangeError", message: "not a port: http" });
});

Integration test across a real HTTP boundary

A real node:http server on 127.0.0.1, port 0, exercised with fetch: the client's URL building, status handling and JSON decoding all run for real, with no network.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";
import { after, before, test } from "node:test";

type Order = { id: string; total: number };

async function fetchOrder(baseUrl: string, id: string): Promise<Order> {
  const response = await fetch(new URL(`/orders/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, baseUrl));
  if (!response.ok) {
    await response.body?.cancel();             // release the keep-alive connection instead of waiting for GC
    throw new Error(response.status === 404 ? `order ${id} not found` : `HTTP ${response.status}`);
  }
  return (await response.json()) as Order;
}

const routes: Record<string, [status: number, body: unknown]> = {
  "/orders/A-1042": [200, { id: "A-1042", total: 19.5 }],
  "/orders/A-500": [500, { error: "database down" }],
};
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  const [status, body] = routes[req.url ?? ""] ?? [404, { error: "not found" }];
  res.writeHead(status, { "content-type": "application/json" }).end(JSON.stringify(body));
});
let baseUrl = "";

before(async () => {
  // port 0: the OS picks a free port, so parallel runs never collide
  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1", resolve));
  baseUrl = `http://127.0.0.1:${(server.address() as AddressInfo).port}`;
});
after(() => server.close());                   // or the open socket keeps the process alive

test("decodes an order", async () => {
  assert.deepEqual(await fetchOrder(baseUrl, "A-1042"), { id: "A-1042", total: 19.5 });
});

test("turns 404 and 5xx into distinct errors", async () => {
  await assert.rejects(fetchOrder(baseUrl, "A-9999"), { message: "order A-9999 not found" });
  await assert.rejects(fetchOrder(baseUrl, "A-500"), { message: "HTTP 500" });
});
Result

✔ decodes an order, ✔ turns 404 and 5xx into distinct errors, pass 2, exit status 0 — and the process exits because the server is closed.

Test doubles: fake, stub, spy — and mock.method

A fake for anything with state, a stub to choose a path, a spy to check a call you care about; Node's mock.method swaps one method of a real object and restores it.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { mock, test } from "node:test";

type User = { id: string; email: string };
interface Users { find(id: string): Promise<User | undefined>; save(user: User): Promise<void> }
interface Mailer { send(to: string, subject: string): Promise<void> }

async function changeEmail(users: Users, mailer: Mailer, id: string, email: string): Promise<void> {
  const user = await users.find(id);
  if (!user) throw new Error(`no user ${id}`);
  await users.save({ ...user, email });
  await mailer.send(user.email, "Your email was changed");   // tell the OLD address
}

class InMemoryUsers implements Users {        // fake: a working implementation, kept in memory
  #rows: Map<string, User>;
  constructor(seed: User[] = []) { this.#rows = new Map(seed.map((u) => [u.id, u])); }
  async find(id: string) { return this.#rows.get(id); }
  async save(user: User) { this.#rows.set(user.id, user); }
}
const ada: User = { id: "u1", email: "ada@old.example" };

test("fake + spy: the state changes and the old address is told", async () => {
  const users = new InMemoryUsers([ada]);
  const send = mock.fn<Mailer["send"]>(async () => {});
  await changeEmail(users, { send }, "u1", "ada@new.example");
  assert.equal((await users.find("u1"))?.email, "ada@new.example");   // assert on state, via the fake
  assert.deepEqual(send.mock.calls.map((c) => c.arguments), [["ada@old.example", "Your email was changed"]]);
});

test("stub + mock.method: a failing save sends no email", async (t) => {
  const users = new InMemoryUsers([ada]);
  t.mock.method(users, "save", async () => { throw new Error("disk full"); });   // restored after the test
  const send = mock.fn<Mailer["send"]>(async () => {});
  await assert.rejects(changeEmail(users, { send }, "u1", "ada@new.example"), { message: "disk full" });
  assert.equal(send.mock.callCount(), 0);              // no email for a change that did not happen
});
Result

✔ fake + spy: the state changes and the old address is told, ✔ stub + mock.method: a failing save sends no email, pass 2, exit status 0.

Principles worth stating

The same in every language.

  • Fakes you own (an in-memory repository, a clock function) over mocks of code you do not.
  • Test behaviour through the public surface; a refactor should not break a test.
  • Real timers, real network and shared state between tests — the three sources of flakiness.
  • Type-check the tests as strictly as the code: tsc --noEmit catches a wrong mock shape.

Clean Code in TypeScript

Names, small functions, options over flags, errors as values, guard clauses, branded types and clean tests — every before/after proved to behave the same.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • any ES2023 engine; the examples run on Node.js

Sources: Google TypeScript Style Guide · Narrowing — TypeScript Handbook · Test runner — Node.js

Uncle Bob rule → TypeScript idiom

The classic rules still hold; TypeScript's type system enforces most of them for you.

Clean Code ruleThe TypeScript way to satisfy it
Avoid nullstrict on; one convention for absence per codebase, read with ?. and ??; return [], not undefined
Don't return error codesa discriminated-union result for expected failures; throw new Error(msg, { cause }) for the unexpected
Prefer polymorphism to switcha closed union with an exhaustive switch (a never check), or a Record<Kind, Handler> when the set grows
Encapsulate conditionalsa named predicate: const isRefundable = (order: Order) => …
Avoid output argumentsreturn a new value; readonly parameters make mutation a compile error
No flag argumentsan options object, or a string-literal union such as "compact" | "full"
Avoid primitive obsessionbranded types, created by one parser at the boundary
Keep classes smallmodules of functions; a class only when it owns state over time
Separate construction from usea composition root (main.ts) wires dependencies; functions receive them as parameters
Comments explain whyTSDoc (/ … */) on exported API; // why beside surprising code; never // what

Naming

Intention-revealing, pronounceable, searchable — camelCase values, PascalCase types, is/has booleans, no I prefix, no Hungarian notation.

Don't
type O = { i: string; t: number; s: number; d: number };

const list1: O[] = [
  { i: "A-1", t: 4200, s: 2, d: 3 },
  { i: "A-2", t: 1500, s: 1, d: 12 },
  { i: "A-3", t: 9900, s: 2, d: 45 },
];

function proc(a: O[]): string[] {
  const r: string[] = [];
  for (const o of a) if (o.s === 2 && o.d < 30) r.push(o.i);   // 2? 30?
  return r;
}

const flag = proc(list1).length > 0;
console.log(proc(list1), flag);
Do
type OrderStatus = "placed" | "delivered";
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number; status: OrderStatus; ageInDays: number };

const REFUND_WINDOW_DAYS = 30;

const orders: Order[] = [
  { id: "A-1", totalCents: 4200, status: "delivered", ageInDays: 3 },
  { id: "A-2", totalCents: 1500, status: "placed", ageInDays: 12 },
  { id: "A-3", totalCents: 9900, status: "delivered", ageInDays: 45 },
];

function refundableOrderIds(orders: readonly Order[]): string[] {
  return orders
    .filter((order) => order.status === "delivered" && order.ageInDays < REFUND_WINDOW_DAYS)
    .map((order) => order.id);
}

const refundableIds = refundableOrderIds(orders);
const hasRefundableOrders = refundableIds.length > 0;
console.log(refundableIds, hasRefundableOrders);
Result
[ 'A-1' ] true

Small functions, one level of abstraction

When a function needs a comment to separate its steps, each step wants to be a function with that name.

Before
type Item = { sku: string; priceCents: number; quantity: number; onSale: boolean };
type Cart = { tier: "free" | "pro"; items: Item[] };

function checkout(cart: Cart) {
  let total = 0;
  for (const item of cart.items) {
    let price = item.priceCents;
    if (item.onSale) price = Math.round(price * 0.8);
    if (cart.tier === "pro") price = Math.round(price * 0.9);
    total += price * item.quantity;
  }
  if (total > 10_000) total -= 500;
  const tax = Math.round(total * 0.21);
  return { totalCents: total + tax, taxCents: tax };
}

console.log(checkout({
  tier: "pro",
  items: [
    { sku: "mug", priceCents: 1200, quantity: 2, onSale: true },
    { sku: "lamp", priceCents: 9900, quantity: 1, onSale: false },
  ],
}));
After
type Tier = "free" | "pro";
type Item = { sku: string; priceCents: number; quantity: number; onSale: boolean };
type Cart = { tier: Tier; items: Item[] };

const SALE_MULTIPLIER = 0.8;
const TIER_MULTIPLIER: Record<Tier, number> = { free: 1, pro: 0.9 };
const BULK = { thresholdCents: 10_000, discountCents: 500 };
const TAX_RATE = 0.21;

function checkout(cart: Cart) {
  const subtotal = subtotalCents(cart);
  const discounted = applyBulkDiscount(subtotal);
  const tax = taxCents(discounted);
  return { totalCents: discounted + tax, taxCents: tax };
}

const taxCents = (cents: number) => Math.round(cents * TAX_RATE);

function subtotalCents(cart: Cart): number {
  return cart.items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + unitPriceCents(item, cart.tier) * item.quantity, 0);
}

function unitPriceCents(item: Item, tier: Tier): number {
  const onSale = item.onSale ? Math.round(item.priceCents * SALE_MULTIPLIER) : item.priceCents;
  return Math.round(onSale * TIER_MULTIPLIER[tier]);
}

function applyBulkDiscount(cents: number): number {
  return cents > BULK.thresholdCents ? cents - BULK.discountCents : cents;
}

console.log(checkout({
  tier: "pro",
  items: [
    { sku: "mug", priceCents: 1200, quantity: 2, onSale: true },
    { sku: "lamp", priceCents: 9900, quantity: 1, onSale: false },
  ],
}));
Result
{ totalCents: 12267, taxCents: 2129 }

Options objects and unions over flag arguments

A positional boolean means the function does two things and the call site cannot say which; name the choice.

Don't
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number; status: string };

function renderOrder(order: Order, compact: boolean, withStatus: boolean, currency: string): string {
  const total = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency })
    .format(order.totalCents / 100);
  if (compact) return withStatus ? `${order.id} ${total} [${order.status}]` : `${order.id} ${total}`;
  const line = `Order ${order.id} — total ${total}`;
  return withStatus ? `${line} — ${order.status}` : line;
}

const order = { id: "A-1", totalCents: 4250, status: "shipped" };
console.log(renderOrder(order, true, false, "EUR"));     // true what? false what?
console.log(renderOrder(order, false, true, "USD"));
Do
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number; status: string };
type RenderOptions = {
  layout: "compact" | "full";
  currency: "EUR" | "USD";
  showStatus?: boolean;
};

function renderOrder(order: Order, { layout, currency, showStatus = false }: RenderOptions): string {
  const total = formatMoney(order.totalCents, currency);
  const line = layout === "compact" ? `${order.id} ${total}` : `Order ${order.id} — total ${total}`;
  if (!showStatus) return line;
  return layout === "compact" ? `${line} [${order.status}]` : `${line} — ${order.status}`;
}

function formatMoney(cents: number, currency: RenderOptions["currency"]): string {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency }).format(cents / 100);
}

const order = { id: "A-1", totalCents: 4250, status: "shipped" };
console.log(renderOrder(order, { layout: "compact", currency: "EUR" }));
console.log(renderOrder(order, { layout: "full", currency: "USD", showStatus: true }));
Result
A-1 €42.50
Order A-1 — total $42.50 — shipped

Comments that earn their place

Code says what and a comment says why — the bug, the constraint, the decision — so delete the rest and let git keep the old code.

Noise
type ApiResponse = { status: number; body: string };

// check the response
function isSignedIn(res: ApiResponse): boolean {
  // if the status is 200
  if (res.status === 200) {
    // and the body is not empty
    if (res.body.length > 0) return true;   // return true
  }
  // function isSignedInOld(res) { return res.status < 400; }
  return false; // TODO: fix this
}

console.log(isSignedIn({ status: 200, body: '{"user":"ada"}' }));
console.log(isSignedIn({ status: 200, body: "" }));
console.log(isSignedIn({ status: 401, body: "" }));
Useful
type ApiResponse = { status: number; body: string };

/**
 * Whether the response proves an authenticated session.
 *
 * @remarks An expired token still gets `200`, with an empty body (vendor bug AUTH-4821),
 * so an empty body counts as signed out.
 */

function isSignedIn(response: ApiResponse): boolean {
  const isSuccess = response.status === 200;
  const hasSessionPayload = response.body.length > 0;
  return isSuccess && hasSessionPayload;
}

console.log(isSignedIn({ status: 200, body: '{"user":"ada"}' }));
console.log(isSignedIn({ status: 200, body: "" }));
console.log(isSignedIn({ status: 401, body: "" }));
Result
true
false
false

Errors as values, not sentinel codes

Expected failures become a union the compiler makes every caller handle; keep throw (with a cause) for the unexpected.

Sentinels
// -1 = not a whole number, -2 = out of range. Every caller must remember.
function parseQuantity(input: string): number {
  const n = Number(input);
  if (!Number.isInteger(n)) return -1;
  if (n < 1 || n > 99) return -2;
  return n;
}

for (const input of ["3", "three", "250"]) {
  const quantity = parseQuantity(input);
  if (quantity === -1) console.log(`"${input}": not a whole number`);
  else if (quantity === -2) console.log(`"${input}": must be 1–99`);
  else console.log(`"${input}": ok, ${quantity}`);
  // Forget the check and -1 flows into the cart total.
}
Typed result
type QuantityError =
  | { kind: "not-a-whole-number"; input: string }
  | { kind: "out-of-range"; value: number; min: number; max: number };

type Parsed<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

function parseQuantity(input: string): Parsed<number, QuantityError> {
  const n = Number(input);
  if (!Number.isInteger(n)) return { ok: false, error: { kind: "not-a-whole-number", input } };
  if (n < 1 || n > 99) return { ok: false, error: { kind: "out-of-range", value: n, min: 1, max: 99 } };
  return { ok: true, value: n };
}

function describe(error: QuantityError): string {
  switch (error.kind) {
    case "not-a-whole-number": return "not a whole number";
    case "out-of-range": return `must be ${error.min}–${error.max}`;
  }
}

for (const input of ["3", "three", "250"]) {
  const result = parseQuantity(input);
  // `result.value` does not type-check until `ok` has been checked.
  console.log(`"${input}": ${result.ok ? `ok, ${result.value}` : describe(result.error)}`);
}
Result
"3": ok, 3
"three": not a whole number
"250": must be 1–99

Guard clauses over the arrow anti-pattern

Reject the edge cases first and return; the happy path stays at the left margin and every else disappears.

Nested
type Payment = { id: string; amountCents: number };
type WebhookEvent = { type: string; signatureValid: boolean; payment?: Payment };

function handleWebhook(event: WebhookEvent | undefined): string {
  if (event) {
    if (event.signatureValid) {
      if (event.type === "payment.succeeded") {
        if (event.payment) {
          return `fulfil ${event.payment.id}`;
        } else {
          return "ignored: no payment";
        }
      } else {
        return `ignored: ${event.type}`;
      }
    } else {
      return "rejected: bad signature";
    }
  }
  return "ignored: empty";
}

const payment = { id: "pay_1", amountCents: 4250 };
console.log(handleWebhook({ type: "payment.succeeded", signatureValid: true, payment }));
console.log(handleWebhook({ type: "payment.succeeded", signatureValid: false, payment }));
console.log(handleWebhook({ type: "refund.created", signatureValid: true }));
console.log(handleWebhook(undefined));
Flat
type Payment = { id: string; amountCents: number };
type WebhookEvent = { type: string; signatureValid: boolean; payment?: Payment };

function handleWebhook(event: WebhookEvent | undefined): string {
  if (!event) return "ignored: empty";
  if (!event.signatureValid) return "rejected: bad signature";
  if (event.type !== "payment.succeeded") return `ignored: ${event.type}`;
  if (!event.payment) return "ignored: no payment";

  return `fulfil ${event.payment.id}`;   // narrowed: `payment` is defined here
}

const payment = { id: "pay_1", amountCents: 4250 };
console.log(handleWebhook({ type: "payment.succeeded", signatureValid: true, payment }));
console.log(handleWebhook({ type: "payment.succeeded", signatureValid: false, payment }));
console.log(handleWebhook({ type: "refund.created", signatureValid: true }));
console.log(handleWebhook(undefined));
Result
fulfil pay_1
rejected: bad signature
ignored: refund.created
ignored: empty

Branded types over bare primitives

Two string ids are interchangeable to the compiler; a brand makes swapping them a type error, at zero runtime cost.

declare const brand: unique symbol;

type Brand<T, Name extends string> = T & { readonly [brand]: Name };

type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;
type CustomerId = Brand<string, "CustomerId">;
type Email = Brand<string, "Email">;

// Parse once, at the edge: everything downstream can trust the type.
function parseEmail(raw: string): Email | undefined {
  const normalized = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
  return /^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$/.test(normalized) ? (normalized as Email) : undefined;
}

const orderId = (raw: string) => raw as OrderId;
const customerId = (raw: string) => raw as CustomerId;

function sendReceipt(order: OrderId, customer: CustomerId, to: Email): string {
  return `receipt for ${order} → ${customer} <${to}>`;
}

const email = parseEmail("  Ada@Example.com ");
if (email) {
  console.log(sendReceipt(orderId("ord_42"), customerId("cus_7"), email));
  // @ts-expect-error — swapped arguments: a CustomerId is not an OrderId
  sendReceipt(customerId("cus_7"), orderId("ord_42"), email);
}

console.log(parseEmail("not-an-email"));
Result
receipt for ord_42 → cus_7 <ada@example.com>
undefined

A clean test: arrange, act, assert

Name the behaviour, build inputs with a factory, inject the clock — so the test is fast, independent and repeatable.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { describe, test } from "node:test";

type Order = { id: string; status: "placed" | "delivered"; deliveredAt?: number };
type Eligibility = { eligible: true } | { eligible: false; reason: "not-delivered" | "window-closed" };
const DAY_MS = 86_400_000;

function refundEligibility(order: Order, now: () => number, windowDays = 30): Eligibility {
  if (order.status !== "delivered" || order.deliveredAt === undefined) {
    return { eligible: false, reason: "not-delivered" };
  }
  const ageInDays = (now() - order.deliveredAt) / DAY_MS;
  return ageInDays <= windowDays ? { eligible: true } : { eligible: false, reason: "window-closed" };
}

const NOW = Date.UTC(2026, 10, 16);   // a fixed instant, never the real clock
const deliveredDaysAgo = (days: number): Order =>
  ({ id: "ord_1", status: "delivered", deliveredAt: NOW - days * DAY_MS });

describe("refundEligibility", () => {
  test("rejects an order delivered more than 30 days ago", () => {
    const order = deliveredDaysAgo(31);                     // Arrange

    const result = refundEligibility(order, () => NOW);    // Act

    assert.deepEqual(result, { eligible: false, reason: "window-closed" });   // Assert
  });

  test("accepts an order on the last day of the window", () => {
    assert.deepEqual(refundEligibility(deliveredDaysAgo(30), () => NOW), { eligible: true });
  });

  test("rejects an order that has not been delivered", () => {
    const placed: Order = { id: "ord_2", status: "placed" };
    assert.deepEqual(refundEligibility(placed, () => NOW), { eligible: false, reason: "not-delivered" });
  });
});
Result

Three passing tests under ▶ refundEligibility — tests 3, pass 3, fail 0 — and exit status 0 (the timings vary).

Smell checklist, and F.I.R.S.T. tests

Name the smell out loud in review; it turns a taste argument into a shared vocabulary.

  • Long function / god module — many reasons to change, and no honest name for it.
  • Deep nesting — invert the condition and return early.
  • Duplicated logic — the third copy is when you extract; two copies may still be a coincidence.
  • Primitive obsession — string for an id, an email, a currency; brand it or give it a union.
  • Boolean blindness — isLoading, hasError, isEmpty encoding one state; use a discriminated union.
  • any and as — each one switches the checker off; prefer unknown plus a narrowing guard.
  • Feature envy — a function that mostly reads another module's data belongs in that module.
  • Temporal coupling — init() must run before start(); make the constructor or factory return a ready value.
  • F.I.R.S.T. tests are Fast (no network, no sleeps), Independent (no shared state, any order), Repeatable (inject the clock, ids and randomness), Self-validating (an assertion, never a log to eyeball) and Timely (written with the change).
  • The boy scout rule — leave the file cleaner than you found it, in small commits that keep the tests green.

SOLID in TypeScript

Five principles in TypeScript's own idiom — small structural types, functions and factories instead of class hierarchies — each before/after proved to print the same.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • any ES2023 engine; the examples run on Node.js

Sources: Object Types — TypeScript Handbook · Type Compatibility — TypeScript Handbook

The one-line versions

Say the name, then the smell it prevents.

  • Single Responsibility — a module has one reason to change. Smell: one class that fetches, parses, caches and formats.
  • Open/Closed — add behaviour by adding code, not by editing a shipped switch. Smell: every feature touches the same function.
  • Liskov Substitution — anything typed as T must keep T's promises. Smell: instanceof checks in the caller, or an override that throws.
  • Interface Segregation — accept the narrowest type you use. Smell: test fakes full of throw new Error("not implemented").
  • Dependency Inversion — depend on a type you declare, and let the caller pass the implementation. Smell: imported singletons and Date.now() inside logic.
  • Liskov, TypeScript edition — a member written in method syntax (refund(cents: number): T) is checked bivariantly, so tsc accepts an implementation that demands a narrower parameter; declare it as a property (refund: (cents: number) => T) and strictFunctionTypes catches it in any implementation of that type. An override in a subclass is always checked bivariantly, so for a class hierarchy only tests and review catch it.
  • Structural typing does much of the work: any object with the right shape satisfies a type, so small types, functions and factories replace most interfaces and hierarchies.

S — Single Responsibility

Split by reason to change — transport, parsing, caching, presentation — and compose the pieces in one thin function.

Violates
type User = { id: string; firstName: string; lastName: string };
const fakeApi: Record<string, string> = { u1: '{"id":"u1","first_name":"Ada","last_name":"Lovelace"}' };

class UserManager {
  #cache = new Map<string, User>();
  readonly events: string[] = [];

  async displayName(id: string): Promise<string> {
    let user = this.#cache.get(id);
    if (!user) {
      const body = fakeApi[id];                                    // transport
      if (body === undefined) throw new Error(`no user ${id}`);
      const raw = JSON.parse(body) as { id: string; first_name: string; last_name: string };
      user = { id: raw.id, firstName: raw.first_name, lastName: raw.last_name };   // parsing
      this.#cache.set(id, user);                                   // caching
      this.events.push("user_fetched");                            // analytics
    }
    return `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName.charAt(0)}.`;        // presentation
  }
}

const users = new UserManager();
console.log(await users.displayName("u1"));
console.log(await users.displayName("u1"));
console.log(users.events);
Respects
type User = { id: string; firstName: string; lastName: string };
type Transport = (id: string) => Promise<string>;
const fakeApi: Record<string, string> = { u1: '{"id":"u1","first_name":"Ada","last_name":"Lovelace"}' };

const transport: Transport = async (id) => {
  const body = fakeApi[id];
  if (body === undefined) throw new Error(`no user ${id}`);
  return body;
};

function parseUser(body: string): User {
  const raw = JSON.parse(body) as { id: string; first_name: string; last_name: string };
  return { id: raw.id, firstName: raw.first_name, lastName: raw.last_name };
}

const displayName = (user: User) => `${user.firstName} ${user.lastName.charAt(0)}.`;

function createUserRepository(fetchUser: Transport, track: (event: string) => void) {
  const cache = new Map<string, User>();
  return {
    async user(id: string): Promise<User> {
      const hit = cache.get(id);
      if (hit) return hit;
      const user = parseUser(await fetchUser(id));
      cache.set(id, user);
      track("user_fetched");
      return user;
    },
  };
}

const events: string[] = [];
const users = createUserRepository(transport, (event) => events.push(event));
console.log(displayName(await users.user("u1")));
console.log(displayName(await users.user("u1")));
console.log(events);
Result
Ada L.
Ada L.
[ 'user_fetched' ]
Setup

  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

O — Open/Closed

Both columns add a Black Friday promotion: one edits the shipped switch, the other adds a rule value beside code that never changes.

Violates
type Cart = { subtotalCents: number; customer: { isStudent: boolean; ageYears: number }; coupon?: string };

function discountCents(cart: Cart, kind: string): number {
  switch (kind) {
    case "student": return cart.customer.isStudent ? Math.round(cart.subtotalCents * 0.1) : 0;
    case "senior": return cart.customer.ageYears >= 65 ? Math.round(cart.subtotalCents * 0.15) : 0;
    case "welcome": return cart.coupon === "WELCOME5" ? 500 : 0;
    case "black-friday": return cart.subtotalCents >= 5000 ? 1000 : 0;   // edited shipped code
    default: return 0;
  }
}

const totalDiscountCents = (cart: Cart, kinds: string[]) =>
  kinds.reduce((sum, kind) => sum + discountCents(cart, kind), 0);

const cart: Cart = { subtotalCents: 8000, customer: { isStudent: true, ageYears: 20 }, coupon: "WELCOME5" };
const standard = ["student", "senior", "welcome"];
console.log("standard:", totalDiscountCents(cart, standard));

// The new promotion meant editing discountCents — and retesting every case in it.
console.log("black friday:", totalDiscountCents(cart, [...standard, "black-friday"]));
Respects
type Cart = { subtotalCents: number; customer: { isStudent: boolean; ageYears: number }; coupon?: string };
type DiscountRule = { name: string; discountCents: (cart: Cart) => number };

const standardRules: readonly DiscountRule[] = [
  { name: "student",
    discountCents: (cart) => (cart.customer.isStudent ? Math.round(cart.subtotalCents * 0.1) : 0) },
  { name: "senior",
    discountCents: (cart) => (cart.customer.ageYears >= 65 ? Math.round(cart.subtotalCents * 0.15) : 0) },
  { name: "welcome", discountCents: (cart) => (cart.coupon === "WELCOME5" ? 500 : 0) },
];

function totalDiscountCents(cart: Cart, rules: readonly DiscountRule[]): number {
  return rules.reduce((sum, rule) => sum + rule.discountCents(cart), 0);
}

// Added later, in its own module: nothing above was edited or needs retesting.
const blackFriday: DiscountRule = {
  name: "black-friday",
  discountCents: (cart) => (cart.subtotalCents >= 5000 ? 1000 : 0),
};

const cart: Cart = { subtotalCents: 8000, customer: { isStudent: true, ageYears: 20 }, coupon: "WELCOME5" };
console.log("standard:", totalDiscountCents(cart, standardRules));
console.log("black friday:", totalDiscountCents(cart, [...standardRules, blackFriday]));

// When the set is genuinely closed (order states), a union with an exhaustive switch is the better tool.
Result
standard: 1300
black friday: 2300

L — Liskov Substitution

If the caller must ask which subclass it got, substitution is broken; the fix keeps the classes and widens the contract so every outcome is a return value.

Violates
class PaymentMethod {
  refund(cents: number): string {
    return `refunded ${cents} to the original method`;
  }
}

class Card extends PaymentMethod {
  readonly last4: string;
  constructor(last4: string) {
    super();
    this.last4 = last4;
  }
  override refund(cents: number): string {
    return `refunded ${cents} to card ••${this.last4}`;
  }
}

class GiftCard extends PaymentMethod {
  override refund(_cents: number): string {
    throw new Error("gift cards cannot be refunded");   // breaks the parent's promise
  }
}

function refundOrder(method: PaymentMethod, cents: number): string {
  // The smell: the caller has to know which subtype it was handed.
  if (method instanceof GiftCard) return `issued ${cents} as store credit`;
  return method.refund(cents);
}

console.log(refundOrder(new Card("4242"), 4250));
console.log(refundOrder(new GiftCard(), 4250));
Respects
type RefundOutcome =
  | { kind: "returned"; description: string }
  | { kind: "store-credit"; cents: number };

// The fix is the contract, not the classes: every outcome is in the return type, and no override throws.
class PaymentMethod {
  refund(cents: number): RefundOutcome {
    return { kind: "returned", description: `refunded ${cents} to the original method` };
  }
}

class Card extends PaymentMethod {
  readonly last4: string;
  constructor(last4: string) {
    super();
    this.last4 = last4;
  }
  override refund(cents: number): RefundOutcome {
    return { kind: "returned", description: `refunded ${cents} to card ••${this.last4}` };
  }
}

class GiftCard extends PaymentMethod {
  override refund(cents: number): RefundOutcome {
    return { kind: "store-credit", cents };   // a different outcome, inside the same promise
  }
}

function refundOrder(method: PaymentMethod, cents: number): string {
  const outcome = method.refund(cents);       // no instanceof: any PaymentMethod will do
  return outcome.kind === "store-credit" ? `issued ${outcome.cents} as store credit` : outcome.description;
}

console.log(refundOrder(new Card("4242"), 4250));
console.log(refundOrder(new GiftCard(), 4250));
Result
refunded 4250 to card ••4242
issued 4250 as store credit

I — Interface Segregation

Declare the parameter as the slice you use; structural typing lets the full repository — or a one-method fake — satisfy it.

Violates
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number; placedOnDay: number };

interface OrderRepository {
  listSince(day: number): Order[];
  save(order: Order): void;
  delete(id: string): void;
  exportCsv(): string;
}

function weeklyRevenueCents(repository: OrderRepository, today: number): number {
  return repository.listSince(today - 7).reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.totalCents, 0);
}

const fixture: Order[] = [
  { id: "A-1", totalCents: 9900, placedOnDay: 90 },
  { id: "A-2", totalCents: 4250, placedOnDay: 95 },
  { id: "A-3", totalCents: 1500, placedOnDay: 99 },
];

// To exercise one method, the fake has to stub four.
const fakeRepository: OrderRepository = {
  listSince: (day) => fixture.filter((order) => order.placedOnDay >= day),
  save: () => { throw new Error("not implemented"); },
  delete: () => { throw new Error("not implemented"); },
  exportCsv: () => { throw new Error("not implemented"); },
};

console.log(weeklyRevenueCents(fakeRepository, 100));
Respects
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number; placedOnDay: number };

type OrderLister = { listSince: (day: number) => Order[] };
type OrderWriter = { save: (order: Order) => void; delete: (id: string) => void };
type OrderExporter = { exportCsv: () => string };
export type OrderRepository = OrderLister & OrderWriter & OrderExporter;   // the adapter implements all

function weeklyRevenueCents(orders: OrderLister, today: number): number {
  return orders.listSince(today - 7).reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.totalCents, 0);
}

const fixture: Order[] = [
  { id: "A-1", totalCents: 9900, placedOnDay: 90 },
  { id: "A-2", totalCents: 4250, placedOnDay: 95 },
  { id: "A-3", totalCents: 1500, placedOnDay: 99 },
];

const fakeOrders: OrderLister = {
  listSince: (day) => fixture.filter((order) => order.placedOnDay >= day),
};

console.log(weeklyRevenueCents(fakeOrders, 100));
Result
5750

D — Dependency Inversion

The business code declares the type it needs; a composition root passes the real client in production and a fake in tests.

Violates
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number };

// Module-level singletons: the only implementations checkout can ever use.
const stripeClient = { charge: async (cents: number) => `ch_${cents}` };
const paymentsTable = new Map<string, string>();

async function checkout(order: Order): Promise<string> {
  const chargeId = await stripeClient.charge(order.totalCents);
  paymentsTable.set(order.id, chargeId);
  return `${order.id} paid with ${chargeId}`;
}

// A test of checkout now charges "Stripe" and writes the real table.
console.log(await checkout({ id: "ord_1", totalCents: 4250 }));
console.log([...paymentsTable]);
Respects
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number };

// Declared by the code that needs it, in the business code's own words.
type CheckoutDeps = {
  charge: (cents: number) => Promise<string>;
  recordPayment: (orderId: string, chargeId: string) => void;
};

function createCheckout({ charge, recordPayment }: CheckoutDeps) {
  return async function checkout(order: Order): Promise<string> {
    const chargeId = await charge(order.totalCents);
    recordPayment(order.id, chargeId);
    return `${order.id} paid with ${chargeId}`;
  };
}

// Composition root. Production passes the Stripe client and the database;
// a test passes these in-memory fakes and asserts on `payments`.
const payments = new Map<string, string>();
const checkout = createCheckout({
  charge: async (cents) => `ch_${cents}`,
  recordPayment: (orderId, chargeId) => payments.set(orderId, chargeId),
});

console.log(await checkout({ id: "ord_1", totalCents: 4250 }));
console.log([...payments]);
Result
ord_1 paid with ch_4250
[ [ 'ord_1', 'ch_4250' ] ]

Composition over inheritance

Wrap a function in functions of the same type, and every combination — and order — of behaviours is one expression.

Inheritance
type Product = { id: string; name: string };

class ProductApi {
  calls = 0;
  async product(id: string): Promise<Product> {
    this.calls++;
    return { id, name: `Product ${id}` };
  }
}

class CachedProductApi extends ProductApi {
  #cache = new Map<string, Product>();
  override async product(id: string): Promise<Product> {
    const hit = this.#cache.get(id);
    if (hit) return hit;
    const product = await super.product(id);
    this.#cache.set(id, product);
    return product;
  }
}

// Logged but not cached? Cached and retried? One subclass per combination.
class LoggedCachedProductApi extends CachedProductApi {
  readonly log: string[] = [];
  override async product(id: string): Promise<Product> {
    this.log.push(`get ${id}`);
    return super.product(id);
  }
}

const api = new LoggedCachedProductApi();
await api.product("p1");
await api.product("p1");
console.log(api.log, "network calls:", api.calls);
Composition
type Product = { id: string; name: string };
type ProductSource = (id: string) => Promise<Product>;

function withCache(source: ProductSource): ProductSource {
  const cache = new Map<string, Product>();
  return async (id) => {
    const hit = cache.get(id);
    if (hit) return hit;
    const product = await source(id);
    cache.set(id, product);
    return product;
  };
}

function withLog(source: ProductSource, log: string[]): ProductSource {
  return (id) => {
    log.push(`get ${id}`);
    return source(id);
  };
}

let calls = 0;
const fromNetwork: ProductSource = async (id) => {
  calls++;
  return { id, name: `Product ${id}` };
};

const log: string[] = [];
const product = withLog(withCache(fromNetwork), log);   // any combination, any order
await product("p1");
await product("p1");
console.log(log, "network calls:", calls);
Result
[ 'get p1', 'get p1' ] network calls: 1

Related design principles

Each one is a trade-off; say when you would break it.

  • DRY — one source of truth for each piece of knowledge; but prefer duplication over the wrong abstraction, and wait for the third copy.
  • KISS — the plain function beats the generic framework; a switch over a closed union beats a plugin system nobody plugs into.
  • YAGNI — do not add a type parameter or an interface until a second caller needs it.
  • Composition over inheritance — wrap functions, spread objects, pass collaborators in; keep extends for framework base classes you do not own.
  • Law of Demeter — order.customer.address.country.code couples you to four shapes; ask for shippingCountry(order) or take the value as a parameter.
  • Tell, don't ask — call cart.applyCoupon(code) rather than reading its fields and deciding outside.
  • SOLID as ceremony — an IUserService interface with exactly one class behind it is not Dependency Inversion; a function parameter is.
  • In React or Redux terms: a reducer per slice is SRP, a hook that takes its dependencies is DIP, and composing components is composition over inheritance.

Functional Programming in TypeScript

Pure functions over immutable data, typed pipe and curry, Option and Result as discriminated unions, lazy iterators and memoization — with the trade-offs.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.6
  • node >=22.18
  • any ES2025 engine (iterator helpers); the examples run on Node.js

Sources: More on Functions — TypeScript Handbook · Narrowing — TypeScript Handbook · Array — MDN

Core ideas

TypeScript is multi-paradigm; use these where they make code easier to test and reason about.

  • Pure function — same input, same output, no observable side effects. Trivially testable, safe to cache, safe to run twice.
  • Immutability — const bindings, readonly types, and new values via spread instead of mutation. JavaScript objects are references, so this is a discipline the types enforce, not a language default.
  • Functions are values — pass them, return them, store them in a Record; a callback type is the lightest interface there is.
  • Declarative — say what you want (filter, map, groupBy), not the loop mechanics.
  • Algebraic data types — an object type is AND, a union is OR. A discriminated union with an exhaustive switch makes illegal states unrepresentable.
  • Push effects to the edges — a pure core decides, a thin shell does the I/O (fetch, DOM, Date.now()).
  • Libraries such as fp-ts and Effect go much further; the patterns below need none of them.

Imperative → declarative

The declarative version names each step, has no mutable accumulator to get wrong, and leaves orders untouched.

Imperative
type Order = { customer: string; status: "placed" | "delivered" | "cancelled"; totalCents: number };
const orders: Order[] = [
  { customer: "ada", status: "delivered", totalCents: 4250 },
  { customer: "grace", status: "cancelled", totalCents: 9900 },
  { customer: "linus", status: "placed", totalCents: 1500 },
  { customer: "ada", status: "placed", totalCents: 1500 },
  { customer: "grace", status: "delivered", totalCents: 3000 },
];

const totals: Record<string, number> = {};
for (const order of orders) {
  if (order.status !== "cancelled") {
    totals[order.customer] = (totals[order.customer] ?? 0) + order.totalCents;
  }
}

const entries: [string, number][] = [];
for (const customer in totals) entries.push([customer, totals[customer]!]);
entries.sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]);
const topCustomers: string[] = [];
for (let i = 0; i < entries.length && i < 2; i++) {
  topCustomers.push(`${entries[i]![0]}: ${entries[i]![1]}`);
}

console.log(topCustomers);
Declarative
type Order = { customer: string; status: "placed" | "delivered" | "cancelled"; totalCents: number };
const orders: readonly Order[] = [
  { customer: "ada", status: "delivered", totalCents: 4250 },
  { customer: "grace", status: "cancelled", totalCents: 9900 },
  { customer: "linus", status: "placed", totalCents: 1500 },
  { customer: "ada", status: "placed", totalCents: 1500 },
  { customer: "grace", status: "delivered", totalCents: 3000 },
];

const sum = (values: readonly number[]) => values.reduce((total, n) => total + n, 0);
const isActive = (order: Order) => order.status !== "cancelled";

const byCustomer = Map.groupBy(orders.filter(isActive), (order) => order.customer);
const topCustomers = [...byCustomer]
  .map(([customer, list]) => ({ customer, totalCents: sum(list.map((o) => o.totalCents)) }))
  .toSorted((a, b) => b.totalCents - a.totalCents)
  .slice(0, 2)
  .map(({ customer, totalCents }) => `${customer}: ${totalCents}`);

console.log(topCustomers);
Result
[ 'ada: 5750', 'grace: 3000' ]

  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts

Higher-order functions to know cold

Prefer the copying methods (toSorted, toReversed, with) — sort and reverse mutate in place.

FunctionWhat it doesExample
maptransform each elementorders.map((o) => o.totalCents)
filterkeep matches; since TS 5.5 an inferred type predicate narrows the resultids.filter((id) => id !== undefined) is string[]
flatMapmap, then flatten one level; return [] to drop an elementorders.flatMap((o) => o.items)
reducefold to one value; always pass the initial valueitems.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.cents, 0)
Object.groupBy / Map.groupBybucket by a key (ES2024)Object.groupBy(orders, (o) => o.status)
toSorted / toReversed / withcopying sort, reverse and index assignment (ES2023)orders.toSorted((a, b) => a.totalCents - b.totalCents)
find / findLastfirst or last match, else undefinedorders.findLast((o) => o.status === "placed")
some / everyshort-circuiting predicatesitems.every((i) => i.inStock)
Object.entries / fromEntriesmap over an object's keys and valuesObject.fromEntries(Object.entries(prices).map(([k, v]) => [k, v * 2]))
Array.frombuild an array from a length and a functionArray.from({ length: 3 }, (_, i) => i + 1)
iterator helperslazy map, filter, take, drop, toArray on any iterator (ES2025)ids.values().filter(isActive).take(10).toArray()

pipe, compose and currying — with types that flow

Overloads give pipe a checked type at every step — add one overload per extra step (libraries go to about 20), and expect a wrong step's error to point at its neighbour; currying fixes the first argument now and takes the rest later.

// Left to right: each step's input is the previous step's output, checked by the compiler.
function pipe<A, B>(ab: (a: A) => B): (a: A) => B;
function pipe<A, B, C>(ab: (a: A) => B, bc: (b: B) => C): (a: A) => C;
function pipe<A, B, C, D>(ab: (a: A) => B, bc: (b: B) => C, cd: (c: C) => D): (a: A) => D;
function pipe(...steps: Array<(value: unknown) => unknown>) {
  return (input: unknown) => steps.reduce((value, step) => step(value), input);
}

// Right to left, as in mathematics: compose(f, g)(x) === f(g(x)).
const compose = <A, B, C>(f: (b: B) => C, g: (a: A) => B) => (a: A): C => f(g(a));

const normalize = (query: string) => query.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, " ");
const tokenize = (query: string) => query.split(" ");
const dropStopWords = (tokens: string[]) => tokens.filter((t) => !["the", "a", "of"].includes(t));

const searchTerms = pipe(normalize, tokenize, dropStopWords);    // (query: string) => string[]
console.log(searchTerms("  The   History of  TypeScript "));

const countTerms = compose((terms: string[]) => terms.length, searchTerms);
console.log(countTerms("a cup of coffee"));

// Currying: a two-argument function becomes a chain of one-argument functions.
const curry = <A, B, R>(fn: (a: A, b: B) => R) => (a: A) => (b: B): R => fn(a, b);
const addTax = (rate: number, cents: number) => Math.round(cents * (1 + rate));

const withSpanishVat = curry(addTax)(0.21);                     // (b: number) => number
const withGermanVat = addTax.bind(null, 0.19);                  // partial application, also typed
console.log([1000, 2500].map(withSpanishVat), withGermanVat(1000));
Result
[ 'history', 'typescript' ]
2
[ 1210, 3025 ] 1190

Option and Result as discriminated unions

map and flatMap chain the happy path and carry the first failure through untouched — no try, no null checks in between.

type Option<T> = { kind: "some"; value: T } | { kind: "none" };
type Result<T, E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

const none: Option<never> = { kind: "none" };

function some<T>(value: T): Option<T> { return { kind: "some", value }; }
function ok<T>(value: T): Result<T, never> { return { ok: true, value }; }
function err<E>(error: E): Result<never, E> { return { ok: false, error }; }

const map = <T, U, E>(r: Result<T, E>, f: (value: T) => U): Result<U, E> => (r.ok ? ok(f(r.value)) : r);
const flatMap = <T, U, E, F>(r: Result<T, E>, f: (value: T) => Result<U, F>): Result<U, E | F> =>
  r.ok ? f(r.value) : r;
const okOr = <T, E>(o: Option<T>, error: E): Result<T, E> => (o.kind === "some" ? ok(o.value) : err(error));

type LineError = { kind: "unknown-sku"; sku: string } | { kind: "bad-quantity"; raw: string };

const catalog = new Map([["mug", 1200], ["lamp", 9900]]);
const priceOf = (sku: string): Option<number> => {
  const price = catalog.get(sku);
  return price === undefined ? none : some(price);
};

const parseQuantity = (raw: string): Result<number, LineError> =>
  /^[1-9]\d*$/.test(raw) ? ok(Number(raw)) : err({ kind: "bad-quantity", raw });
const unknownSku = (sku: string): LineError => ({ kind: "unknown-sku", sku });

const lineTotal = (sku: string, rawQuantity: string) =>
  flatMap(okOr(priceOf(sku), unknownSku(sku)), (price) =>
    map(parseQuantity(rawQuantity), (quantity) => price * quantity));

for (const [sku, quantity] of [["mug", "2"], ["vase", "2"], ["mug", "two"]] as const) {
  const line = lineTotal(sku, quantity);
  console.log(line.ok ? `ok ${line.value}` : `error ${line.error.kind}`);
}

// Day to day, Option is just `T | undefined`, read with `?.` and `??`:
console.log(catalog.get("vase")?.toFixed(2) ?? "not sold");
Result
ok 2400
error unknown-sku
error bad-quantity
not sold

Make illegal states unrepresentable

Three independent fields allow eight shapes, most of them nonsense; a union allows exactly the states the screen can be in.

Flags
type Order = { id: string };
type OrdersState = { isLoading: boolean; orders: Order[]; error?: string };

function render(state: OrdersState): string {
  if (state.isLoading) return "spinner";
  if (state.error) return `error: ${state.error}`;   // and if orders are set too?
  if (state.orders.length === 0) return "empty";      // never loaded, or loaded nothing?
  return `${state.orders.length} orders`;
}

const states: OrdersState[] = [
  { isLoading: true, orders: [] },
  { isLoading: false, orders: [], error: "offline" },
  { isLoading: false, orders: [{ id: "A-1" }, { id: "A-2" }] },
  { isLoading: false, orders: [] },
];

for (const state of states) console.log(render(state));

// Compiles, and means nothing:
export const nonsense: OrdersState = { isLoading: true, orders: [{ id: "A-1" }], error: "offline" };
Union
type Order = { id: string };
type OrdersState =
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "failed"; error: string }
  | { status: "loaded"; orders: readonly Order[] };

function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`unhandled state: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

function render(state: OrdersState): string {
  switch (state.status) {
    case "loading": return "spinner";
    case "failed": return `error: ${state.error}`;
    case "loaded": return state.orders.length === 0 ? "empty" : `${state.orders.length} orders`;
    default: return assertNever(state);   // add a state and this line stops compiling
  }
}

const states: OrdersState[] = [
  { status: "loading" },
  { status: "failed", error: "offline" },
  { status: "loaded", orders: [{ id: "A-1" }, { id: "A-2" }] },
  { status: "loaded", orders: [] },
];

for (const state of states) console.log(render(state));

// @ts-expect-error — a loading state cannot carry orders or an error
export const nonsense: OrdersState = { status: "loading", orders: [{ id: "A-1" }], error: "offline" };
Result
spinner
error: offline
2 orders
empty

readonly, as const and structural sharing

readonly is checked at compile time and free at run time; an update copies only the path it changes and shares the rest.

type Item = { readonly sku: string; readonly quantity: number };
type Cart = Readonly<{ id: string; items: readonly Item[] }>;

const SHIPPING_CENTS = { standard: 499, express: 1299 } as const;   // readonly, literal types

type ShippingSpeed = keyof typeof SHIPPING_CENTS;                  // "standard" | "express"

function setQuantity(cart: Cart, sku: string, quantity: number): Cart {
  return {
    ...cart,
    items: cart.items.map((item) => (item.sku === sku ? { ...item, quantity } : item)),
  };
}

const before: Cart = { id: "c1", items: [{ sku: "mug", quantity: 1 }, { sku: "lamp", quantity: 1 }] };
const after = setQuantity(before, "mug", 3);

console.log(before.items[0]?.quantity, after.items[0]?.quantity);   // the old value is intact
console.log(before.items[1] === after.items[1]);                   // unchanged item is shared
console.log(before === after, before.items === after.items);        // changed path is new
console.log(after.items.toSorted((a, b) => a.sku.localeCompare(b.sku)).map((i) => i.sku));

const speed: ShippingSpeed = "express";
console.log(SHIPPING_CENTS[speed]);

// `readonly` vanishes at run time; Object.freeze enforces it there too (shallowly).
const defaults = Object.freeze({ currency: "EUR", taxRate: 0.21 });
try {
  // @ts-expect-error — taxRate is readonly
  defaults.taxRate = 0;
} catch (error) {
  console.log((error as Error).name);   // modules run in strict mode, so this throws
}

Laziness with generators and iterator helpers

A generator computes on demand, so an infinite source is safe; iterator helpers chain over it without building intermediate arrays.

function* orderIds(): Generator<string> {
  for (let n = 1; ; n++) yield `ord_${n}`;     // infinite: only safe because nothing runs until pulled
}

let loaded = 0;

function loadOrder(id: string) {
  loaded++;                                     // stand-in for a lookup
  return { id, totalCents: Number(id.slice(4)) * 1000 };
}

const firstThreeLarge = orderIds()
  .map(loadOrder)
  .filter((order) => order.totalCents >= 3000)
  .take(3)
  .toArray();

console.log(firstThreeLarge.map((order) => order.id), "loaded:", loaded);

// The eager version must load everything before it can slice.
loaded = 0;
const ids = Array.from({ length: 100 }, (_, i) => `ord_${i + 1}`);
const eager = ids.map(loadOrder).filter((order) => order.totalCents >= 3000).slice(0, 3);
console.log(eager.length, "loaded:", loaded);

// Built-in iterators (Set, Map, arrays' .values()) already have the helpers;
// Iterator.from wraps a hand-written one that lacks them, such as a cursor from an older library.
let page = 0;
const cursor = {
  next: () => (page < 3 ? { done: false, value: `page ${++page}` } : { done: true, value: undefined }),
};

console.log(Iterator.from(cursor).drop(1).toArray());

Memoization

Only a pure function can be cached safely; memoizing an async function caches the promise, which also dedupes concurrent calls.

function memoize<Args extends unknown[], R>(
  fn: (...args: Args) => R,
  keyOf: (...args: Args) => string = (...args) => JSON.stringify(args),
): (...args: Args) => R {
  const cache = new Map<string, R>();
  return (...args) => {
    const key = keyOf(...args);
    if (cache.has(key)) return cache.get(key)!;
    const value = fn(...args);
    cache.set(key, value);
    return value;
  };
}

let computed = 0;

function shippingQuoteCents(country: string, weightGrams: number): number {
  computed++;
  const base = country === "ES" ? 399 : 1299;
  return base + Math.ceil(weightGrams / 500) * 150;
}

const quote = memoize(shippingQuoteCents);
console.log(quote("ES", 1200), quote("ES", 1200), quote("FR", 1200), "computed:", computed);

let requests = 0;
const loadProfile = memoize(async (userId: string) => {
  requests++;                                   // stand-in for fetch(`/users/${userId}`)
  return { userId, name: "Ada" };
});

const [first, second] = await Promise.all([loadProfile("u1"), loadProfile("u1")]);
console.log(first === second, "requests:", requests);

// In production: bound the cache (LRU or a TTL), and evict a rejected promise so a retry can succeed.
Result

true requests: 1
