Trade-offs to say out loud

FP in TypeScript is a set of habits, not a framework — know where each one costs.

  • Pure functions need no mocks: pass inputs, assert on the output. Most of a reducer, a selector or a price calculation should look like this.
  • Immutable updates make change detection a reference check (prev !== next) — the model React and Redux are built on; a signal compares with === on set, so a mutated object does not notify (proxy-based stores such as Solid's, Vue's and MobX track mutation instead).
  • Copying is not free: spreading a 10 000-item array on every keystroke shows up in a profile. Use a Map, batch updates, or mutate a local copy you own.
  • readonly is compile-time only, and shallow by default; data from JSON.parse or another module can still be mutated.
  • Long point-free chains and deep generic helpers hurt readability, error messages and type-check time — name the intermediate steps.
  • Local mutation inside a function that returns a new value is still pure from the outside; a for loop that pushes into a fresh array is fine.
  • throw remains the right tool for bugs and broken invariants; use Result for failures the caller is expected to handle.

Architectural Approaches

MVC, MVVM, Flux and clean/hexagonal layering for web and Node apps — compared, then built without a framework so the shape is visible.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • any ES2023 engine; the examples run on Node.js

Sources: The Clean Architecture — Robert C. Martin · Hexagonal Architecture — Alistair Cockburn · Redux · Feature-Sliced Design

The common approaches compared

The question is always the same three things — which way data flows, where the logic lives, and what you can test without a browser or a server.

ApproachData flowWhere logic livesTestabilityBest for
MVC (server)request → controller → model → view templatecontrollers and models; controllers grow fatmedium: controllers need HTTP fakesserver-rendered apps, small APIs
MVVMview ⇄ view model (observable state) → modelview models: hooks, composables, Angular services, signal storeshigh: a view model is plain codecomponent UIs in React, Vue, Angular, Solid
Flux / Reduxaction → reducer → one store → view → actionpure reducers; thunks or middleware for effectsvery high: reducers are pure functionsstate shared by many screens; undo, devtools, replay
Clean / hexagonaladapters → use cases → domain; dependencies point inwarddomain and use cases, free of frameworksvery high: swap adapters for in-memory oneslong-lived business rules, Node services, several front ends over one core
Route loaders and actionsthe route loads on the server, the component renders, a form posts backroute modules (React Router, Remix, Next.js server code)medium: needs a request to testdata-heavy web apps where the server owns the data
By feature: Feature-Sliced Design, vertical sliceseach feature (front end) or each request handler (back end) owns its UI, state and data accessinside the feature or the slicehigh: one feature's tests at a timegrowing teams; combines with any row above

MVVM done properly

The view model owns state and logic, takes its repository and error reporter as parameters, and knows nothing about the DOM — bind it in React with useSyncExternalStore(vm.subscribe, vm.getState).

type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number };
type OrdersViewState = { status: "loading" } | { status: "failed"; message: string }
  | { status: "loaded"; rows: string[]; total: string };

const eur = (cents: number) => `€${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)}`;   // Intl.NumberFormat in a real app

function createOrdersViewModel(repository: { list(): Promise<Order[]> }, report: (error: unknown) => void) {
  let state: OrdersViewState = { status: "loading" };
  let latest = 0;                                    // only the newest load may write (next card)
  const listeners = new Set<() => void>();

  const set = (next: OrdersViewState) => {
    state = next;
    listeners.forEach((notify) => notify());
  };

  return {
    getState: () => state,
    subscribe(notify: () => void) {
      listeners.add(notify);
      return () => listeners.delete(notify);
    },
    async load() {
      const request = ++latest;
      set({ status: "loading" });
      try {
        const orders = await repository.list();
        if (request !== latest) return;
        const total = eur(orders.reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.totalCents, 0));
        set({ status: "loaded", rows: orders.map((o) => `${o.id} ${eur(o.totalCents)}`), total });
      } catch (error) {
        report(error);                               // the cause, for diagnostics
        if (request === latest) set({ status: "failed", message: "Could not load your orders." });
      }
    },
  };
}

const replies = [() => Promise.resolve([{ id: "A-1", totalCents: 4250 }, { id: "A-2", totalCents: 1500 }]),
  () => Promise.reject<Order[]>(new Error("503 Service Unavailable"))];
const vm = createOrdersViewModel({ list: () => replies.shift()!() },
  (error) => console.log("reported:", String(error)));

vm.subscribe(() => console.log(JSON.stringify(vm.getState())));   // the view: renders on each change
await vm.load();
await vm.load();                                     // the refresh fails

Stale responses: only the newest request may write

Requests overlap whenever the user is faster than the network, so a view model numbers each one and drops any answer that is no longer the newest (aborting the superseded fetch as well saves the bandwidth).

// A search box's view model: one request per keystroke, and the answers can arrive in any order.
function createSearchViewModel(search: (query: string) => Promise<string[]>, show: (text: string) => void) {
  let latest = 0;
  return {
    async onInput(query: string) {
      const request = ++latest;
      const results = await search(query);
      if (request !== latest) return;                // a newer query was typed: this answer is stale
      show(`${query} → ${results.join(", ")}`);
    },
  };
}

// A fake backend whose replies the demo releases by hand, newest first.
const pending = new Map<string, PromiseWithResolvers<string[]>>();
function search(query: string): Promise<string[]> {
  const reply = Promise.withResolvers<string[]>();
  pending.set(query, reply);
  return reply.promise;
}

const vm = createSearchViewModel(search, (text) => console.log("shown:", text));
const typing = [vm.onInput("mu"), vm.onInput("mug")];

pending.get("mug")!.resolve(["mug", "travel mug"]);              // the newer query answers first…
pending.get("mu")!.resolve(["mug", "muffin tin", "mustard"]);    // …the older one lands late: dropped
await Promise.all(typing);
console.log("rendered once, for the newest query");
Result

rendered once, for the newest query

The clean core: a repository and a use case

The domain declares the repository type it needs and adapters outside implement it, so dependencies point inward and the core runs with an in-memory adapter.

// ---- domain: no fetch, no SQL, no framework ----
type OrderState = { kind: "placed" } | { kind: "shipped" } | { kind: "cancelled"; at: string };
type Order = { id: string; totalCents: number; state: OrderState };
type OrderRepository = {                          // declared BY the domain, implemented outside it
  byId(id: string): Promise<Order | undefined>;
  save(order: Order): Promise<void>;
};

type CancelResult = { ok: true; order: Order } | { ok: false; reason: "not-found" | "not-cancellable" };

// A use case is one verb, with its dependencies passed in.
function makeCancelOrder(deps: { orders: OrderRepository; now: () => Date }) {
  return async function cancelOrder(id: string): Promise<CancelResult> {
    const order = await deps.orders.byId(id);
    if (!order) return { ok: false, reason: "not-found" };
    if (order.state.kind !== "placed") return { ok: false, reason: "not-cancellable" };
    const cancelled: Order = { ...order, state: { kind: "cancelled", at: deps.now().toISOString() } };
    await deps.orders.save(cancelled);
    return { ok: true, order: cancelled };
  };
}

// ---- data layer: one adapter per technology (SQL, REST, and in-memory for tests) ----
function inMemoryOrders(seed: Order[]): OrderRepository {
  const rows = new Map(seed.map((order) => [order.id, order]));
  return {
    byId: async (id) => rows.get(id),
    save: async (order) => {
      rows.set(order.id, order);
    },
  };
}

// ---- composition root: the only place that knows both sides ----
const orders = inMemoryOrders([
  { id: "A-1", totalCents: 4250, state: { kind: "placed" } },
  { id: "A-2", totalCents: 1500, state: { kind: "shipped" } },
]);

const cancelOrder = makeCancelOrder({ orders, now: () => new Date("2026-11-16T09:30:00Z") });

for (const id of ["A-1", "A-2", "A-9"]) {
  const result = await cancelOrder(id);
  if (result.ok) console.log(id, "cancelled at", JSON.stringify(result.order.state));
  else console.log(id, "refused:", result.reason);
}

Hexagonal in Node: HTTP is just an adapter

The HTTP handler translates a request into a use-case call and the result into a status code; swap it for a CLI or a queue consumer and the core does not change.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { createServer, type IncomingMessage, type ServerResponse } from "node:http";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";

// The core (from the use-case card), reduced to its signature and an in-memory store.
type CancelResult = { ok: true; id: string } | { ok: false; reason: "not-found" | "not-cancellable" };
const states = new Map([["A-1", "placed"], ["A-2", "shipped"]]);

async function cancelOrder(id: string): Promise<CancelResult> {
  const state = states.get(id);
  if (state !== "placed") return { ok: false, reason: state === undefined ? "not-found" : "not-cancellable" };
  states.set(id, "cancelled");
  return { ok: true, id };
}

// The driving adapter owns everything HTTP: routes, methods, status codes, JSON.
const STATUS = { "not-found": 404, "not-cancellable": 409 } as const;

async function handle(request: IncomingMessage, response: ServerResponse): Promise<void> {
  const match = /^\/orders\/([\w-]+)\/cancel$/.exec(request.url ?? "");
  if (request.method !== "POST" || !match) {
    response.writeHead(404).end();
    return;
  }
  const result = await cancelOrder(match[1]!);
  response.writeHead(result.ok ? 200 : STATUS[result.reason], { "content-type": "application/json" });
  response.end(JSON.stringify(result.ok ? { id: result.id, state: "cancelled" } : { error: result.reason }));
}

// A throw in the core becomes a 500, not an unhandled rejection that kills the process.
const server = createServer((request, response) => {
  handle(request, response).catch((error: unknown) => {
    console.error(error);
    if (!response.headersSent) response.writeHead(500);
    response.end();
  });
});

await once(server.listen(0, "127.0.0.1"), "listening");
const { port } = server.address() as AddressInfo;

for (const id of ["A-1", "A-1", "A-9"]) {
  const response = await fetch(`http://127.0.0.1:${port}/orders/${id}/cancel`, { method: "POST" });
  console.log(response.status, await response.text());
}

server.close();
server.closeAllConnections();   // fetch keeps connections alive; let the process exit now
Result
200 {"id":"A-1","state":"cancelled"}
409 {"error":"not-cancellable"}
404 {"error":"not-found"}

Routing as its own concern

Routes are a union of values: views ask to go to { name: "order", id }, and only the router knows URLs, encoding, guards and history.

type Route =
  | { name: "orders" }
  | { name: "order"; id: string }
  | { name: "checkout" }
  | { name: "sign-in"; returnTo: string }
  | { name: "not-found"; path: string };

function hrefFor(route: Route): string {
  switch (route.name) {
    case "orders": return "/orders";
    case "order": return `/orders/${encodeURIComponent(route.id)}`;
    case "checkout": return "/checkout";
    case "sign-in": return `/sign-in?returnTo=${encodeURIComponent(route.returnTo)}`;
    case "not-found": return route.path;
  }
}

// A guard is a pure function of the route and the session.
function guard(to: Route, session: { signedIn: boolean }): Route {
  if (to.name === "checkout" && !session.signedIn) return { name: "sign-in", returnTo: hrefFor(to) };
  return to;
}

// Views call navigate({ name: "order", id }); only the router knows URLs, guards and history.
// In a browser, `push` is history.pushState, and a popstate listener parses location.href.
function createRouter(session: { signedIn: boolean }, push: (href: string) => void) {
  return {
    navigate(to: Route) {
      push(hrefFor(guard(to, session)));
    },
  };
}

const session = { signedIn: false };
const router = createRouter(session, (href) => console.log("pushState", href));

router.navigate({ name: "order", id: "A/1 é" });     // encoded once, here
router.navigate({ name: "checkout" });               // guarded: sign in first, then come back
session.signedIn = true;
router.navigate({ name: "checkout" });
Result
pushState /orders/A%2F1%20%C3%A9
pushState /sign-in?returnTo=%2Fcheckout
pushState /checkout
Setup

  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts (top-level await needs a module: the .mts extension makes it one)
  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

Parsing links you did not write

Every URL a user can paste is hostile input, so parsing never throws — a malformed link becomes not-found — and returnTo can only point back at this site.

type Route =
  | { name: "orders" }
  | { name: "order"; id: string }
  | { name: "checkout" }
  | { name: "sign-in"; returnTo: string }
  | { name: "not-found"; path: string };

const SITE = "https://shop.example";                // in a browser: location.origin

// Only a same-origin path may come back, or sign-in becomes an open redirect; comparing origins
// also catches "//evil.example" and "/\evil.example".
function safeReturnTo(target: string | null): string {
  if (target === null || !URL.canParse(target, SITE)) return "/orders";
  const url = new URL(target, SITE);
  return url.origin === SITE ? url.pathname + url.search : "/orders";
}

// Links come from anywhere, so nothing here may throw: a malformed one is simply "not found".
function parseRoute(url: string): Route {
  if (!URL.canParse(url, SITE)) return { name: "not-found", path: url };
  const { pathname, searchParams } = new URL(url, SITE);
  const [section, id, ...rest] = pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean);
  if (section === "orders" && rest.length === 0) {
    if (id === undefined) return { name: "orders" };
    try {
      return { name: "order", id: decodeURIComponent(id) };
    } catch {
      return { name: "not-found", path: pathname };    // a broken %-escape
    }
  }
  if (section === "checkout" && id === undefined) return { name: "checkout" };
  if (section === "sign-in") return { name: "sign-in", returnTo: safeReturnTo(searchParams.get("returnTo")) };
  return { name: "not-found", path: pathname };
}

console.log(parseRoute("/orders/A%2F1%20%C3%A9"), parseRoute("/orders/%E0%A4%A"));

const targets = ["/checkout", "https://evil.example/phish", "//evil.example", "/\\evil.example", "http://["];
for (const target of targets) {
  const route = parseRoute(`/sign-in?returnTo=${encodeURIComponent(target)}`);
  console.log(target, "→", route.name === "sign-in" ? route.returnTo : route.name);
}
Result
{ name: 'order', id: 'A/1 é' } { name: 'not-found', path: '/orders/%E0%A4%A' }
/checkout → /checkout
https://evil.example/phish → /orders
//evil.example → /orders
/\evil.example → /orders
http://[ → /orders

Unidirectional flow without a library

A pure reducer returns the next state and a description of the effect; the store runs it and feeds the result back as an action, which says what it was computed for so a late answer cannot overwrite newer state.

type State = { items: string[]; quoteCents?: number; pending: boolean };
type Action =
  | { type: "itemAdded"; sku: string }
  | { type: "quoteRequested" }
  | { type: "quoteReceived"; skus: string[]; cents: number };   // says which cart it priced
type Effect = { type: "fetchQuote"; skus: string[] };            // a description, not a promise

function reduce(state: State, action: Action): [State, Effect?] {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "itemAdded":                                    // any quote, even one in flight, is now stale
      return [{ items: [...state.items, action.sku], pending: false }];
    case "quoteRequested":
      return [{ ...state, pending: true }, { type: "fetchQuote", skus: state.items }];
    case "quoteReceived":
      if (action.skus.join() !== state.items.join()) return [state];   // a late answer for an old cart
      return [{ ...state, pending: false, quoteCents: action.cents }];
  }
}

type Listener = (action: Action, state: State) => void;

function createStore(initial: State, runEffect: (effect: Effect) => Promise<Action>) {
  let state = initial;
  const listeners = new Set<Listener>();
  async function dispatch(action: Action): Promise<void> {
    const [next, effect] = reduce(state, action);
    state = next;
    listeners.forEach((listener) => listener(action, state));
    if (effect) await dispatch(await runEffect(effect));        // effects re-enter as actions
  }
  return { dispatch, subscribe: (listener: Listener) => { listeners.add(listener); } };
}

const quoteApi = async ({ skus }: Effect): Promise<Action> =>
  ({ type: "quoteReceived", skus, cents: skus.length * 499 });
const store = createStore({ items: ["mug"], pending: false }, quoteApi);
store.subscribe((action, state) => console.log(action.type.padEnd(14), JSON.stringify(state)));
const firstQuote = store.dispatch({ type: "quoteRequested" });
await store.dispatch({ type: "itemAdded", sku: "lamp" });        // the user keeps shopping meanwhile
await firstQuote;                                                 // its answer arrives late: ignored
await store.dispatch({ type: "quoteRequested" });
Result
quoteRequested {"items":["mug"],"pending":true}
itemAdded      {"items":["mug","lamp"],"pending":false}
quoteReceived  {"items":["mug","lamp"],"pending":false}
quoteRequested {"items":["mug","lamp"],"pending":true}
quoteReceived  {"items":["mug","lamp"],"pending":false,"quoteCents":998}
Setup

  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts (top-level await needs a module: the .mts extension makes it one)
  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

Feature-Sliced Design structure

Organise by what the product does, not by file type; each layer imports only the layers below it, and a change to checkout should touch one folder.

FolderHoldsMay import
app/the composition root: providers, router, store setup, validated configeverything
pages/ (or routes/)one module per route, composing widgets and featureswidgets, features, entities, shared
widgets/composite UI blocks reused across pages: a header, an order summary panelfeatures, entities, shared
features/checkout/one user-facing capability: its components, view model, use cases, API calls and testsentities, shared — never another feature
features/checkout/index.tsthe feature's public surface; everything else in the folder is private—
entities/order/domain types and pure rules several features shareshared
shared/design system, HTTP client, formatting — no business wordsnothing above it
enforcementSteiger (the FSD linter), import/no-restricted-paths or eslint-plugin-boundaries; package exports once features become packages—

How to answer "which architecture would you use?"

Constraints first, then the lightest structure that protects them.

  • Start with the constraints: team size, app lifetime, how much state is shared between screens, server- or client-rendered, how strict the testing bar is.
  • Name the invariants: one owner per piece of state, no business logic in components, routes as data, a domain that imports no framework.
  • Then pick the lightest fit — usually components with hooks or view models plus a repository per backend; a store (Redux Toolkit, Zustand) when many screens share state; a hexagonal core when the rules outlive the UI.
  • Say what you would not do: no clean-architecture layers on a three-screen app, no global store for state one component owns.
  • The seams matter more than the acronym: dependencies passed in, server state cached in one place (TanStack Query, RTK Query), navigation owned by the router.
  • Answering with one acronym and no trade-off is the actual failure mode — so is choosing by framework fashion rather than by the data flow.

Modularization Approaches

ES modules, package `exports` as the boundary, workspaces and project references, interface modules, lazy `import()` — most module graphs built in a temporary folder and run for real.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • Node.js ES modules; bundlers (Vite, esbuild, webpack) follow the same rules in the browser

Sources: Modules — TypeScript Handbook · Modules — Node.js packages · Project References — TypeScript

Why modularize, and the unit of modularity

Have concrete reasons ready; "cleanliness" is not one.

  • Enforced boundaries — a package's exports map blocks deep imports by package name (@shop/checkout/src/…) in Node and in tsc under node16, nodenext or bundler resolution. A relative path into the package folder or a tsconfig paths alias walks straight past it, so pair it with a lint rule (import/no-relative-packages, no-restricted-imports) in CI.
  • Faster feedback — type-check, test and lint only the packages a change affects (project references, --filter in pnpm, Nx or Turborepo affected runs).
  • Smaller bundles — a feature behind import() is a separate chunk the user downloads only when needed.
  • Ownership and reuse — a web app, a server and a CLI share one @shop/domain package; CODEOWNERS routes reviews per folder.
  • Units, smallest first: a file (an ES module), a folder with an index.ts surface, a package (package.json with exports), a workspace of packages, a TypeScript project (composite + references).
  • Cost: more package.json files, build wiring, version and dependency hygiene, and a dependency-injection seam wherever two packages meet.

What a barrel costs

Importing one name through an index that re-exports everything evaluates everything — in Node, in tests and in dev servers; bundlers can drop it only when the package declares "sideEffects": false.

import { mkdirSync, mkdtempSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { dirname, join } from "node:path";
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const root = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "barrels-"));
const write = (file: string, source: string) => {
  mkdirSync(dirname(join(root, file)), { recursive: true });
  writeFileSync(join(root, file), source);
};

// Two copies of one small catalog library, so each import starts cold.
for (const copy of ["a", "b"]) {
  write(`${copy}/price.mjs`, `console.log("  evaluated price");
  export const formatPrice = (c) => (c / 100).toFixed(2);`);
  write(`${copy}/search.mjs`, `console.log("  evaluated search, and its 300 kB index");
  export const search = () => [];`);
  write(`${copy}/index.mjs`, `export * from "./price.mjs"; export * from "./search.mjs";`);
}

write("direct.mjs", `import { formatPrice } from "./a/price.mjs"; console.log("  " + formatPrice(4250));`);
write("via-barrel.mjs", `import { formatPrice } from "./b/index.mjs";
console.log("  " + formatPrice(4250));`);

console.log("direct import:");
await import(pathToFileURL(join(root, "direct.mjs")).href);
console.log("through the barrel:");
await import(pathToFileURL(join(root, "via-barrel.mjs")).href);
rmSync(root, { recursive: true });
Result
direct import:
  evaluated price
  42.50
through the barrel:
  evaluated price
  evaluated search, and its 300 kB index
  42.50
Setup
  1. Node.js 22.18 or later (it runs .mts files directly by stripping the types)
  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts — it writes the small module graph to a temporary folder, imports it, and deletes it
  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

Circular imports fail by entry order

A cycle works or throws depending on which module is loaded first, so break it with a leaf module that imports nothing.

import { mkdirSync, mkdtempSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { dirname, join } from "node:path";
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const root = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "cycles-"));
const write = (file: string, source: string) => {
  mkdirSync(dirname(join(root, file)), { recursive: true });
  writeFileSync(join(root, file), source);
};

const load = (file: string) => import(pathToFileURL(join(root, file)).href);

// money ⇄ config, written twice so each entry point starts cold. It throws below only because
// `format` is a `const`: `function` declarations are initialised early, so a cycle can hide
// until someone changes one into a `const`.
for (const copy of ["a", "b"]) {
  write(`${copy}/money.mjs`, `import { CURRENCY } from "./config.mjs";
export const format = (cents) => (cents / 100).toFixed(2) + " " + CURRENCY;`);
  write(`${copy}/config.mjs`, `import { format } from "./money.mjs";
export const CURRENCY = "EUR";
export const FREE_SHIPPING = "Free over " + format(5000);`);
}

console.log("enter at config:", (await load("a/config.mjs")).FREE_SHIPPING);
await load("b/money.mjs").catch((error: unknown) => console.log("enter at money: ", String(error)));

// The fix: the shared constant moves to a leaf module, and the graph becomes a tree.
write("fixed/currency.mjs", `export const CURRENCY = "EUR";`);
write("fixed/money.mjs", `import { CURRENCY } from "./currency.mjs";
export const format = (cents) => (cents / 100).toFixed(2) + " " + CURRENCY;`);
write("fixed/shipping.mjs", `import { format } from "./money.mjs";
export const FREE_SHIPPING = "Free over " + format(5000);`);
const { format } = await load("fixed/money.mjs");
console.log("fixed:", format(5000), "|", (await load("fixed/shipping.mjs")).FREE_SHIPPING);
rmSync(root, { recursive: true });
Result
enter at config: Free over 50.00 EUR
enter at money:  ReferenceError: Cannot access 'format' before initialization
fixed: 50.00 EUR | Free over 50.00 EUR

  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts — it writes the small module graph to a temporary folder, imports it, and deletes it
  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

package.json `exports` is the enforcement mechanism

Only the subpaths listed in exports can be imported by package name — in Node, and in tsc with moduleResolution node16, nodenext or bundler; a relative path bypasses it, which is why a lint rule (import/no-relative-packages) closes the gap.

import { mkdirSync, mkdtempSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { dirname, join } from "node:path";
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const root = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "exports-"));
const write = (file: string, source: string) => {
  mkdirSync(dirname(join(root, file)), { recursive: true });
  writeFileSync(join(root, file), source);
};

const pkg = "node_modules/@shop/checkout";
write(`${pkg}/package.json`, JSON.stringify({
  name: "@shop/checkout",
  type: "module",
  // A TypeScript package puts a "types" condition first:
  // { "types": "./dist/index.d.ts", "default": "./dist/index.js" }
  exports: { ".": "./src/index.mjs", "./testing": "./src/testing.mjs" },
}));

write(`${pkg}/src/index.mjs`, `export { startCheckout } from "./flow.mjs";`);
write(`${pkg}/src/flow.mjs`, `export const startCheckout = (cartId) => "checkout for " + cartId;
export const retryPolicy = { attempts: 3 };   // internal: not in the public surface`);
write(`${pkg}/src/testing.mjs`, `export const fakeCheckout = () => "fake checkout";`);

write("app.mjs", `import { startCheckout } from "@shop/checkout";
import { fakeCheckout } from "@shop/checkout/testing";
console.log(startCheckout("cart_1"), "|", fakeCheckout());
try {
  await import("@shop/checkout/src/flow.mjs");
} catch (error) {
  console.log(error.code);
}
const bypass = await import("./node_modules/@shop/checkout/src/flow.mjs");   // a relative path is not checked
console.log("relative path bypass:", bypass.retryPolicy);`);

await import(pathToFileURL(join(root, "app.mjs")).href);
rmSync(root, { recursive: true });
Result
checkout for cart_1 | fake checkout
ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED
relative path bypass: { attempts: 3 }

Workspaces: packages linked by name

A workspace is packages linked by name into node_modules — npm and Yarn hoist the links to the root; pnpm links each package into its dependents' own node_modules, so an undeclared dependency fails to resolve.

import { mkdirSync, mkdtempSync, rmSync, symlinkSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { dirname, join } from "node:path";
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const root = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "workspace-"));
const write = (file: string, content: string | object) => {
  mkdirSync(dirname(join(root, file)), { recursive: true });
  writeFileSync(join(root, file), typeof content === "string" ? content : JSON.stringify(content, null, 2));
};

write("package.json", { name: "shop", private: true, workspaces: ["packages/*"] });
write("packages/catalog/package.json", { name: "@shop/catalog", type: "module", exports: "./index.mjs" });
write("packages/catalog/index.mjs", `export const featured = () => ["mug", "lamp"];`);
write("packages/web/package.json", {
  name: "@shop/web", type: "module", dependencies: { "@shop/catalog": "*" },
});

write("packages/web/main.mjs", `import { featured } from "@shop/catalog";
console.log("web shows", featured());`);

// The link `npm install` (or Yarn) creates in the ROOT node_modules. pnpm instead links it into
// packages/web/node_modules — so an undeclared dependency fails there instead of resolving by accident.
mkdirSync(join(root, "node_modules/@shop"), { recursive: true });
symlinkSync(join(root, "packages/catalog"), join(root, "node_modules/@shop/catalog"), "dir");

await import(pathToFileURL(join(root, "packages/web/main.mjs")).href);
rmSync(root, { recursive: true });
Result
web shows [ 'mug', 'lamp' ]
Setup
  1. Node.js 22.18 or later (it runs .mts files directly by stripping the types)
  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts — it lays out a two-package workspace in a temporary folder and creates the link npm install would
  3. In a real repository, npm install creates the links; with pnpm, declare the dependency as "@shop/catalog": "workspace:*" and list the packages in pnpm-workspace.yaml

Ran with Node 24.16.0, TypeScript 5.9.3 on 2026-11-16: the output matched the result shown.

Sources: workspaces — npm Docs · Workspaces — pnpm

Project references: `tsc -b` in dependency order

Each package is a composite project that references what it imports; tsc -b builds them in order, writes .d.ts for the dependents, and rebuilds only the projects whose inputs changed.

import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import { mkdirSync, mkdtempSync, rmSync, symlinkSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { createRequire } from "node:module";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { dirname, join } from "node:path";

const root = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "references-"));
const write = (file: string, content: string | object) => {
  mkdirSync(dirname(join(root, file)), { recursive: true });
  writeFileSync(join(root, file), typeof content === "string" ? content : JSON.stringify(content, null, 2));
};

const compilerOptions = { composite: true, module: "nodenext", rootDir: "src", outDir: "dist" };
write("packages/catalog/tsconfig.json", { compilerOptions, include: ["src"] });
write("packages/catalog/package.json", {
  name: "@shop/catalog",
  type: "module",
  exports: { ".": { types: "./dist/index.d.ts", default: "./dist/index.js" } },
});

write("packages/catalog/src/index.ts", `export const featured = (): string[] => ["mug", "lamp"];`);
write("packages/web/tsconfig.json",
  { compilerOptions, include: ["src"], references: [{ path: "../catalog" }] });
write("packages/web/package.json", { name: "@shop/web", type: "module" });
const writeMain = (verb: string) => write("packages/web/src/main.ts",
  `import { featured } from "@shop/catalog";\nconsole.log("web ${verb}", featured());`);
writeMain("shows");
mkdirSync(join(root, "node_modules/@shop"), { recursive: true });   // the link a workspace install makes
symlinkSync(join(root, "packages/catalog"), join(root, "node_modules/@shop/catalog"), "dir");

const tsc = createRequire(import.meta.url).resolve("typescript/lib/tsc.js");
const run = (...args: string[]) => execFileSync(process.execPath, args, { cwd: root, encoding: "utf8" });
const STATUS = /Project 'packages\/(\w+)\/tsconfig\.json' is (up to date|out of date)/g;
const build = () =>
  [...run(tsc, "-b", "packages/web", "--verbose").matchAll(STATUS)].map(([, p, s]) => `${p}: ${s}`);

console.log("first build:", build());                 // catalog first: web references it
console.log("no change:  ", build());
writeMain("lists");
console.log("web edited: ", build());
console.log(run("packages/web/dist/main.js").trim());
rmSync(root, { recursive: true });
Result
first build: [ 'catalog: out of date', 'web: out of date' ]
no change:   [ 'catalog: up to date', 'web: up to date' ]
web edited:  [ 'catalog: up to date', 'web: out of date' ]
web lists [ 'mug', 'lamp' ]
Setup
  1. Node.js 22.18 or later (it runs .mts files directly by stripping the types)
  2. npm i -D typescript — the snippet runs that package's tsc -b on a two-package workspace it writes to a temporary folder
  3. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts; in a real repository the same build is npx tsc -b

Interface modules and the composition root

Features depend on a types-only package, never on each other or on an implementation; the app's entry point is the one module that imports both sides.

// ── packages/catalog-api: the interface module — types only, no dependencies ──
type Product = { sku: string; name: string; priceCents: number };
type CatalogService = { related(sku: string): Promise<Product[]> };

// ── packages/checkout: `import type { CatalogService } from "@shop/catalog-api"` ──
// A type-only import is erased, so it adds no runtime edge (and no runtime cycle).
function createSuggestions(catalog: CatalogService) {
  return async (cartSkus: string[]) => {
    const candidates = await Promise.all(cartSkus.map((sku) => catalog.related(sku)));
    return [...new Set(candidates.flat().map((p) => p.name))];
  };
}

// ── packages/catalog-live: the heavy implementation (HTTP client, cache, retries) ──
function createLiveCatalog(getJson: (path: string) => Promise<Product[]>): CatalogService {
  return { related: (sku) => getJson(`/products/${encodeURIComponent(sku)}/related`) };
}

// ── apps/web/main.ts: the composition root ──
const fakeHttp = async (path: string): Promise<Product[]> =>
  path.includes("mug") ? [{ sku: "coaster", name: "Cork coaster", priceCents: 400 }] : [];
const suggestions = createSuggestions(createLiveCatalog(fakeHttp));
console.log(await suggestions(["mug-white", "lamp"]));

// ── a test or a Storybook story wires an in-memory catalog instead ──
const inMemory: CatalogService = {
  related: async () => [{ sku: "tray", name: "Oak tray", priceCents: 2500 }],
};

console.log(await createSuggestions(inMemory)(["anything"]));
Result
[ 'Cork coaster' ]
[ 'Oak tray' ]

  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

Lazy loading with dynamic import()

import() loads and evaluates a module the first time it is needed, and only once; bundlers turn each one into a separate chunk (React.lazy(() => import("./Checkout"))).

import { mkdtempSync, rmSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { tmpdir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const root = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "lazy-"));
writeFileSync(join(root, "pdf-export.mjs"), `console.log("loading the PDF exporter and its fonts");
export function exportPdf(orderId) { return "invoice-" + orderId + ".pdf"; }`);

type PdfExporter = { exportPdf(orderId: string): string };

// With a literal path, `await import("./pdf-export.js")` is typed for you; this path is built at run time.
const loadExporter = () => import(pathToFileURL(join(root, "pdf-export.mjs")).href) as Promise<PdfExporter>;

async function onDownloadInvoice(orderId: string): Promise<void> {
  const { exportPdf } = await loadExporter();
  console.log("downloaded", exportPdf(orderId));
}

console.log("app started");              // nothing PDF-related has been evaluated yet
await onDownloadInvoice("A-1");
await onDownloadInvoice("A-2");         // the module registry returns the same instance
rmSync(root, { recursive: true });
Result
app started
loading the PDF exporter and its fonts
downloaded invoice-A-1.pdf
downloaded invoice-A-2.pdf

Choosing a strategy

Start at the top and move down only when a concrete cost forces you to.

StrategyLooks likeUse when
Folders in one packagesrc/features/*, each with an index.ts surface, boundaries enforced by lintone app, one team — start here
Workspace packagespackages/* with exports, linked by npm, pnpm or Yarn workspacesa web app, a server or a CLI share code, and the boundary must hold
Project referencescomposite tsconfigs, references, tsc -btype-checking the whole repository has become slow
Monorepo task runnerNx or Turborepo over the workspacemany packages: cached, affected-only builds and tests
Published packagessemver releases to a registry, one package per concernreuse across repositories or organisations; adds release overhead
Micro-frontendsindependently deployed bundles, module federationteams that must deploy independently — and can pay the runtime and consistency cost

Pitfalls

Most module problems are graph problems; look at the graph before the code.

  • Barrels everywhere — every import of @/components evaluates the whole folder: slow tests, slow dev server, and cycles hidden behind one index.ts.
  • Cycles — they fail by entry order, so they pass locally and break in a test; find them with madge --circular or the import/no-cycle lint rule.
  • A shared/utils package everything depends on — it becomes the new monolith and invalidates every cache when it changes.
  • Feature imports feature — features are siblings; they meet in the app or through an interface package.
  • Two copies of a dependency (two Reacts, two zod schemas) — declare frameworks as peerDependencies and check npm ls react.
  • The dual package hazard — shipping CommonJS and ESM builds lets both load at once, with two copies of module state; prefer ESM-only packages.
  • Named exports over export default — one name everywhere, reliable auto-import and rename, and a typo is a compile error instead of a silently different local name.
  • Use import type (enforced by verbatimModuleSyntax) so type-only dependencies never become runtime edges.
  • Give each package its own tests and an exports map from day one; enforce the dependency graph in CI — documentation alone never holds.

TypeScript Engineering Best Practices

The habits that keep a TypeScript codebase honest in its second year — strict types, modelled errors, validated config, structured logs, disciplined async, and a review you can run in five minutes.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • any ES2023 engine; the examples run on Node.js

Sources: TSConfig Reference — TypeScript · TSDoc · typescript-eslint

The ten that matter most

If you say nothing else in a review, say these.

  • strict on, any out. Use unknown and narrow; every as, ! and @ts-expect-error carries a reason.
  • Make illegal states unrepresentable. A discriminated union beats four booleans and an optional error.
  • Parse at the boundary. Types vanish at run time: validate JSON, process.env, localStorage and form input once, then trust the type.
  • Inject what you do not own. The clock, fetch, storage and randomness are parameters, so tests need no patching.
  • Keep the public surface small. Export deliberately; a package's exports map and a folder's index.ts are promises.
  • Errors carry codes. Never throw "string"; keep the cause; map codes to user messages in one place.
  • One source of truth per piece of state; derive the rest instead of syncing copies.
  • No floating promises. Every promise is awaited, returned or handled; long work takes an AbortSignal.
  • Tests are part of the change — if it is hard to test, the dependencies are hidden.
  • Measure before optimising, and delete code — dead exports, expired flags and speculative abstractions all cost.

API design

Precise types in and out, an options object, private state, and a doc comment on every public member; both versions are classes, so the difference is the API, not the style (TSDoc tags are on the next card).

Don't
export class Cache {
  data = new Map<string, any>();      // storage is public and untyped
  ttl: number;
  clock: () => number;
  constructor(ttl: number, clock: () => number) {
    this.ttl = ttl;
    this.clock = clock;
  }
  get(key: string): any {
    const e = this.data.get(key);
    return e && e.exp > this.clock() ? e.val : null;   // null, undefined, or a value?
  }
  set(key: string, val: any, ttl?: number, overwrite = true): boolean {
    if (!overwrite && this.data.has(key)) return false;   // a flag that changes what set means
    this.data.set(key, { val, exp: this.clock() + (ttl ?? this.ttl) });
    return true;
  }
}

let time = 0;
const prices = new Cache(60_000, () => time);
prices.set("mug", 1200);
console.log(prices.get("mug"), prices.data.size);
time = 60_000;
console.log(prices.get("mug") ?? "expired");
Do
export type CacheOptions = {
  /** How long an entry stays fresh, in milliseconds. */
  ttlMs: number;
  /** The clock. Defaults to `Date.now`; pass a fake one in tests. */
  now?: () => number;
};

/** An in-memory cache whose entries expire after {@link CacheOptions.ttlMs}. */
export class TtlCache<V> {
  readonly #entries = new Map<string, { value: V; expiresAt: number }>();   // truly private
  readonly #ttlMs: number;
  readonly #now: () => number;
  constructor({ ttlMs, now = Date.now }: CacheOptions) {
    this.#ttlMs = ttlMs;
    this.#now = now;
  }
  /** The fresh value for `key`, or `undefined` when it is missing or expired. */
  get(key: string): V | undefined {
    const entry = this.#entries.get(key);
    return entry && entry.expiresAt > this.#now() ? entry.value : undefined;
  }
  /** Stores `value` under `key` for {@link CacheOptions.ttlMs}. */
  set(key: string, value: V): void {
    // The old per-call TTL and no-overwrite flag are gone on purpose: no caller needed them.
    this.#entries.set(key, { value, expiresAt: this.#now() + this.#ttlMs });
  }
  /** How many entries are stored, fresh or expired. */
  get size(): number {
    return this.#entries.size;
  }
}

let time = 0;
const prices = new TtlCache<number>({ ttlMs: 60_000, now: () => time });
prices.set("mug", 1200);
console.log(prices.get("mug"), prices.size);
time = 60_000;
console.log(prices.get("mug") ?? "expired");
Result
1200 1
expired

Documentation with TSDoc

TSDoc on an export shows on hover in every editor and feeds TypeDoc; @deprecated strikes the old name through at each call site, and typescript-eslint's no-deprecated rule flags it in CI.

type Order = { id: string; state: "placed" | "shipped" | "cancelled"; cancelReason?: string };
const orders = new Map<string, Order>([
  ["A-1", { id: "A-1", state: "placed" }],
  ["A-2", { id: "A-2", state: "shipped" }],
]);

/**
 * Cancels an order that has not shipped yet.
 *
 * @remarks
 * Idempotent: cancelling a cancelled order returns it unchanged. A shipped order has to go
 * through the returns flow instead.
 *
 * @param orderId - The order to cancel.
 * @param reason - Free text for the support team; never shown to the customer.
 * @returns The order, now in the `cancelled` state.
 * @throws `Error` with `code: "not-found"` when no order has that id.
 * @throws `Error` with `code: "not-cancellable"` when the order has already shipped.
 *
 * @example
 * ```ts
 * const order = await cancelOrder("A-1", "customer changed their mind");
 * ```
 */

export async function cancelOrder(orderId: string, reason: string): Promise<Order> {
  const order = orders.get(orderId);
  if (!order) throw Object.assign(new Error(`${orderId} does not exist`), { code: "not-found" });
  if (order.state === "cancelled") return order;
  if (order.state === "shipped") {
    throw Object.assign(new Error(`${orderId} has shipped`), { code: "not-cancellable" });
  }
  const cancelled: Order = { ...order, state: "cancelled", cancelReason: reason };
  orders.set(orderId, cancelled);
  return cancelled;
}

/** @deprecated Use {@link cancelOrder}, which records a reason. Removed in v3. */
export const cancel = (orderId: string) => cancelOrder(orderId, "not given");

const order = await cancelOrder("A-1", "customer changed their mind");
console.log(order.state, "—", order.cancelReason, "| idempotent:", (await cancel("A-1")) === order);
const codeOf = (error: unknown) => (error instanceof Error && "code" in error ? error.code : error);
console.log(await cancelOrder("A-2", "late").catch(codeOf), await cancelOrder("A-9", "typo").catch(codeOf));
Result
cancelled — customer changed their mind | idempotent: true
not-cancellable not-found

Model errors; don't stringly-type them

Translate transport failures into a small set of codes at the boundary, keep the original as cause, and map codes to user messages in one exhaustive table.

type ErrorCode = "offline" | "unauthorized" | "not-found" | "server";

class ApiError extends Error {
  override readonly name = "ApiError";
  readonly code: ErrorCode;
  constructor(code: ErrorCode, message: string, options?: ErrorOptions) {
    super(message, options);
    this.code = code;
  }
}

// At the boundary, translate transport failures into the codes the app understands.
type Fetch = (url: string) => Promise<Response>;

async function getOrder(fetchFn: Fetch, id: string): Promise<{ status: string }> {
  const response = await fetchFn(`https://api.shop.example/orders/${id}`).catch((cause: unknown) => {
    throw new ApiError("offline", "network request failed", { cause });
  });
  if (response.status === 401) throw new ApiError("unauthorized", "session expired");
  if (response.status === 404) throw new ApiError("not-found", `order ${id} does not exist`);
  if (!response.ok) throw new ApiError("server", `HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();   // in production, validate the body with a schema here
}

// What the USER sees, in one place. A Record over the union stops compiling when a code is added.
const USER_MESSAGE: Record<ErrorCode, string> = {
  offline: "You appear to be offline.",
  unauthorized: "Please sign in again.",
  "not-found": "We couldn't find that order.",
  server: "Something went wrong. Try again.",
};

const fakeFetch = async (url: string) => {
  if (url.endsWith("/A-1")) return Response.json({ status: "shipped" });
  if (url.endsWith("/A-2")) return new Response(null, { status: 503 });
  throw new TypeError("fetch failed");
};

for (const id of ["A-1", "A-2", "A-3"]) {
  const outcome = await getOrder(fakeFetch, id).then((order) => order.status, (error: unknown) => {
    if (!(error instanceof ApiError)) throw error;           // `unknown`: narrow before use
    const cause = error.cause instanceof Error ? ` (cause: ${error.cause.message})` : "";
    return `${error.code}: ${USER_MESSAGE[error.code]}${cause}`;
  });
  console.log(id, outcome);
}
Result
A-1 shipped
A-2 server: Something went wrong. Try again.
A-3 offline: You appear to be offline. (cause: fetch failed)

null and undefined discipline

Pick one convention for absence per codebase (many choose undefined, matching Map.get and optional properties), convert at the boundary, keep null where a wire format needs an explicit "cleared", default with ?? rather than ||, and narrow instead of asserting with !.

type Profile = { legalName: string; nickname?: string; address?: { city?: string }; tags?: string[] };

// `||` replaces every falsy value; `??` replaces only null and undefined.
const saved = { pageSize: 0, greeting: "" };
console.log(saved.pageSize || 20, saved.pageSize ?? 20);
console.log(JSON.stringify(saved.greeting || "Hello"), JSON.stringify(saved.greeting ?? "Hello"));

// This codebase's convention is `undefined` (it matches Map.get and optional properties),
// so the API's null is converted once, where the data enters.
type ApiProfile = { legalName: string; nickname: string | null };
const fromApi = JSON.parse('{"legalName":"Ada Lovelace","nickname":null}') as ApiProfile;
const profile: Profile = { legalName: fromApi.legalName, nickname: fromApi.nickname ?? undefined };

const displayName = (p: Profile) => p.nickname ?? p.legalName;
const city = (p: Profile) => p.address?.city?.toUpperCase() ?? "unknown";
const tagsOf = (p: Profile): readonly string[] => p.tags ?? [];   // callers never check for undefined
console.log(displayName(profile), city(profile), tagsOf(profile).length);

// The wire is where null earns its keep: JSON drops `undefined`, so only null can say "clear this field".
console.log(JSON.stringify({ nickname: undefined }), JSON.stringify({ nickname: null }));

// Map.get (and, with noUncheckedIndexedAccess, array[i] and record[key]) may be undefined:
// narrow it, don't `!` it.
const users = new Map([["u1", profile]]);
const user = users.get("u2");
console.log(user === undefined ? "u2: not found" : displayName(user));
Result
20 0
"Hello" ""
Ada Lovelace unknown 0
{} {"nickname":null}
u2: not found

Structured logging and diagnostics

The ideas pino gives you — one JSON object per line, levels, child loggers carrying request context, redaction, and errors with their stack and cause; pino itself writes numeric levels and epoch-millisecond times.

type Level = "debug" | "info" | "warn" | "error";
type Fields = Record<string, unknown>;
type Logger = Record<Level, (msg: string, fields?: Fields) => void> & { child: (context: Fields) => Logger };

const SEVERITY: Record<Level, number> = { debug: 10, info: 20, warn: 30, error: 40 };

// Top-level keys only, to stay short; pino redacts by path: redact: { paths: ["req.headers.authorization"] }.
const SECRET_KEY = /token|password|secret|authorization|cookie/i;

// Keep the stack: it is the field that tells you where a failure came from.
const serialize = (value: unknown): unknown => value instanceof Error
  ? { name: value.name, message: value.message, stack: value.stack, cause: serialize(value.cause) }
  : value;

type Sink = { minLevel: Level; now: () => string; write: (line: string) => void };

function createLogger(sink: Sink, context: Fields = {}): Logger {
  const at = (level: Level) => (msg: string, fields: Fields = {}) => {
    if (SEVERITY[level] < SEVERITY[sink.minLevel]) return;
    const entries = Object.entries({ ...context, ...fields })
      .map(([key, value]) => [key, SECRET_KEY.test(key) ? "[redacted]" : serialize(value)]);
    sink.write(JSON.stringify({ time: sink.now(), level, msg, ...Object.fromEntries(entries) }));
  };
  return { debug: at("debug"), info: at("info"), warn: at("warn"), error: at("error"),
    child: (extra) => createLogger(sink, { ...context, ...extra }) };
}

// Stacks hold paths and line numbers; this demo strips them only so that its output is reproducible.
const withoutStacks = (line: string) => line.replace(/,"stack":"(?:[^"\\]|\\.)*"/g, "");
const write = (line: string) => console.log(withoutStacks(line));
const logger = createLogger({ minLevel: "info", now: () => "2026-11-16T09:30:00.000Z", write });
const log = logger.child({ requestId: "req_7f3a", route: "POST /checkout" });
log.debug("cart loaded");                                   // below minLevel: dropped
log.info("payment authorised", { orderId: "A-1", amountCents: 4250, authorization: "Bearer eyJhbGci" });
const err = new Error("SMTP timeout", { cause: new Error("ETIMEDOUT") });
log.error("receipt email failed", { orderId: "A-1", err });
Result
{"time":"2026-11-16T09:30:00.000Z","level":"info","msg":"payment authorised","requestId":"req_7f3a","route":"POST /checkout","orderId":"A-1","amountCents":4250,"authorization":"[redacted]"}
{"time":"2026-11-16T09:30:00.000Z","level":"error","msg":"receipt email failed","requestId":"req_7f3a","route":"POST /checkout","orderId":"A-1","err":{"name":"Error","message":"SMTP timeout","cause":{"name":"Error","message":"ETIMEDOUT"}}}

Configuration, secrets and feature flags, validated at startup

Parse the environment once, at startup, into a frozen typed object — a bad deploy then fails on boot with every problem listed, not on the first request that reads the missing value.

import { z } from "zod";

const ConfigSchema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "production"]).default("development"),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65_535).default(3000),
  API_BASE_URL: z.url(),
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: z.string().startsWith("sk_"),          // from the secret store, never from git
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: z.stringbool().default(false),      // owner: payments; remove by 2027-03
});

type Config = z.infer<typeof ConfigSchema>;

function loadConfig(env: Record<string, string | undefined>): Readonly<Config> {
  const parsed = ConfigSchema.safeParse(env);               // unknown keys are dropped
  if (!parsed.success) throw new Error(`Invalid configuration:\n${z.prettifyError(parsed.error)}`);
  return Object.freeze(parsed.data);
}

// Production passes process.env; literals keep this example deterministic.
const config = loadConfig({
  API_BASE_URL: "https://api.shop.example",
  STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: "sk_test_example_only",
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: "true",
  PORT: "8080",
});

const flags = { newCheckout: config.FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT };   // read flags through one typed object
console.log(flags.newCheckout ? "new checkout" : "classic checkout");
console.log(JSON.stringify({ ...config, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: "[redacted]" }));   // the only view that is logged

try {
  loadConfig({ API_BASE_URL: "not a url", PORT: "eighty" });
} catch (error) {
  console.log((error as Error).message);
}
Result
new checkout
{"NODE_ENV":"development","PORT":8080,"API_BASE_URL":"https://api.shop.example","STRIPE_SECRET_KEY":"[redacted]","FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT":true}
Invalid configuration:
✖ Invalid input: expected number, received NaN
  → at PORT
✖ Invalid URL
  → at API_BASE_URL
✖ Invalid input: expected string, received undefined
  → at STRIPE_SECRET_KEY

Async practices

Bound the fan-out, stop starting work after the first failure, give every wait a deadline (AbortSignal.timeout, with an abortable wait written as on the Async/Await, Promises & Cancellation sheet), and let @typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises find the promises you missed.

// At most `limit` tasks at once. After the first failure no new task starts, and the caller hears
// about it only when the tasks already running have settled, so nothing is left floating.
async function mapWithConcurrency<T, R>(
  items: readonly T[], limit: number, task: (item: T) => Promise<R>,
): Promise<R[]> {
  const results = new Array<R>(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  let failed = false;
  const worker = async () => {
    while (!failed && next < items.length) {
      const index = next++;
      try {
        results[index] = await task(items[index]!);
      } catch (error) {
        failed = true;
        throw error;
      }
    }
  };
  const settled = await Promise.allSettled(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker));
  const failure = settled.find((outcome) => outcome.status === "rejected");
  if (failure) throw failure.reason;
  return results;
}

const started: string[] = [];
let inFlight = 0;
let peak = 0;

async function sendReceipt(orderId: string): Promise<string> {
  started.push(orderId);
  peak = Math.max(peak, ++inFlight);
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 10));   // stand-in for an email API call
  inFlight--;
  if (orderId === "A-4") throw new Error(`mailbox for ${orderId} is full`);
  return orderId;
}

const orderIds = Array.from({ length: 10 }, (_, i) => `A-${i + 1}`);
await mapWithConcurrency(orderIds, 3, sendReceipt).catch((error: unknown) => console.log(String(error)));
console.log("started", started.join(" "), "| at most", peak, "at once; none after the failure");
Result
Error: mailbox for A-4 is full
started A-1 A-2 A-3 A-4 A-5 A-6 | at most 3 at once; none after the failure

Performance checklist

Roughly in order of how often each one is the actual culprit — and measure first.

SymptomLook atFix
Slow first loadbundle visualizer, Lighthousesplit routes with import(), drop heavy dependencies, avoid barrel imports
Requests in seriesthe network waterfallstart independent requests together (Promise.all); prefetch on hover or route intent
Janky typing or scrollingPerformance panel, long tasks over 50 msdebounce input, virtualize long lists, move CPU work to a Web Worker
Too many React rendersReact DevTools Profilerstable props, narrow store selectors, split contexts; memo only where measured
Memory keeps growingheap snapshots, allocation timelineremove listeners (pass signal to addEventListener), clear timers, bound caches
Slow Node endpointnode --cpu-prof, a flame graphno sync I/O on the hot path; stream large bodies; cache what is pure
Event-loop stallsperf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay()chunk CPU work, or move it to worker_threads
Slow tsctsc --extendedDiagnostics, --generateTraceproject references, simpler conditional types, explicit return types on exports
Silent regressions—a budget in CI: bundle size, Lighthouse CI, a benchmark on the hot path

Project hygiene

What a healthy TypeScript repository has before anyone argues about architecture.

AreaPractice
tsconfigstrict, noUncheckedIndexedAccess, noImplicitOverride, verbatimModuleSyntax; one base config that every package extends
Type-check in CItsc --noEmit as its own step — Vite, esbuild and Node strip types without checking them
Linttypescript-eslint with type-aware rules (no-floating-promises, no-misused-promises, no-explicit-any); warnings fail CI
FormatPrettier or Biome on save and in a pre-commit hook — never a review comment
Lockfilecommit it; CI installs with npm ci or pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
Node versionengines in package.json plus .nvmrc; CI runs the same version
Dependenciesjustify each one; Renovate or Dependabot for updates; npm audit in CI
CIinstall, type-check, lint, test, build — under about ten minutes, on every pull request
Releasessemver, a generated changelog (Changesets), a tagged commit per release
OwnershipCODEOWNERS per package or feature folder, so reviews route themselves

A review checklist you can run in five minutes

Review the design before the syntax; formatting is the tools' job.

  • Correctness — what happens on empty, undefined, an error, an abort, a slow network and a double click?
  • Types — any new any, as, ! or @ts-expect-error? Each needs a reason in a comment.
  • Async — every promise awaited or handled; a stale response cannot overwrite a newer one.
  • Errors — expected failures are modelled; no empty catch {} swallowing the cause.
  • Surface — does this need to be exported? Does the new API corner future callers?
  • Tests — is there one test that fails if the core behaviour regresses?
  • Accessibility — native elements before ARIA, a label on every control, keyboard and focus order work, contrast passes, axe runs in CI; see the Accessibility on the Web sheet.
  • Localization — strings go through the i18n layer; numbers, dates and plurals through Intl; no sentences built by concatenation; tested with dir="rtl" and a pseudo-locale; see the Localization with Intl sheet.
  • Privacy — no personal data or tokens in logs, URLs or analytics events; collect only what the feature needs; ask for permissions (notifications, geolocation) in context, not on load; see the Security, Authentication & Privacy sheet.
  • Size and deletion — under about 400 lines gets a real review; dead code and expired flags leave with the change.

TypeScript Language Essentials

Structural types, unions and narrowing, null and undefined, generics, errors, exhaustiveness.

  • node
  • browser
  • typescript >=5.0
  • node >=22.18
  • TypeScript compiler; the examples run on Node.js

Sources: The TypeScript Handbook · Narrowing — TypeScript Handbook

Swift idea → TypeScript

Types are erased at runtime — they check, they never convert.

SwiftTypeScriptWatch out
protocolinterface / typestructural: any value of the right shape fits
enum with associated valuesdiscriminated unionswitch on the tag; never proves exhaustiveness
Optional<T>, ?., ??T | undefined, ?., ??there are two empties: null and undefined
generics with wheregenerics with extendsconstraints are structural too
struct value semanticsnone — objects are referencescopy with spread or structuredClone
throws / do-catchthrow anything / catch (e: unknown)the type system does not track throws
some P / any P—no existential distinction; inference does the work

Structural typing

A value fits a type when it has the members — no declaration of conformance needed.

interface Point { x: number; y: number }
function length(p: Point): number {
  return Math.hypot(p.x, p.y);
}

const reading = { x: 3, y: 4, label: "sensor" };
console.log(length(reading));                 // extra members are fine on a variable…
// length({ x: 3, y: 4, label: "s" });        // …but an object literal with them is error TS2353
Result
5
Setup
  1. Node.js 22.18 or later (it runs .mts files directly by stripping the types)
  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts
  3. Optional type-check: npm i -D typescript @types/node, then npx tsc --noEmit --strict --target esnext --module nodenext main.mts

Ran with Node 24.16.0, TypeScript 5.9.3 on 2026-11-11: the output matched the result shown.

Narrowing, null and undefined

typeof, in, instanceof and == null narrow a union; ?. and ?? handle both empties.

function describe(value: string | number | null | undefined): string {
  if (value == null) return "nothing";       // == null matches null and undefined
  if (typeof value === "string") return `text of ${value.length}`;
  return `number ${value.toFixed(1)}`;
}
console.log(describe("hey"), "|", describe(2), "|", describe(undefined));

const user: { name?: string; address?: { city?: string } } = {};
console.log(user.address?.city ?? "unknown city", user.name?.toUpperCase());
Result
text of 3 | number 2.0 | nothing
unknown city undefined

Generics and constraints

K extends keyof T ties a key to its object; the compiler rejects a key that does not exist.

function maxBy<T>(items: readonly T[], key: (item: T) => number): T | undefined {
  let best: T | undefined;
  let bestKey = -Infinity;
  for (const item of items) {
    const k = key(item);
    if (k > bestKey) {
      best = item;
      bestKey = k;
    }
  }
  return best;
}
function pluck<T, K extends keyof T>(items: readonly T[], key: K): T[K][] {
  return items.map((item) => item[key]);
}

const files = [{ name: "a.txt", size: 10 }, { name: "b.png", size: 2048 }];
console.log(maxBy(files, (f) => f.size)?.name, pluck(files, "name"));
// pluck(files, "owner");   // error TS2345: '"owner"' is not assignable to '"name" | "size"'
Result
b.png [ 'a.txt', 'b.png' ]

Errors — thrown, or returned as values

A catch variable is unknown; a Result union makes failure part of the signature.

type Result<T, E = Error> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E };

function parsePort(text: string): Result<number> {
  const n = Number(text);
  return Number.isInteger(n) && n > 0 && n < 65536
    ? { ok: true, value: n }
    : { ok: false, error: new RangeError(`not a port: ${text}`) };
}

for (const input of ["8080", "http"]) {
  const r = parsePort(input);
  console.log(r.ok ? `port ${r.value}` : r.error.message);
}

try {
  JSON.parse("{bad");
} catch (e: unknown) {                       // narrow before use
  console.log(e instanceof SyntaxError ? "SyntaxError" : "something else");
}
Result
port 8080
not a port: http
SyntaxError

Exhaustive switch with never

Assigning the leftover to never turns a forgotten case into a compile error.

type Shape =
  | { kind: "circle"; radius: number }
  | { kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number };

function area(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case "circle":
      return Math.PI * s.radius ** 2;
    case "rect":
      return s.width * s.height;
    default: {
      const unreachable: never = s;          // a new Shape without a case fails here
      return unreachable;
    }
  }
}
console.log(area({ kind: "rect", width: 2, height: 3 }), area({ kind: "circle", radius: 1 }).toFixed(2));
Result
6 3.14

References and copies

Spread copies one level; structuredClone copies deeply; Object.freeze is shallow too.

const a = { tags: ["x"] };
const shallow = { ...a };
const deep = structuredClone(a);
a.tags.push("y");
console.log(shallow.tags, deep.tags, a === shallow);

const frozen = Object.freeze({ n: 1 });
// frozen.n = 2;   // error TS2540: Cannot assign to 'n' because it is a read-only property
console.log(Object.isFrozen(frozen));
Result
[ 'x', 'y' ] [ 'x' ] false
true

Modeling with the Type System

Branded ids, satisfies, utility and mapped types, and validating what the types cannot see.

Branded ids

Structural typing makes every string interchangeable; a brand makes UserId and OrderId distinct at no runtime cost.

type Brand<T, B extends string> = T & { readonly __brand: B };
type UserId = Brand<string, "UserId">;
type OrderId = Brand<string, "OrderId">;

const userId = (raw: string) => raw as UserId;     // the one place a raw string becomes an id
function ordersOf(user: UserId): string {
  return `orders of ${user}`;
}

console.log(ordersOf(userId("u-42")));
// ordersOf("o-7" as OrderId);   // error TS2345: 'OrderId' is not assignable to 'UserId'
Result
orders of u-42

satisfies — check without widening

An annotation would widen the keys to string; satisfies checks the shape and keeps the literal keys.

type Route = { path: string; auth: boolean };
const routes = {
  home: { path: "/", auth: false },
  settings: { path: "/settings", auth: true },
} satisfies Record<string, Route>;

console.log(routes.settings.path, Object.keys(routes));   // routes.home is known to exist
Result
/settings [ 'home', 'settings' ]

Utility types

Derive the variants from one source of truth instead of copying fields.

interface User { id: string; name: string; email: string; admin: boolean }
type UserPatch = Partial<Omit<User, "id">>;  // the id never changes
type PublicUser = Pick<User, "id" | "name">;

function apply(user: User, patch: UserPatch): Readonly<User> {
  return { ...user, ...patch };
}
const ana: User = { id: "1", name: "Ana", email: "ana@example.com", admin: false };
const shown: PublicUser = { id: ana.id, name: ana.name };
console.log(apply(ana, { admin: true }).admin, Object.keys(shown));
Result
true [ 'id', 'name' ]

Mapped and template literal types

Generate a family of keys from a union; the compiler then knows every one of them.

type EventName = "click" | "focus";
type Handlers = { [E in EventName as `on${Capitalize<E>}`]: (at: number) => void };

const handlers: Handlers = {
  onClick: (at) => console.log("click at", at),
  onFocus: (at) => console.log("focus at", at),
};
handlers.onClick(10);
// handlers.onHover(1);   // error TS2339: Property 'onHover' does not exist on type 'Handlers'
Result
click at 10

Validate what the types cannot see

JSON.parse returns any. Treat it as unknown and narrow with a type guard (or a schema library such as zod).

interface Config { port: number; hosts: string[] }

function isConfig(x: unknown): x is Config {
  if (typeof x !== "object" || x === null) return false;
  const c = x as Record<string, unknown>;
  return typeof c.port === "number" && Array.isArray(c.hosts) && c.hosts.every((h) => typeof h === "string");
}

for (const text of ['{"port":8080,"hosts":["a"]}', '{"port":"8080"}']) {
  const data: unknown = JSON.parse(text);
  console.log(isConfig(data) ? `ok ${data.port}` : "rejected");
}
Result
ok 8080
rejected

Rules

Make illegal states unrepresentable — within what erasure allows.

  • A discriminated union over a bag of optional fields: { status: "error"; error: E } cannot lack its error.
  • String-literal unions over enum: they erase completely (Node's type stripping rejects enum).
  • as is an assertion, not a conversion — x as User on unchecked data is a bug waiting.
  • any switches checking off for everything it touches; unknown forces a check.
  • Types vanish at runtime: anything crossing a boundary (network, storage, user input) needs validation.

React — Components, Layout & Animation

Typed function components, children and slots, keyed lists, flex and grid layout, routing, CSS and view transitions, and what makes a re-render cheap.

Sources: Learn React — react.dev · React reference — react.dev

SwiftUI idea → React

The same declarative contract — describe the UI for a state, the framework applies the difference.

SwiftUIReactNote
struct TaskRow: Viewfunction TaskRow(props: TaskRowProps)a component is a function of its props; it re-runs on every render
let task: Task (init parameter)a typed props object, destructuredprops are read-only; never mutate them
@ViewBuilder content: () -> Contentchildren: ReactNode, or named slot props (actions: ReactNode)composition over configuration
ForEach(tasks) { … } + Identifiabletasks.map((t) => <TaskRow key={t.id} … />)key is the identity; never the array index for editable lists
if / switch in bodyearly return, cond ? a : b, cond && a0 && x renders 0 — compare explicitly
VStack / HStack / Spacer()display: flex with flex-direction, gap; flex: 1layout is CSS, not components
LazyVGrid(.adaptive(minimum:))grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(12rem, 1fr))no laziness: virtualise long lists with a library
NavigationStack + navigationDestinationa router (<Routes>, useParams, useNavigate)the URL is the navigation path
withAnimation / .transitionCSS transition on a state-driven style or class; <ViewTransition>the browser animates; React only changes the DOM
ViewModifiera wrapper component or a shared classNameprops spread onto the native element keep it accessible
Equatable + .equatable()memo(Component)skips a render when props are shallow-equal

Function components, typed props and children

Type props as an object type; take children (and named slots) as ReactNode so callers compose instead of configure.

import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from "react-dom/server";

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean; due?: string };

type TaskRowProps = {
  task: Task;
  onToggle?: (id: string) => void;          // optional: a read-only list omits it
};

function TaskRow({ task, onToggle }: TaskRowProps) {
  return (
    <li className={task.done ? "task done" : "task"}>
      <label>
        <input type="checkbox" checked={task.done} disabled={!onToggle}
          onChange={() => onToggle?.(task.id)} />
        {task.title}
      </label>
      {task.due !== undefined && <small> due {task.due}</small>}
    </li>
  );
}

type PanelProps = { title: string; actions?: ReactNode; children: ReactNode };

function Panel({ title, actions, children }: PanelProps) {
  return (
    <section className="panel">
      <header><h2>{title}</h2>{actions}</header>
      {children}
    </section>
  );
}

const task: Task = { id: "t1", title: "Renew TLS certificate", done: false, due: "Fri" };
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<TaskRow task={task} />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Panel title="Today" actions={<button>Add</button>}><p>3 open</p></Panel>));
Result
<li class="task"><label><input type="checkbox" disabled=""/>Renew TLS certificate</label><small> due Fri</small></li>
<section class="panel"><header><h2>Today</h2><button>Add</button></header><p>3 open</p></section>

  3. Save as main.tsx, then npx esbuild main.tsx --jsx=automatic --format=esm --outfile=main.mjs && node main.mjs

Lists with stable keys, conditional rendering

Key rows by the data's own id; return early for empty states; never let a number reach &&.

import { renderToStaticMarkup } from "react-dom/server";

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };

function TaskList({ tasks, filter }: { tasks: readonly Task[]; filter: string }) {
  const shown = tasks.filter((t) => t.title.toLowerCase().includes(filter.toLowerCase()));
  if (shown.length === 0) return <p className="empty">No tasks match {filter}.</p>;

  const open = shown.filter((t) => !t.done).length;
  return (
    <>
      <p>{open > 0 ? `${open} open` : "All done"}</p>
      <ul>
        {shown.map((t) => (
          <li key={t.id}>{t.done ? <s>{t.title}</s> : t.title}</li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </>
  );
}

const UnreadBadge = ({ count }: { count: number }) => <span>{count && <b>{count} new</b>}</span>;
const FixedBadge = ({ count }: { count: number }) => <span>{count > 0 && <b>{count} new</b>}</span>;

const tasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "t1", title: "Rotate API keys", done: true },
  { id: "t2", title: "Review deploy PR", done: false },
];
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<TaskList tasks={tasks} filter="" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<TaskList tasks={tasks} filter="audit" />));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<UnreadBadge count={0} />), renderToStaticMarkup(<FixedBadge count={0} />));
Result
<p>1 open</p><ul><li><s>Rotate API keys</s></li><li>Review deploy PR</li></ul>
<p class="empty">No tasks match audit.</p>
<span>0</span> <span></span>

Layout with flexbox and grid

Stacks are flex, adaptive grids are grid with auto-fill; in an app put these in CSS classes — inline styles here keep the example to one file.

import type { CSSProperties, ReactNode } from "react";
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from "react-dom/server";

type StackProps = {
  direction?: "row" | "column";
  gap?: number;                              // a number becomes px
  align?: CSSProperties["alignItems"];
  children: ReactNode;
};

function Stack({ direction = "column", gap = 8, align = "stretch", children }: StackProps) {
  return <div style={{ display: "flex", flexDirection: direction, gap, alignItems: align }}>{children}</div>;
}

const Spacer = () => <div style={{ flex: 1 }} />;

function CardGrid({ minColumn = "12rem", children }: { minColumn?: string; children: ReactNode }) {
  // as many columns as fit, each at least `minColumn` wide — no media query needed
  const columns = `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(${minColumn}, 1fr))`;
  return <div style={{ display: "grid", gap: 12, gridTemplateColumns: columns }}>{children}</div>;
}

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <Stack direction="row" align="center"><h1>Tasks</h1><Spacer /><button>Add</button></Stack>,
));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<CardGrid><article>Inbox</article><article>Done</article></CardGrid>));
Result
<div style="display:flex;flex-direction:row;gap:8px;align-items:center"><h1>Tasks</h1><div style="flex:1"></div><button>Add</button></div>
<div style="display:grid;gap:12px;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill, minmax(12rem, 1fr))"><article>Inbox</article><article>Done</article></div>

Routing between screens

The URL is the navigation stack — a list route, a detail route with a dynamic segment, links for users and navigate for code.

import { useEffect } from "react";
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { BrowserRouter, Link, Navigate, Outlet, Route, Routes, useNavigate, useParams } from "react-router";

type Task = { id: string; title: string };
const tasks: Task[] = [{ id: "t1", title: "Rotate API keys" }, { id: "t2", title: "Review deploy PR" }];

function TasksLayout() {
  // <Outlet /> is where the matched child route renders
  return <main><nav><Link to="/tasks">All tasks</Link></nav><Outlet /></main>;
}

function TaskIndex() {
  return <ul>{tasks.map((t) => <li key={t.id}><Link to={`/tasks/${t.id}`}>{t.title}</Link></li>)}</ul>;
}

function TaskDetail() {
  const { taskId } = useParams();            // string | undefined: it comes from the URL
  const navigate = useNavigate();
  useEffect(() => {                          // navigation from code: Escape closes the detail
    const onKey = (e: KeyboardEvent) => { if (e.key === "Escape") navigate("/tasks"); };
    window.addEventListener("keydown", onKey);
    return () => window.removeEventListener("keydown", onKey);
  }, [navigate]);

  const task = tasks.find((t) => t.id === taskId);
  if (!task) return <p>Task not found.</p>;
  return <article><h2>{task.title}</h2><Link to="/tasks">Back to tasks</Link></article>;
}

createRoot(document.getElementById("root")!).render(
  <BrowserRouter>
    <Routes>
      <Route path="/" element={<Navigate to="/tasks" replace />} />
      <Route path="tasks" element={<TasksLayout />}>
        <Route index element={<TaskIndex />} />
        <Route path=":taskId" element={<TaskDetail />} />
      </Route>
    </Routes>
  </BrowserRouter>,
);
Result

/ redirects to /tasks, which lists the tasks; a link pushes /tasks/t2 and shows its detail inside the same layout; Back to tasks or Escape returns to the list, even after a deep link.

Setup
  1. A React project (npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts)
  2. npm i react-router

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a React app with react-router installed and a <div id="root"> in its page.

CSS transitions driven by state

The owner flips open with useState; the browser animates the style change that causes — here a height animation with grid-template-rows.

import { act, useState, type ReactNode } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");

type DisclosureProps = { open: boolean; title: string; onToggle: () => void; children: ReactNode };

function Disclosure({ open, title, onToggle, children }: DisclosureProps) {
  // 0fr → 1fr animates to the content's real height, which `height: auto` cannot
  const rows = open ? "1fr" : "0fr";
  const panel = { display: "grid", gridTemplateRows: rows, transition: "grid-template-rows 200ms ease-out" };
  return (
    <section>
      <button aria-expanded={open} onClick={onToggle}>{title}</button>
      <div inert={!open} style={panel}><div style={{ overflow: "hidden" }}>{children}</div></div>
    </section>
  );
}

function ReleaseChecklist() {
  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);                  // the state the animation follows
  return (
    <Disclosure open={open} title="Release checklist" onToggle={() => setOpen((o) => !o)}>
      <p>Back up the database</p>
    </Disclosure>
  );
}

// In the stylesheet: @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { * { transition: none !important } }
await act(() => createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!).render(<ReleaseChecklist />));

const button = document.querySelector("button")!;
const show = () => {
  const panel = button.nextElementSibling!;

show();
