View transitions between list and detail

Wrap what should animate in <ViewTransition> and change state inside startTransition; a shared name morphs the row's title into the detail heading.

import { startTransition, useState, ViewTransition } from "react";

type Task = { id: string; title: string; notes: string };

export function TaskBoard({ tasks }: { tasks: readonly Task[] }) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const selected = tasks.find((t) => t.id === selectedId);
  // Only transitions animate: a plain setState commits immediately, with no animation.
  const show = (id: string | null) => startTransition(() => setSelectedId(id));

  if (selected) {
    return (
      <article>
        <ViewTransition name={`task-${selected.id}`}><h2>{selected.title}</h2></ViewTransition>
        <p>{selected.notes}</p>
        <button type="button" onClick={() => show(null)}>Back</button>
      </article>
    );
  }
  return (
    <ul>
      {tasks.map((t) => (
        <li key={t.id}>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => show(t.id)}>
            <ViewTransition name={`task-${t.id}`}><span>{t.title}</span></ViewTransition>
          </button>
        </li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// Tune it in CSS: ::view-transition-group(*) { animation-duration: 250ms; }
// Before React 19.3: document.startViewTransition(() => flushSync(() => setSelectedId(id)))
Result

Activating a row (click, Enter or Space) cross-fades the list into the detail while the title glides into the heading's position; Back plays it in reverse.

Setup

  2. A browser with the View Transitions API (without it the update simply applies, unanimated)

Reusable building blocks

Extend the native element's props so a wrapper stays a real button; make a list generic so the type of each item flows into renderItem.

import type { ComponentProps, Key, ReactNode } from "react";
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from "react-dom/server";

type ButtonProps = ComponentProps<"button"> & { variant?: "primary" | "ghost" };

// `...rest` forwards aria-*, onClick, disabled and (React 19) ref to the real <button>
function Button({ variant = "primary", type = "button", className = "", ...rest }: ButtonProps) {
  return <button type={type} className={`btn btn-${variant} ${className}`.trim()} {...rest} />;
}

type ListProps<T> = {
  items: readonly T[];
  getKey: (item: T) => Key;
  renderItem: (item: T) => ReactNode;
  empty?: ReactNode;
};

function List<T>({ items, getKey, renderItem, empty = <p>Nothing here.</p> }: ListProps<T>) {
  if (items.length === 0) return empty;
  return <ul>{items.map((item) => <li key={getKey(item)}>{renderItem(item)}</li>)}</ul>;
}

type Assignee = { login: string; open: number };
const people: Assignee[] = [{ login: "ada", open: 3 }, { login: "grace", open: 0 }];

console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<Button variant="ghost" aria-label="Archive task">Archive</Button>));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <List items={people} getKey={(p) => p.login} renderItem={(p) => `${p.login} (${p.open})`} />,
));
console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(
  <List items={[] as Assignee[]} getKey={(p) => p.login} renderItem={(p) => p.login} />,
));
Result
<button type="button" class="btn btn-ghost" aria-label="Archive task">Archive</button>
<ul><li>ada (3)</li><li>grace (0)</li></ul>
<p>Nothing here.</p>

Keep re-renders cheap — memo, keys, stable callbacks

A state change re-renders its component and every child; memo lets a row skip when its props are unchanged, which needs callbacks with a stable identity.

import { act, memo, useCallback, useState } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");
const { fireEvent } = await import("@testing-library/dom");

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };
const seed: Task[] = [{ id: "t1", title: "Triage", done: false }, { id: "t2", title: "Ship", done: false }];
const rendered: string[] = [];                          // demo instrumentation only

type RowProps = { task: Task; onToggle: (id: string) => void };

const TaskRow = memo(function TaskRow({ task, onToggle }: RowProps) {
  rendered.push(task.id);
  const box = <input type="checkbox" checked={task.done} onChange={() => onToggle(task.id)} />;
  return <li><label>{box} {task.title}</label></li>;
});

function TaskScreen() {
  const [tasks, setTasks] = useState(seed);
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState("");

  // the functional update reads no `tasks`, so `toggle` keeps one identity for good
  const toggle = useCallback((id: string) =>
    setTasks((ts) => ts.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t))), []);

  return (
    <>
      <input aria-label="New task" value={draft} onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)} />
      <ul>{tasks.map((t) => <TaskRow key={t.id} task={t} onToggle={toggle} />)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}

const root = createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!);
async function step(label: string, update: () => void) {
  await act(update);
  console.log(`${label}: ${rendered.splice(0).join(",") || "no rows"}`);
}

await step("first render", () => root.render(<TaskScreen />));
await step("typing", () => fireEvent.change(document.querySelector("input")!, { target: { value: "x" } }));
await step("toggle t2", () => document.querySelectorAll<HTMLInputElement>("li input")[1]!.click());
Result
first render: t1,t2
typing: no rows
toggle t2: t2

Rendering and performance rules

What re-renders, and how to keep it cheap.

  • Keep render pure and cheap — it runs on every state change of the component and of every ancestor. No fetches, no subscriptions, no Date.now() in the body.
  • Put state as low as it can go: a filter box that owns its own draft re-renders itself, not the whole screen.
  • key = the row's own stable id. An index key reuses the wrong row's state (focus, an open editor, a checkbox) after an insert or sort.
  • memo only helps when props are stable: pass ids and primitives, keep callbacks stable (useCallback, functional setState), and do not create {} or [] literals as props.
  • The React Compiler (babel-plugin-react-compiler) memoises components and values automatically; with it on, hand-written memo/useCallback is mostly unnecessary.
  • Defining a component inside another component: every render creates a new type, so React unmounts and remounts the subtree and its state is lost.
  • Rendering thousands of rows: React has no lazy stack — virtualise (@tanstack/react-virtual, react-window) or paginate.
  • React DevTools: the Profiler records what rendered and why; the "Highlight updates when components render" setting flashes renders live.

React — State & Data Flow

Pick the right hook, lift state to the closest common owner, inject with context, reset with keys, and tie async work to the component's lifetime.

  • browser
  • React
  • typescript >=5.5
  • react >=19.0
  • react-dom >=19.0
  • node >=22.18
  • a browser page with React (the examples run in Node with `react-dom/server` or jsdom)

Sources: Managing state — react.dev · Built-in React hooks — react.dev

Hook decision table

Reach for the first row that fits; most bugs come from storing in state what should be derived.

HookRe-renders on change?Use when
a plain const in render—anything computable from props and state (a filtered list, a total, isDirty): never mirror it into state
useStateyesa value this component owns: a draft, a toggle, the selected id
useReduceryesseveral fields that change together under named actions (an edit form, a wizard); the reducer is pure and testable
useRefnoa value that must survive renders but not be shown: a DOM node, a timer id, an AbortController
useMemo / useCallback—an expensive derivation, or a stable identity for a memo child or an effect dependency; never for correctness
useContext / use(Context)yes, when the provided value changes identitywhat many levels need: session, theme, feature flags
useEffect—synchronise with something outside React (subscriptions, requests, browser APIs) and return its cleanup
useSyncExternalStoreyes, when the snapshot changes (Object.is)read a store React does not own (a cache, a websocket client, matchMedia) without tearing
use(promise) + <Suspense>suspends, then rendersread async data during render; the nearest <Suspense> shows the fallback meanwhile
useActionStateyes, when the action returnsa form or button submission: the action's result (saved value, errors) and its isPending flag
useOptimisticyes, until the action settlesshow the expected result at once; it falls back to the real state when the action ends
useFormStatus (react-dom)yes, while the form submitsa submit button that knows its <form> is pending, with no props passed down
useTransition / useDeferredValueyes, at lower prioritykeep typing responsive while an expensive re-render catches up
useEffectEvent—read the latest props inside an effect without making them dependencies (React 19.2+)

Lifting state and controlled inputs

Move state up to the closest component that every reader needs; pass the value down and a callback up.

import { act, useState } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");
const { fireEvent } = await import("@testing-library/dom");

type Person = { id: string; name: string; team: string };

const people: Person[] = [
  { id: "p1", name: "Ada Lovelace", team: "Platform" },
  { id: "p2", name: "Grace Hopper", team: "Compilers" },
  { id: "p3", name: "Alan Turing", team: "Platform" },
];

// Controlled: the parent owns the value; the input only reports what the user typed.
function SearchBox({ value, onChange }: { value: string; onChange: (next: string) => void }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <input aria-label="Search people" value={value} onChange={(e) => onChange(e.target.value)} />
      <button disabled={value === ""} onClick={() => onChange("")}>Clear</button>
    </div>
  );
}

function Directory() {
  const [query, setQuery] = useState("");          // lifted: the box and the list both need it
  const shown = people.filter((p) => `${p.name} ${p.team}`.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase()));
  return (
    <>
      <SearchBox value={query} onChange={setQuery} />
      <ul>{shown.map((p) => <li key={p.id}>{p.name}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}

const root = createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!);
const names = () => [...document.querySelectorAll("li")].map((li) => li.textContent).join(", ");
await act(() => root.render(<Directory />));

const input = document.querySelector("input")!;
await act(() => fireEvent.change(input, { target: { value: "platform" } }));
console.log(`typed [${input.value}]: ${names()}`);

await act(() => document.querySelector("button")!.click());
console.log(`cleared [${input.value}]: ${names()}`);

useReducer for state that changes together

Name the events and keep every transition — saving and a failed save included — in one pure function; the component is type-checked, and the output replays a failed save through the reducer alone, with no rendering.

import { useReducer, type ChangeEvent, type FormEvent } from "react";

type EditState = { saved: string; draft: string; saving: boolean; error: string | null };

type EditAction =
  | { type: "edit"; value: string }
  | { type: "save-started" }
  | { type: "saved"; value: string }
  | { type: "save-failed"; error: string };

function editReducer(state: EditState, action: EditAction): EditState {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "edit": return { ...state, draft: action.value };
    case "save-started": return { ...state, saving: true, error: null };
    case "saved": return { ...state, saved: action.value, saving: false };
    case "save-failed": return { ...state, saving: false, error: action.error };   // the draft survives
  }
}

export function NameEditor({ name, onSave }: { name: string; onSave: (n: string) => Promise<string> }) {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(editReducer, { saved: name, draft: name, saving: false, error: null });
  const edit = (e: ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) => dispatch({ type: "edit", value: e.target.value });

  const save = (e: FormEvent) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (state.saving) return;                         // already saving: a second Enter sends nothing
    dispatch({ type: "save-started" });
    onSave(state.draft).then(
      (saved) => dispatch({ type: "saved", value: saved }),
      (err: unknown) => dispatch({ type: "save-failed", error: String(err) }),
    );
  };

  return (
    <form onSubmit={save}>
      <label>Display name <input value={state.draft} onChange={edit} /></label>
      <button disabled={state.saving}>{state.saving ? "Saving…" : "Save"}</button>
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

let state: EditState = { saved: "Ada", draft: "Ada", saving: false, error: null };
state = editReducer(state, { type: "edit", value: "Ada Lovelace" });
state = editReducer(state, { type: "save-started" });
state = editReducer(state, { type: "save-failed", error: "Network error" });
console.log(state);
Result
{
  saved: 'Ada',
  draft: 'Ada Lovelace',
  saving: false,
  error: 'Network error'
}

Submit with an action — useActionState and useFormStatus

Give the form an action; React tracks its pending state, keeps what it returned and resets the form afterwards — so echo a rejected value back.

import { act, useActionState } from "react";
import { useFormStatus } from "react-dom";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
const { document, FormData } = window;                  // Node's own FormData cannot read a jsdom <form>
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document, FormData, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");

let reply: (error: string | null) => void = () => {};   // the demo answers for the server
const saveEmail = (_email: string) => new Promise<string | null>((resolve) => { reply = resolve; });

function SaveButton() {
  const { pending } = useFormStatus();                   // the enclosing <form>'s submission
  return <button disabled={pending}>{pending ? "Saving…" : "Save"}</button>;
}

type SaveState = { saved: string; value: string; error: string | null };

function EmailForm({ current }: { current: string }) {
  const [state, saveAction] = useActionState<SaveState, FormData>(async (prev, form) => {
    const email = String(form.get("email"));
    const error = await saveEmail(email);
    return error ? { ...prev, value: email, error } : { saved: email, value: email, error: null };
  }, { saved: current, value: current, error: null });

  return (
    <form action={saveAction}>
      <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" defaultValue={state.value} /></label>
      <SaveButton />
      {state.error && <p role="alert">{state.error}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

await act(() => createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!).render(<EmailForm current="ada@example.com" />));
const show = (step: string) => console.log(`${step}: [${document.querySelector("button")!.textContent}]`,
  document.querySelector("input")!.value, document.querySelector("[role=alert]")?.textContent ?? "");

// The browser's own validation runs first: this address passes `type="email"`, then the server rejects it.
document.querySelector("input")!.value = "ada@gmail.com";
await act(() => document.querySelector("form")!.requestSubmit());
show("submitting");

await act(async () => reply("Use your @example.com address"));
show("rejected");
Result
submitting: [Saving…] ada@gmail.com
rejected: [Save] ada@gmail.com Use your @example.com address

Optimistic updates — useOptimistic

Show the row the user just added while the request runs; when the action ends React drops the optimistic copy for the real state, so a failure undoes itself.

import { act, useActionState, useOptimistic } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
const { document, FormData } = window;                  // Node's own FormData cannot read a jsdom <form>
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document, FormData, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");

type Invite = { email: string; sending?: boolean };

let settle: (accepted: boolean) => void = () => {};     // the demo answers for the server
const sendInvite = (_email: string) => new Promise<boolean>((resolve) => { settle = resolve; });

function InviteForm() {
  // a real form would also return an error to show, as in the previous card
  const [invites, inviteAction, isPending] = useActionState<Invite[], FormData>(async (prev, form) => {
    const email = String(form.get("email"));
    return (await sendInvite(email)) ? [...prev, { email }] : prev;
  }, []);
  const [shown, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(invites, (list, added: Invite) => [...list, added]);

  const submit = (form: FormData) => {
    addOptimistic({ email: String(form.get("email")), sending: true });   // visible until the action ends
    inviteAction(form);
  };

  return (
    <form action={submit}>
      <label>Email <input name="email" type="email" /></label>
      <button disabled={isPending}>Invite</button>
      <ul>{shown.map((i) => <li key={i.email}>{i.email}{i.sending ? " (sending…)" : ""}</li>)}</ul>
    </form>
  );
}

await act(() => createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!).render(<InviteForm />));
const text = (sel: string) => [...document.querySelectorAll(sel)].map((el) => el.textContent).join(", ");

async function invite(email: string, accepted: boolean) {
  document.querySelector("input")!.value = email;
  await act(() => document.querySelector("form")!.requestSubmit());
  console.log(`sending: ${text("li")}`);
  await act(async () => settle(accepted));
  console.log(`${accepted ? "accepted" : "rejected"}: ${text("li")}`);
}

await invite("grace@example.com", true);
await invite("alan@example.com", false);

sending: grace@example.com, alan@example.com (sending…)

Inject with context

Provide once near the root, read through a custom hook that fails loudly when the provider is missing.

import { createContext, use, type ReactNode } from "react";
import { renderToStaticMarkup } from "react-dom/server";

type Permission = "invite" | "billing";
type Session = { userId: string; displayName: string; can: (permission: Permission) => boolean };

const SessionContext = createContext<Session | null>(null);   // null: a missing provider is detectable

function useSession(): Session {
  const session = use(SessionContext);
  if (!session) throw new Error("useSession() needs a <SessionContext> above it");
  return session;
}

function Greeting() {
  const { displayName } = useSession();
  return <p>Signed in as {displayName}</p>;
}

function InviteButton() {
  return useSession().can("invite") ? <button>Invite teammate</button> : null;
}

// React 19: the context object is its own provider (`<SessionContext.Provider>` still works)
function AppShell({ session, children }: { session: Session; children: ReactNode }) {
  return <SessionContext value={session}>{children}</SessionContext>;
}

const admin: Session = { userId: "u1", displayName: "Ada", can: () => true };
const viewer: Session = { userId: "u2", displayName: "Grace", can: (p) => p !== "invite" };
for (const session of [admin, viewer]) {
  console.log(renderToStaticMarkup(<AppShell session={session}><Greeting /><InviteButton /></AppShell>));
}
Result
<p>Signed in as Ada</p><button>Invite teammate</button>
<p>Signed in as Grace</p>

Identity — a key resets state

State belongs to a position in the tree; the same component at the same position keeps its state across new props unless its key changes.

import { act, useState } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");
const { fireEvent } = await import("@testing-library/dom");

type Person = { id: string; name: string; note: string };
const ada: Person = { id: "p1", name: "Ada", note: "" };
const grace: Person = { id: "p2", name: "Grace", note: "Prefers email" };

function NoteEditor({ person }: { person: Person }) {
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState(person.note);   // read on mount only, not on every new prop
  const label = `Note for ${person.name}`;

  return <textarea aria-label={label} value={draft} onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)} />;
}

function Inspector({ selected, keyed }: { selected: Person; keyed: boolean }) {
  return keyed ? <NoteEditor key={selected.id} person={selected} /> : <NoteEditor person={selected} />;
}

for (const keyed of [false, true]) {
  const root = createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!);
  await act(() => root.render(<Inspector selected={ada} keyed={keyed} />));
  const note = document.querySelector("textarea")!;
  await act(() => fireEvent.change(note, { target: { value: "Call Ada back" } }));
  await act(() => root.render(<Inspector selected={grace} keyed={keyed} />));   // then picks Grace
  const editor = document.querySelector("textarea")!;
  console.log(`${keyed ? "key={id}" : "no key  "} → ${editor.ariaLabel}: "${editor.value}"`);
  await act(() => root.unmount());
}
Result
no key   → Note for Grace: "Call Ada back"
key={id} → Note for Grace: "Prefers email"
Setup
  1. A React project (npm create vite@latest app -- --template react-ts), or standalone as shown here
  2. npm i react react-dom jsdom @testing-library/dom and npm i -D esbuild @types/react @types/react-dom @types/jsdom
  3. The JSDOM lines give Node a DOM before react-dom loads (hence the dynamic import); a browser page needs none of them
  4. Save as main.tsx, then npx esbuild main.tsx --jsx=automatic --format=esm --outfile=main.mjs && node main.mjs

Ran with Node 24.16.0, TypeScript 5.9.3 on 2026-11-16: the output matched the result shown.

Sources: Preserving and resetting state — react.dev

Subscribe to a browser API with useSyncExternalStore

For a value React does not own — here navigator.onLine — the hook gives every render one consistent value (no tearing) and re-renders only when the snapshot changes; binding a view model this way is on the MVVM sheet.

import { act, useSyncExternalStore } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");

let online = true;                                       // jsdom cannot go offline: stub the flag
Object.defineProperty(window.navigator, "onLine", { get: () => online });

// Module-level, so their identity is stable: a new `subscribe` each render would resubscribe each time.
function subscribe(onChange: () => void) {
  window.addEventListener("online", onChange);
  window.addEventListener("offline", onChange);
  return () => {
    window.removeEventListener("online", onChange);
    window.removeEventListener("offline", onChange);
  };
}

const getSnapshot = () => window.navigator.onLine;     // a boolean: equal by value, nothing to cache
const getServerSnapshot = () => true;                    // what a server render assumes

let renders = 0;

function SaveButton() {
  const isOnline = useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot);
  renders++;
  return <button disabled={!isOnline}>{isOnline ? "Save" : "Offline — reconnecting…"}</button>;
}

await act(() => createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!).render(<SaveButton />));
const show = (step: string) =>
  console.log(`${step}: ${document.querySelector("button")!.textContent} (renders: ${renders})`);

async function network(event: "online" | "offline", isUp: boolean) {
  online = isUp;
  await act(() => window.dispatchEvent(new window.Event(event)));
}

show("mounted");
await network("offline", false);
show("offline");
await network("offline", false);                         // event fired, snapshot unchanged
show("repeat event");
await network("online", true);
show("online");
Result
mounted: Save (renders: 1)
offline: Offline — reconnecting… (renders: 2)
repeat event: Offline — reconnecting… (renders: 2)
online: Save (renders: 3)

Async work tied to the component — abort on change

The effect starts the request for the current id and its cleanup aborts it, so a slow reply for an old id can never overwrite the new one.

import { act, useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");

type Person = { id: string; name: string };
type Phase =
  | { status: "loading" }
  | { status: "loaded"; person: Person }
  | { status: "failed"; message: string };
type Loader = (id: string, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<Person>;

function PersonCard({ personId, load }: { personId: string; load: Loader }) {
  const [result, setResult] = useState<{ id: string; phase: Phase } | null>(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const controller = new AbortController();
    load(personId, controller.signal)
      .then((person): Phase => ({ status: "loaded", person }))
      .catch((e: unknown): Phase => ({ status: "failed", message: String(e) }))
      .then((phase) => { if (!controller.signal.aborted) setResult({ id: personId, phase }); });
    return () => controller.abort();               // new id or unmount: the old request is moot
  }, [personId, load]);

  // a result for another id is stale: show loading, not the wrong person
  const phase: Phase = result?.id === personId ? result.phase : { status: "loading" };
  if (phase.status === "loading") return <p>Loading…</p>;
  return phase.status === "failed" ? <p role="alert">{phase.message}</p> : <h2>{phase.person.name}</h2>;
}

// A fake transport the test resolves by hand; in the app this is `fetch(url, { signal })`.
const calls: { id: string; signal: AbortSignal; reply: (p: Person) => void }[] = [];
const load: Loader = (id, signal) => new Promise((reply) => calls.push({ id, signal, reply }));

const root = createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!);
const screen = () => document.querySelector("main")!.textContent;
await act(() => root.render(<PersonCard personId="p1" load={load} />));
await act(() => root.render(<PersonCard personId="p2" load={load} />));   // the user moved on
console.log(calls.map((c) => `${c.id}:${c.signal.aborted ? "aborted" : "live"}`).join(" "));

await act(async () => calls[0]!.reply({ id: "p1", name: "Ada Lovelace" }));  // the stale reply lands late
console.log("after stale reply:", screen());

await act(async () => calls[1]!.reply({ id: "p2", name: "Grace Hopper" }));
console.log("after p2 reply:", screen());
Result
p1:aborted p2:live
after stale reply: Loading…
after p2 reply: Grace Hopper

Read a promise with use and Suspense

Start the request outside render (an event handler, a cache, a router loader, or a parent's state), pass the promise down, and let <Suspense> own the loading state.

import { act, Suspense, use } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main></main>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");

type Member = { id: string; name: string };

function TeamMembers({ members }: { members: Promise<Member[]> }) {
  const list = use(members);                // suspends until settled; a rejection reaches an error boundary
  return <ul>{list.map((m) => <li key={m.id}>{m.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}

function TeamPage({ members }: { members: Promise<Member[]> }) {
  return (
    <section>
      <h1>Platform team</h1>
      <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading members…</p>}>
        <TeamMembers members={members} />
      </Suspense>
    </section>
  );
}

// One promise per request, created outside render: a new promise on every render would suspend forever.
const { promise, resolve } = Promise.withResolvers<Member[]>();
const root = createRoot(document.querySelector("main")!);
await act(() => root.render(<TeamPage members={promise} />));
console.log(document.querySelector("section")!.innerHTML);

await act(async () => resolve([{ id: "p1", name: "Ada" }, { id: "p3", name: "Alan" }]));
console.log(document.querySelector("section")!.innerHTML);
Result
<h1>Platform team</h1><p>Loading members…</p>
<h1>Platform team</h1><ul><li>Ada</li><li>Alan</li></ul>

Identity and lifetime rules

Where most React state bugs come from.

  • Copying props into state (useState(props.x)) and "syncing" it in an effect: the copy goes stale, and every change renders twice. Derive in render, or reset with a key.
  • An object or array literal as a context value re-renders every consumer on each parent render; memoise it (useMemo) or split the context.
  • Reading state right after setState: you get the old value. Updates are queued; use the functional form setX((x) => x + 1) when the next value depends on the last.
  • State lives at a position in the tree: changing the component type or the key at that position destroys it; the same type at the same position keeps it.
  • Every effect that subscribes, starts a timer or a request returns the cleanup that undoes it; <StrictMode> runs effects twice in development to prove the cleanup works.
  • List every reactive value an effect reads in its dependencies; to read the latest value without re-running, use useEffectEvent — not a stale-closure workaround.
  • Mutating state in place (items.push(x)) does nothing visible: React compares by reference. Replace it ([...items, x]) — or use Immer when updates are deep.
  • Server data (caching, refetching, deduping) is better owned by a data library (TanStack Query, SWR, a router loader) than by hand-rolled effects.

The React sheet's task screen built by hand — elements, events, keyed updates, recycled rows and layout in code — with the DOM API and with jQuery 4.

Build the screen with the DOM API

Create, configure, then insert once; set text with textContent and state with properties, and stamp each row with its id.

import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { document } = new JSDOM(`<main id="app"></main>`).window;

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };

function createTaskRow(task: Task): HTMLLIElement {
  const row = document.createElement("li");
  row.dataset.id = task.id;                       // the key later updates look rows up by
  row.className = task.done ? "task done" : "task";

  const box = document.createElement("input");
  box.type = "checkbox";
  box.checked = task.done;                        // a property: live state, not serialised HTML

  const title = document.createElement("span");
  title.textContent = task.title;                 // text, never markup: a title cannot inject HTML

  const label = document.createElement("label"); // the title names the checkbox for assistive tech
  label.append(box, " ", title);
  row.append(label);
  return row;
}

function createTaskScreen(tasks: readonly Task[]): HTMLElement {
  const heading = Object.assign(document.createElement("h1"), { textContent: "Tasks" });
  const count = Object.assign(document.createElement("p"), { className: "count" });
  count.textContent = `${tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length} open`;

  const list = document.createElement("ul");
  list.append(...tasks.map(createTaskRow));      // build detached, insert once: one layout

  const screen = document.createElement("section");
  screen.append(heading, count, list);
  return screen;
}

const tasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "t1", title: "Rotate API keys", done: true },
  { id: "t2", title: "Review deploy PR", done: false },
];
document.querySelector("#app")!.replaceChildren(createTaskScreen(tasks));

for (const el of document.querySelectorAll("h1, .count, li")) console.log(el.outerHTML);
console.log("checked:", [...document.querySelectorAll("input")].map((box) => box.checked).join(","));
Result
<h1>Tasks</h1>
<p class="count">1 open</p>
<li data-id="t1" class="task done"><label><input type="checkbox"> <span>Rotate API keys</span></label></li>
<li data-id="t2" class="task"><label><input type="checkbox"> <span>Review deploy PR</span></label></li>
checked: true,false
Setup

  2. npm i jsdom and npm i -D @types/jsdom
  3. In a browser drop the JSDOM line: the page's own document is used the same way
  4. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts

The same screen with jQuery 4 — toggle and bulk clear

Bulk work is where jQuery is still terse, because one call acts on every matched row — the whole screen with a count and an add form is on the jQuery vs React vs SolidJS sheet.

import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";
import { jQueryFactory } from "jquery/factory";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main id="app"></main>`);
const $ = jQueryFactory(window as unknown as Window);      // jsdom's window type is narrower than lib.dom's

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };

// The array is the owner: each handler updates it first, then the nodes that show it.
let tasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "t1", title: "Rotate API keys", done: true },
  { id: "t2", title: "Review deploy PR", done: false },
  { id: "t3", title: "Rotate TLS certificate", done: false },
];

function row(t: Task): JQuery<HTMLElement> {
  const $box = $("<input>", { type: "checkbox" }).prop("checked", t.done);
  const $label = $("<label>").append($box, " ", $("<span>").text(t.title));
  return $("<li>", { class: t.done ? "task done" : "task", "data-id": t.id }).append($label);
}

const $app = $("#app").append($("<button>", { type: "button", text: "Clear completed" }), $("<ul>"));
$app.find("ul").append(tasks.map(row));

$app.on("change", "li input", (e) => {                     // delegated: covers every row
  const $row = $(e.currentTarget).closest("li");
  const done = $(e.currentTarget).prop("checked") === true;
  tasks = tasks.map((t) => (t.id === $row.attr("data-id") ? { ...t, done } : t));
  $row.toggleClass("done", done);
});

$app.on("click", "button", () => {
  tasks = tasks.filter((t) => !t.done);
  $app.find("li.done").remove();                            // one call, every matching row
});

const show = (step: string) => {
  const rows = $app.find("li").map((_, li) => $(li).text().trim() + ($(li).hasClass("done") ? " ✓" : ""));
  console.log(`${step}: ${rows.get().join(", ")} | data: ${tasks.map((t) => (t.done ? `${t.id}✓` : t.id))}`);
};

$app.find("[data-id=t2] input").prop("checked", true).trigger("change");   // the user ticks t2…
show("ticked t2");

$app.find("button").trigger("click");                       // …and clears completed
show("cleared");
Result
ticked t2: Rotate API keys ✓, Review deploy PR ✓, Rotate TLS certificate | data: t1✓,t2✓,t3
cleared: Rotate TLS certificate | data: t3

Events — delegation and teardown

Enhance server-rendered rows with one listener per container, and remove every listener at once with an AbortSignal.

import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<ul id="tasks">
  <li data-id="t1"><label><input type=checkbox> Rotate keys</label> <button class=remove>Remove</button></li>
  <li data-id="t2"><label><input type=checkbox> Review PR</label> <button class=remove>Remove</button></li>
</ul>`);
const { document, AbortController } = window;     // jsdom accepts only its own AbortSignal

type TaskEvents = { toggle(id: string, done: boolean): void; remove(id: string): void };

function enhanceTaskList(list: HTMLElement, on: TaskEvents): () => void {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  const options = { signal: controller.signal };
  const rowOf = (target: EventTarget | null) =>
    (target as Element | null)?.closest<HTMLElement>("li[data-id]");

  list.addEventListener("change", (event) => {
    const box = event.target as HTMLInputElement;
    const row = rowOf(box);
    if (row && box.matches("input[type=checkbox]")) on.toggle(row.dataset.id!, box.checked);
  }, options);

  list.addEventListener("click", (event) => {
    const row = rowOf((event.target as Element).closest("button.remove"));
    if (!row) return;
    on.remove(row.dataset.id!);
    row.remove();
  }, options);

  return () => controller.abort();                // one call removes every listener added with `options`
}

const list = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#tasks")!;
const teardown = enhanceTaskList(list, {
  toggle: (id, done) => console.log(`toggle ${id} → ${done}`),
  remove: (id) => console.log(`remove ${id}`),
});

list.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("[data-id=t1] input")!.click();
list.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>("[data-id=t2] button")!.click();

teardown();
list.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("[data-id=t1] input")!.click();   // no longer handled
console.log("rows left:", list.querySelectorAll("li").length);
Result
toggle t1 → true
remove t2
rows left: 1

Keep the list in sync with the data by hand

A keyed patch — remove, update in place, insert, move — reuses each row's node, so listeners and in-progress state survive; a row that insertBefore moves still loses focus, so put it back.

import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { document } = new JSDOM(`<ul id="tasks"></ul>`).window;

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };
const task = (id: string, title: string, done = false): Task => ({ id, title, done });

function createRow(task: Task): HTMLLIElement {
  const label = Object.assign(document.createElement("label"), { textContent: task.title });
  label.prepend(Object.assign(document.createElement("input"), { type: "checkbox" }));
  const row = document.createElement("li");                  // <li><label><input>title</label></li>
  row.append(label);
  return row;
}

function syncList(list: HTMLElement, tasks: readonly Task[], rows: Map<string, HTMLLIElement>): void {
  const focused = list.contains(document.activeElement) ? (document.activeElement as HTMLElement) : null;
  const wanted = new Set(tasks.map((t) => t.id));
  for (const [id, row] of rows) {
    if (wanted.has(id)) continue;
    row.remove();
    rows.delete(id);
  }
  tasks.forEach((task, index) => {
    const row = rows.get(task.id) ?? createRow(task);       // `rows`: task id → its node, across updates
    rows.set(task.id, row);
    const box = row.querySelector("input")!;
    if (box.checked !== task.done) box.checked = task.done;  // update in place: write only what changed
    const current = list.children[index] ?? null;
    if (current !== row) list.insertBefore(row, current);   // insert or move into place
  });
  if (focused?.isConnected && document.activeElement !== focused) focused.focus();   // moving blurred it
}

const list = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#tasks")!;
const rows = new Map<string, HTMLLIElement>();
syncList(list, [task("t1", "Rotate keys"), task("t2", "Review PR"), task("t3", "Tag release")], rows);

// The user is on t2 when an update drops t3, marks t1 done, adds t4 and pins t2 to the top (so t2 moves).
const t2 = rows.get("t2")!;
t2.querySelector("input")!.focus();
syncList(list, [task("t2", "Review PR"), task("t1", "Rotate keys", true), task("t4", "Email QA")], rows);

const shown = [...list.children]
  .map((li) => li.textContent + (li.querySelector("input")!.checked ? " ✓" : ""));
console.log(shown.join(" | "));
console.log("t2 same node:", rows.get("t2") === t2, "| focus on t2:", t2.contains(document.activeElement));
Result
Review PR | Rotate keys ✓ | Email QA
t2 same node: true | focus on t2: true

  2. npm i jsdom and npm i -D @types/jsdom
  3. In a browser drop the JSDOM line: the page's own document is used the same way
  4. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts

What goes wrong when you rebuild with innerHTML

Re-rendering by string is the tempting shortcut — every row becomes a new node, and any user text becomes markup.

import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { document } = new JSDOM(`<ul id="tasks"></ul>`).window;
type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };
const list = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#tasks")!;

function renderWithInnerHTML(tasks: readonly Task[]): void {
  list.innerHTML = tasks
    .map((t) => `<li data-id="${t.id}"><input type="checkbox"${t.done ? " checked" : ""}> ${t.title}</li>`)
    .join("");
}

const tasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "t1", title: "Rotate keys", done: false },
  { id: "t2", title: "Review PR", done: false },
];
renderWithInnerHTML(tasks);
const before = list.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("[data-id=t2] input")!;
before.focus();
let clicks = 0;
before.addEventListener("click", () => clicks++);            // a per-row listener

// a user names a task with markup; one more render later…
renderWithInnerHTML([...tasks, { id: "t3", title: `<img src="x" onerror="stealCookies()">`, done: false }]);
const after = list.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("[data-id=t2] input")!;
after.click();

console.log("same node:", before === after);
console.log("focus on:", document.activeElement?.tagName);
console.log("listener calls:", clicks);
console.log("injected <img> elements:", list.querySelectorAll("img").length);
Result
same node: false
focus on: BODY
listener calls: 0
injected <img> elements: 1
Setup

  2. npm i jsdom and npm i -D @types/jsdom
  3. In a browser drop the JSDOM line: the page's own document is used the same way
  4. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts

Ran with Node 24.16.0, TypeScript 5.9.3 on 2026-11-16: the output matched the result shown.

Recycle rows for a long list

For thousands of rows inside a fixed-height overflow-y: auto viewport, keep a small pool of nodes and re-fill them as the user scrolls — the DOM's version of a reusable cell.

import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<div id="log"></div>`, { pretendToBeVisual: true });   // with rAF
const { document } = window;

function createRecycledList(viewport: HTMLElement, items: readonly string[], rowHeight = 32, visible = 6) {
  const content = document.createElement("div");
  content.style.cssText = `position: relative; height: ${items.length * rowHeight}px`;   // full scroll height
  const pool = Array.from({ length: visible + 2 }, () => {     // +2 covers partly visible rows
    const row = content.appendChild(document.createElement("div"));
    row.style.cssText = `position: absolute; inset-inline: 0; height: ${rowHeight}px`;
    return row;
  });
  viewport.replaceChildren(content);

  function render(): void {
    const first = Math.floor(viewport.scrollTop / rowHeight);
    pool.forEach((row, i) => {
      const index = first + i;
      row.hidden = index >= items.length;
      row.style.transform = `translateY(${index * rowHeight}px)`;
      row.textContent = items[index] ?? "";                  // the same node, new content
    });
  }

  let frame = 0;
  viewport.addEventListener("scroll", () => {                // at most one render per frame
    window.cancelAnimationFrame(frame);
    frame = window.requestAnimationFrame(render);
  }, { passive: true });

  render();
  return pool;
}

const entries = Array.from({ length: 10_000 }, (_, i) => `Task #${i + 1} updated`);
const viewport = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#log")!;
const pool = createRecycledList(viewport, entries);
const firstRows = () => pool.slice(0, 3).map((row) => row.textContent).join(" / ");
console.log(firstRows());

viewport.scrollTop = 3200;                                   // the user scrolls…
viewport.dispatchEvent(new window.Event("scroll"));
await new Promise((resolve) => window.requestAnimationFrame(resolve));   // …and the next frame renders
console.log(firstRows(), `| ${pool[0]!.parentElement!.children.length} nodes for ${entries.length} rows`);
Result
Task #1 updated / Task #2 updated / Task #3 updated
Task #101 updated / Task #102 updated / Task #103 updated | 8 nodes for 10000 rows
Setup
  1. Node.js 22.18 or later (it runs .mts files directly by stripping the types)
  2. npm i jsdom and npm i -D @types/jsdom
  3. In a browser drop the JSDOM line: the page's own document is used the same way
  4. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts

Sources: Window.requestAnimationFrame — MDN

Layout and measurement in code

Let CSS lay out; use code to react to a container's size, to position against a measured element, and to batch reads before writes.

const panel = document.querySelector<HTMLElement>("#tasks-panel")!;

// 1. Container-driven layout: the panel's width, not the window's, picks the layout.
const resizes = new ResizeObserver(([entry]) => {
  if (!entry) return;
  const width = entry.contentBoxSize[0]?.inlineSize ?? entry.contentRect.width;
  panel.classList.toggle("compact", width < 480);
  // read in CSS as grid-template-columns: repeat(var(--columns), 1fr)
  panel.style.setProperty("--columns", String(Math.max(1, Math.floor(width / 240))));
  equaliseRowHeights([...panel.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>(".task")]);   // rows re-wrapped
});
resizes.observe(panel);

// 2. Position a menu under its trigger: measure once, then write.
function placeBelow(menu: HTMLElement, trigger: HTMLElement): void {
  const rect = trigger.getBoundingClientRect();              // viewport coordinates; forces layout
  menu.style.top = `${rect.bottom + window.scrollY + 4}px`;
  menu.style.left = `${rect.left + window.scrollX}px`;
}
const byId = (id: string) => document.getElementById(id)!;
placeBelow(byId("filter-menu"), byId("filter-button"));

// 3. Batch: clear all, read all, write all — alternating forces one layout per row ("layout thrashing").
function equaliseRowHeights(rows: HTMLElement[]): void {
  requestAnimationFrame(() => {
    for (const row of rows) row.style.minHeight = "";                // let rows shrink back first
    const tallest = Math.max(...rows.map((row) => row.getBoundingClientRect().height));
    for (const row of rows) row.style.minHeight = `${tallest}px`;
  });
}

// On teardown: resizes.disconnect()
Result

The panel switches to its compact layout below 480px wide and its grid gains a column per 240px; the filter menu sits 4px under its button; after every resize each row takes the tallest row's height, growing or shrinking.

Setup
  1. A page containing <section id="tasks-panel"> with .task rows and a #filter-button, and a #filter-menu styled position: absolute placed directly under <body> (so page coordinates apply)
  2. Compile with tsc (lib including DOM) or a bundler, and load the output with <script type="module">

Compiled with Node 24.16.0, TypeScript 5.9.3 on 2026-11-16; not run here — running it needs a browser page with the elements named in the setup (jsdom has no layout).

Sources: ResizeObserver — MDN · Element.getBoundingClientRect — MDN

jQuery → modern DOM

Everything jQuery smoothed over now has a native equivalent in every supported browser.

jQueryModern DOMNote

$(fn), $(document).ready(fn)<script type="module"> (deferred) or DOMContentLoaded
.on("click", ".row", fn)addEventListener("click", …) + event.target.closest(".row")delegation by hand

.addClass / .toggleClass(c, on)classList.add(c) / classList.toggle(c, on)jQuery 4 removed the class-less .toggleClass(state) / .toggleClass() forms; .toggleClass(c, on) remains
.attr / .prop / .datasetAttribute / the property / dataset.data() also caches and parses JSON; dataset is always strings
.text(s) / .html(s)textContent / innerHTMLinnerHTML with data is an injection hole
.append .prepend .before .after .remove .empty()the same names natively; replaceChildren() to empty or swap
.closest / .find / .parent() / .children()closest / querySelectorAll / parentElement / childrenchildren is a live HTMLCollection
.css({ … }), .width(), .offset()classes and style.setProperty; getBoundingClientRect()
.fadeIn() / .animate()CSS transitions, or element.animate() (Web Animations)runs off the main thread where it can

$.ajax / $.getJSONfetch + AbortController

$.trim / $.isArray / $.parseJSON / $.nows.trim() / Array.isArray / JSON.parse / Date.now()removed in jQuery 4

When jQuery still earns its place — and what bites by hand

Programmatic UI is fine for small, stable screens; past that, the bookkeeping is the bug source.

  • jQuery earns its place in an existing jQuery codebase and its plugins (DataTables, Select2, a CMS theme): upgrade to 4, keep it, wrap it — rewriting working UI buys little.
  • It is still terse for quick enhancement of server-rendered pages: implicit iteration over every match, delegated and namespaced events, .trigger.
  • New apps: no state model, no keyed updates, no components — you rebuild a worse framework by hand. Use the DOM API for small widgets, a framework for screens.
  • One owner of the data and one update(data) path that patches by key; never let event handlers edit the DOM and the data separately.
  • Delegate events to the container: one listener instead of one closure per row, and rows added later are covered.
  • innerHTML / .html() with data: new nodes on every render (focus, scroll and listeners lost) and an injection hole. Build nodes and set textContent.
  • Combining hand-written DOM code or jQuery plugins with React or Solid (refs, islands, one owner per subtree) is on the jQuery vs React vs SolidJS sheet.
  • Moving a focused node with insertBefore blurs it; querySelectorAll is a snapshot while children is live — re-query after you mutate.

jQuery vs React vs SolidJS

Translate any answer between the imperative DOM, React's re-render-and-diff and Solid's fine-grained signals — and embed one inside another.

  • browser
  • jQuery
  • React
  • SolidJS
  • typescript >=5.5
  • jquery >=4.0
  • react >=19.0
  • solid-js >=1.9
  • node >=22.18
  • a browser page (the examples run in Node against jsdom)

Sources: jQuery API documentation · Learn React — react.dev · SolidJS documentation

Concept mapping

The same job in each model; the jQuery column is also what the other two do for you underneath.

ConceptjQuery (imperative)React (re-render + diff)SolidJS (fine-grained)

local statea variable + your own update()useState / useReducercreateSignal / createStore
derived valuerecomputed in each handler that changes the inputcomputed in render (useMemo if expensive)createMemo or a plain function () => …

events.on("click", ".row", fn) (delegated)onClick={fn} (React delegates at the root)onClick={fn} (delegated for common events)

The same task screen — jQuery and React

Both programs drive the screen identically and print the same result; jQuery keeps data and DOM in step by hand, React derives the DOM from state.

jQuery 4 — imperative
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";
import { jQueryFactory } from "jquery/factory";

const form = `<form><label>New task <input name="title"></label> <button>Add</button></form>`;
const { window } = new JSDOM(`<main>${form}<p class="count"></p><ul></ul></main>`);
const $ = jQueryFactory(window as unknown as Window);

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };

const tasks: Task[] = [
  { id: "t1", title: "Rotate keys", done: true },
  { id: "t2", title: "Review PR", done: false },
];

// Every change must update the data AND each node that shows it.
function appendRow(task: Task): void {
  const $box = $("<input>", { type: "checkbox" }).prop("checked", task.done);
  const $label = $("<label>").append($box, " ", $("<span>").text(task.title));
  $("<li>", { "data-id": task.id }).append($label).appendTo("ul");
}

function updateCount(): void {
  $(".count").text(`${tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length} open`);
}

tasks.forEach(appendRow);
updateCount();

$("ul").on("change", "input", (e) => {
  const id = $(e.currentTarget).closest("li").attr("data-id");
  const task = tasks.find((t) => t.id === id);
  if (task) task.done = $(e.currentTarget).prop("checked") === true;
  updateCount();
});

$("form").on("submit", (e) => {
  e.preventDefault();
  const task: Task = { id: `t${tasks.length + 1}`, title: String($("[name=title]").val()), done: false };
  tasks.push(task);
  appendRow(task);
  updateCount();
  $("[name=title]").val("");
});

$("li[data-id=t2] input").prop("checked", true).trigger("change");   // the user ticks t2…
$("[name=title]").val("Email QA");
$("form").trigger("submit");                                        // …and adds a task

const rows = $("li").map((_, li) => $(li).text().trim() + ($(li).find("input").prop("checked") ? " ✓" : ""));
console.log(`${$(".count").text()} | ${rows.get().join(", ")}`);
React 19 — declarative
import { act, useState, type FormEvent } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<div id="root"></div>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");
const { fireEvent } = await import("@testing-library/dom");

function TaskScreen() {                                      // the screen as a function of state
  const [tasks, setTasks] = useState([
    { id: "t1", title: "Rotate keys", done: true },
    { id: "t2", title: "Review PR", done: false },
  ]);
  const [title, setTitle] = useState("");                    // controlled: each keystroke re-renders

  const toggle = (id: string) => setTasks((ts) => ts.map((t) => (t.id === id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)));
  const add = (e: FormEvent) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    setTasks((ts) => [...ts, { id: `t${ts.length + 1}`, title, done: false }]);
    setTitle("");
  };

  return (
    <main>
      <form onSubmit={add}>
        <input aria-label="New task" name="title" value={title} onChange={(e) => setTitle(e.target.value)} />
        <button>Add</button>
      </form>
      <p className="count">{tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length} open</p>
      <ul>{tasks.map((t) => (
        <li key={t.id} data-id={t.id}><label>
          <input type="checkbox" checked={t.done} onChange={() => toggle(t.id)} /> <span>{t.title}</span>
        </label></li>
      ))}</ul>
    </main>
  );
}

await act(() => createRoot(document.querySelector("#root")!).render(<TaskScreen />));

await act(() => document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("li[data-id=t2] input")!.click());   // ticks t2…
await act(() => fireEvent.change(document.querySelector("[name=title]")!, { target: { value: "Email QA" } }));
await act(() => fireEvent.submit(document.querySelector("form")!));                         // …adds a task

const rows = [...document.querySelectorAll("li")]
  .map((li) => li.textContent!.trim() + (li.querySelector("input")!.checked ? " ✓" : ""));
console.log(`${document.querySelector(".count")!.textContent} | ${rows.join(", ")}`);
Result
1 open | Rotate keys ✓, Review PR ✓, Email QA

  2. The JSDOM lines stand in for a browser page; in a browser use import $ from "jquery" and the page's document

The same task screen — SolidJS

Looks like the React version, behaves like the jQuery one — the component runs once and each signal read in JSX becomes a direct DOM update.

import { createSignal, For } from "solid-js";
import { createStore } from "solid-js/store";
import { render } from "solid-js/web";

type Task = { id: string; title: string; done: boolean };

function TaskScreen(props: { initial: Task[] }) {             // runs once, wiring signals to nodes
  const [tasks, setTasks] = createStore<Task[]>([...props.initial]);
  const [title, setTitle] = createSignal("");
  const open = () => tasks.filter((t) => !t.done).length;   // re-evaluated only where it is read

  const add = (e: Event) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    setTasks((ts) => [...ts, { id: `t${ts.length + 1}`, title: title(), done: false }]);
    setTitle("");
  };

  return (
    <main>
      <form onSubmit={add}>
        <input aria-label="New task" name="title" value={title()}
          onInput={(e) => setTitle(e.currentTarget.value)} />
        <button>Add</button>
      </form>
      <p class="count">{open()} open</p>
      <ul>
        <For each={tasks}>{(task, index) => (
          <li data-id={task.id}>
            <label>
              <input type="checkbox" checked={task.done}
                onChange={(e) => setTasks(index(), "done", e.currentTarget.checked)} />
              <span>{task.title}</span>
            </label>
          </li>
        )}</For>
      </ul>
    </main>
  );
}

const initial: Task[] = [
  { id: "t1", title: "Rotate keys", done: true },
  { id: "t2", title: "Review PR", done: false },
];
render(() => <TaskScreen initial={initial} />, document.querySelector("#app")!);
Result

The same screen as the two above; ticking a box updates only that row's checked and the count text — no component function runs again.

Setup

  2. A page containing <main id="app"></main>

What re-runs on an update

The key distinction between the three UI models.

On…jQueryReactSolidJS
ticking one taskyour change handler: the task's data and the count textTaskScreen re-renders, every row is re-rendered and diffed, one checkbox and the count are patchedthat row's checked binding and the count text node
typing one characternothing — the input holds its own valueTaskScreen and all its rows re-render (unless rows are memo)the input's value binding
adding a taskyour submit handler: one <li>, one counta re-render; the keyed diff inserts one <li><For> creates one row; the count updates
the component function—runs on every renderruns once
what you must get rightevery place a value is shownkeys, stable props and callbacks, effect dependenciesread signals where they are used; never destructure props
how it scalesbookkeeping grows with every featurerender cost grows with subtree size; memoise or let the React Compiler do itcost grows with the number of bindings, not the tree size

A jQuery plugin inside React — through a ref

React owns the element; the plugin owns its behaviour — create it on mount, push props in with an effect, destroy it on unmount.

import { act, useEffect, useEffectEvent, useRef } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";
import { jQueryFactory } from "jquery/factory";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`<div id="root"></div>`);
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document: window.document, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");
const $ = jQueryFactory(window as unknown as Window);

declare global {
  interface JQuery<TElement = HTMLElement> { tagInput(command?: "set" | "destroy", tags?: string[]): this }
}

const parseTags = (text: string) => text.split(",").map((t) => t.trim()).filter(Boolean);

$.fn.tagInput = function (command, tags = []) {
  if (command === "set") return this.val(tags.join(", "));
  if (command === "destroy") return this.off(".tagInput").removeClass("tag-input");
  return this.addClass("tag-input").on("change.tagInput", (e) => {
    $(e.currentTarget).trigger("tags:change", [parseTags(String($(e.currentTarget).val()))]);
  });
};

function TagInput({ tags, onChange }: { tags: string[]; onChange: (tags: string[]) => void }) {
  const input = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
  const emit = useEffectEvent(onChange);            // the latest callback, without re-creating the plugin

  useEffect(() => {
    const $input = $(input.current!).tagInput();
    $input.on("tags:change", (_e, next: string[]) => emit(next));
    return () => {
      $input.off("tags:change").tagInput("destroy");
    };
  }, []);

  useEffect(() => { $(input.current!).tagInput("set", tags); }, [tags]);   // props → plugin

  return <input ref={input} aria-label="Labels" />;
}

const root = createRoot(document.querySelector("#root")!);
const log = (next: string[]) => console.log("onChange", next);
await act(() => root.render(<TagInput tags={["urgent"]} onChange={log} />));

const field = document.querySelector("input")!;
console.log(`mounted: class="${field.className}" value="${field.value}"`);

await act(() => { $(field).val("urgent, backend").trigger("change"); });   // the user edits in the plugin

await act(() => root.unmount());
console.log(`unmounted: plugin destroyed = ${!field.classList.contains("tag-input")}`);
Result
mounted: class="tag-input" value="urgent"
onChange [ 'urgent', 'backend' ]
unmounted: plugin destroyed = true
Setup
  1. npm i jquery react react-dom jsdom and npm i -D esbuild @types/jquery @types/react @types/react-dom @types/jsdom
  2. In an app import $ from "jquery" and the real plugin (Select2, a tag editor…); the JSDOM lines and the stand-in tagInput plugin — init, "set", "destroy" and its own event — make the file runnable alone
  3. Save as main.tsx, then npx esbuild main.tsx --jsx=automatic --format=esm --outfile=main.mjs && node main.mjs

A React island in a server-rendered page

Keep the page server-rendered (Rails, Django, PHP) and mount React only where it is interactive; talk to the rest of the page with DOM events.

import { act, useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { JSDOM } from "jsdom";

const { window } = new JSDOM(`
  <header>Shop <span data-island="cart-badge" data-count="2"></span></header>
  <article><h1>Mechanical keyboard</h1><button class="legacy-add">Add to cart</button></article>`);
const { document, CustomEvent } = window;                // jsdom dispatches only its own event objects
Object.assign(globalThis, { window, document, CustomEvent, IS_REACT_ACT_ENVIRONMENT: true });
const { createRoot } = await import("react-dom/client");

function CartBadge({ initialCount }: { initialCount: number }) {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(initialCount);

  useEffect(() => {
    const onAdd = () => setCount((c) => c + 1);
    document.addEventListener("cart:add", onAdd);    // the page's legacy code announces additions
    return () => document.removeEventListener("cart:add", onAdd);
  }, []);

  // a live region: screen readers announce each new count
  return (
    <span className="badge" role="status">
      {count}<span className="visually-hidden"> items in cart</span>
    </span>
  );
}

// One entry per island type; server-rendered data travels in data-* attributes.
const islands: Record<string, (el: HTMLElement) => void> = {
  "cart-badge": (el) => createRoot(el).render(<CartBadge initialCount={Number(el.dataset.count ?? 0)} />),
};

await act(() => {
  for (const el of document.querySelectorAll<HTMLElement>("[data-island]")) {
    islands[el.dataset.island ?? ""]?.(el);
  }
});
console.log(document.querySelector("header")!.innerHTML);

// The page's existing code keeps working: it only dispatches an event.
const announceAdd = () => document.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:add"));
document.querySelector(".legacy-add")!.addEventListener("click", announceAdd);

await act(() => document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>(".legacy-add")!.click());
console.log(document.querySelector("header")!.innerHTML);
Result
Shop <span data-island="cart-badge" data-count="2"><span class="badge" role="status">2<span class="visually-hidden"> items in cart</span></span></span>
Shop <span data-island="cart-badge" data-count="2"><span class="badge" role="status">3<span class="visually-hidden"> items in cart</span></span></span>
Setup

  2. In a browser the markup is the server's page and the JSDOM lines go; bundle the mount script and load it with <script type="module">
  3. Save as main.tsx, then npx esbuild main.tsx --jsx=automatic --format=esm --outfile=main.mjs && node main.mjs

Key concepts

The answers to "how do jQuery, React and Solid differ?" — one breath each.

  • jQuery is imperative: you find nodes and mutate them; the DOM is the state, and keeping several views of one value in step is your job.
  • React is declarative, re-render and diff: a component is a function of state; on change React re-runs it and patches the difference. Identity is position + key.
  • Solid is declarative, fine-grained: components run once and compile to real DOM nodes; each signal read in JSX is a subscription that updates exactly one place. No virtual DOM.
  • React's cost is re-rendering subtrees (mitigated by memo and the React Compiler); Solid's cost is reactivity rules (no destructuring props, read signals lazily).
  • Same JSX, different semantics: in React {count} is a value captured at render; in Solid {count()} is a live binding the compiler wraps in an effect.
  • Coexistence is normal: jQuery plugins inside React via a ref and effect cleanup; React or Solid islands inside server-rendered pages; migrate leaf-first.
  • Never let two owners mutate the same DOM subtree — the framework's picture of the DOM goes stale and the next update corrupts it.

SolidJS — Components & Fine-Grained Reactivity

Signals, memos and effects and their tracking rules, components that run once, control flow, stores and resources — and the traps a React developer walks into.

  • browser
  • SolidJS
  • typescript >=5.5
  • solid-js >=1.9
  • node >=22.18
  • a browser page with SolidJS (the reactive examples run in Node with Solid's browser build)

Sources: SolidJS documentation · Signals — SolidJS

The primitives and when each one re-runs

Everything is a signal or a computation that reads signals; a computation re-runs only when something it read in its last run changes.

PrimitiveWhat it isRe-runs when
createSignal(v)a [get, set] pair; call get() to read— (it is the source)
() => a() + b()a derived signal: a plain functionevery time it is called
createMemo(fn)a cached derived value; notifies readers only if the result changeda signal it read changes
createEffect(fn)a side effect, run after renderinga signal it read in its last run changes
on(deps, fn, { defer })an effect body with explicit dependenciesone of deps changes
untrack(fn)a read that does not subscribenever
batch(fn)groups writes; dependents run once at the end—
onCleanup(fn)teardown for the current computation or componentbefore the next run, and on dispose
onMount(fn)runs once after the component's DOM existsnever again
createStore(obj)a deeply reactive proxy; one signal per property, created lazilyper property read
createResource(source, fetcher)async data with loading, error, state, latestsource() changes, or refetch()
createRoot(fn)an owner for computations outside a component (render makes one for you)—; dispose() stops everything in it

Signals

A signal is a getter and a setter; reading the getter inside a computation subscribes that computation, reading it anywhere else is a plain read.

import { createEffect, createRoot, createSignal } from "solid-js";

const cart = createRoot((dispose) => {
  const [quantity, setQuantity] = createSignal(1);
  const [coupon, setCoupon] = createSignal<string | null>(null);

  // reads quantity() and coupon(), so it re-runs when either changes
  createEffect(() => console.log(`qty=${quantity()} coupon=${coupon() ?? "none"}`));

  return { quantity, setQuantity, setCoupon, dispose };
});

cart.setQuantity(2);
cart.setQuantity((q) => q + 1);             // updater form: based on the current value
cart.setQuantity(3);                        // same value (===): nothing re-runs
cart.setCoupon("SPRING10");

console.log("plain read:", cart.quantity()); // outside a computation: no subscription

cart.dispose();                             // stops every computation created in the root
cart.setQuantity(10);                       // logs nothing: the effect is gone
Result
qty=1 coupon=none
qty=2 coupon=none
qty=3 coupon=none
qty=3 coupon=SPRING10
plain read: 3
Setup
  1. Node.js 22.18 or later (it runs .mts files directly by stripping the types)
  2. npm i solid-js
  3. Save as main.mts and run node --conditions=browser main.mts — Node's default resolves Solid's server build, where effects never re-run
  4. In a Solid app the same code runs inside a component; render provides the root

Derived values and memos

A plain function is enough for cheap derivations; createMemo caches an expensive one and stops propagation when its result did not change.

import { createEffect, createMemo, createRoot, createSignal } from "solid-js";

type Line = { name: string; unitCents: number; qty: number };

let subtotalRuns = 0;
let bannerRuns = 0;

const checkout = createRoot(() => {
  const [lines, setLines] = createSignal<Line[]>([{ name: "Keyboard", unitCents: 8_900, qty: 1 }]);
  const [shippingCents, setShipping] = createSignal(500);

  const subtotal = createMemo(() => {              // computed once per change, shared by every reader
    subtotalRuns++;
    return lines().reduce((sum, l) => sum + l.unitCents * l.qty, 0);
  });
  const total = () => subtotal() + shippingCents();  // cheap: a derived function, no memo
  const freeShipping = createMemo(() => subtotal() >= 10_000);   // readers wake only when it flips

  createEffect(() => console.log(`subtotal ${subtotal()} total ${total()}`));
  createEffect(() => {                             // e.g. show or hide a free-shipping banner
    freeShipping();
    bannerRuns++;
  });

  return { setLines, setShipping, subtotal };
});

checkout.setShipping(0);                             // subtotal is not recomputed
checkout.setLines((ls) => [...ls, { name: "Mouse", unitCents: 2_500, qty: 1 }]);

checkout.subtotal();                                 // cached reads
checkout.subtotal();
console.log(`subtotal computed ${subtotalRuns} times, banner updated ${bannerRuns} times`);
Result
subtotal 8900 total 9400
subtotal 8900 total 8900
subtotal 11400 total 11400
subtotal computed 2 times, banner updated 2 times

Effects and their tracking rules

Dependencies are whatever the last run read — so a branch not taken is not tracked, untrack opts a read out, on() names them explicitly, and onCleanup undoes the previous run.

import { createEffect, createRoot, createSignal, on, onCleanup, untrack } from "solid-js";

const session = createRoot((dispose) => {
  const [signedIn, setSignedIn] = createSignal(false);
  const [userName, setUserName] = createSignal("guest");
  const [cartCount, setCartCount] = createSignal(0);
  const [currency, setCurrency] = createSignal("EUR");

  // 1. dynamic: while signed out, userName() is never read, so it is not a dependency
  createEffect(() => console.log(signedIn() ? `hello ${userName()}` : "signed out"));

  // 2. untrack: show the currency, but re-run only when the count changes
  createEffect(() => console.log(`cart ${cartCount()} (${untrack(currency)})`));

  // 3. on(): only the listed signal is tracked — userName() inside is not; `defer` skips the first run
  const audit = (isIn: boolean) => console.log(`audit: ${userName()} signed ${isIn ? "in" : "out"}`);
  createEffect(on(signedIn, audit, { defer: true }));

  // 4. onCleanup: runs before the next run and on dispose — subscriptions, timers, sockets
  createEffect(() => {
    const channel = `prices:${currency()}`;
    console.log(`subscribe ${channel}`);
    onCleanup(() => console.log(`unsubscribe ${channel}`));
  });

  return { setSignedIn, setUserName, setCartCount, setCurrency, dispose };
});

session.setUserName("ada");                         // nothing: not tracked yet
session.setSignedIn(true);
session.setUserName("grace");                       // the greeting updates; the audit stays quiet
session.setCurrency("USD");                         // the cart effect stays quiet
session.setCartCount(1);
session.dispose();
Result
signed out
cart 0 (EUR)
subscribe prices:EUR
hello ada
audit: ada signed in
hello grace
unsubscribe prices:EUR
subscribe prices:USD
cart 1 (USD)
unsubscribe prices:USD

batch — event handlers are not batched for you

In Solid 1.x each write outside an effect runs its dependents at once, so two writes in a click handler show an in-between value; wrap related writes in batch.

import { batch, createEffect, createRoot, createSignal } from "solid-js";

const checkout = createRoot(() => {
  const [subtotal, setSubtotal] = createSignal(8_900);
  const [discount, setDiscount] = createSignal(0);
  createEffect(() => console.log(`total shown: ${subtotal() - discount()}`));   // e.g. the price label
  return { setSubtotal, setDiscount };
});

// Handlers are plain functions; Solid's delegated onClick calls them the same way an EventTarget does.
function applyCouponUnbatched() {
  checkout.setSubtotal(8_000);                    // dependents run now: new subtotal, old discount
  checkout.setDiscount(800);
}

function applyCouponBatched() {
  batch(() => {
    checkout.setSubtotal(7_000);
    checkout.setDiscount(700);
  });                                             // dependents run once, with both values
}

const button = new EventTarget();                 // stands in for the button element

button.addEventListener("click", applyCouponUnbatched, { once: true });
console.log("— click, no batch");
button.dispatchEvent(new Event("click"));

button.addEventListener("click", applyCouponBatched, { once: true });
console.log("— click, batch");
button.dispatchEvent(new Event("click"));
Result
total shown: 8900
— click, no batch
total shown: 8000
total shown: 7200
— click, batch
total shown: 6300

Components run once — why destructuring props breaks reactivity

JSX passes props as getters; destructuring calls each getter once, in a function that never runs again, so the value freezes.

import { createComponent, createEffect, createRoot, createSignal, mergeProps } from "solid-js";

type PriceProps = { cents: number; currency?: string };
const format = (cents: number, currency: string) => `${(cents / 100).toFixed(2)} ${currency}`;

function PriceTagBroken({ cents, currency = "EUR" }: PriceProps) {   // read once, here
  createEffect(() => console.log(`broken: ${format(cents, currency)}`));
  return null;
}

function PriceTag(props: PriceProps) {
  console.log("PriceTag body runs");                // once, at creation — never on updates
  const p = mergeProps({ currency: "EUR" }, props);  // defaults that stay reactive
  createEffect(() => console.log(`fixed:  ${format(p.cents, p.currency)}`));   // read lazily, tracked
  return null;
}

const setCents = createRoot(() => {
  const [cents, setCents] = createSignal(8_900);
  // <PriceTag cents={cents()} /> compiles to exactly this: a getter, not a value
  createComponent(PriceTagBroken, { get cents() { return cents(); } });
  createComponent(PriceTag, { get cents() { return cents(); } });
  return setCents;
});

setCents(7_900);                                    // a price drop arrives
Result
PriceTag body runs
broken: 89.00 EUR
fixed:  89.00 EUR
fixed:  79.00 EUR

Control flow — Show, For, Index, Switch

Use the control-flow components instead of && and .map — they create and dispose exactly the nodes that change.

import { For, Index, Match, Show, Switch } from "solid-js";

type Line = { sku: string; name: string; qty: number };
type Checkout =
  | { step: "cart" } | { step: "paying" }
  | { step: "failed"; reason: string } | { step: "done"; orderId: string };
type CartPanelProps = {
  lines: Line[]; coupon?: string; suggestions: string[];
  checkout: Checkout; onRemove: (sku: string) => void;
};

export function CartPanel(props: CartPanelProps) {
  return (
    <section>
      <Show when={props.lines.length > 0} fallback={<p>Your cart is empty.</p>}>
        <ul>
          {/* For: keyed by reference — rows move, not rebuild, while line objects stay the same */}
          <For each={props.lines}>{(line) => (
            <li>{line.name} × {line.qty}
              <button aria-label={`Remove ${line.name}`}
                onClick={() => props.onRemove(line.sku)}>Remove</button>
            </li>
          )}</For>
        </ul>
      </Show>
      {/* a function child receives the narrowed, non-null value as an accessor */}
      <Show when={props.coupon}>{(code) => <p>Coupon {code()} applied</p>}</Show>
      {/* Index: keyed by position — for primitives whose values change in place */}
      <Index each={props.suggestions}>{(name) => <span class="chip">{name()}</span>}</Index>
      <Switch fallback={<button>Pay now</button>}>
        <Match when={props.checkout.step === "paying"}><p>Processing…</p></Match>
        <Match when={props.checkout.step === "failed" && props.checkout}>
          {(failed) => <p role="alert">{failed().reason}</p>}
        </Match>
        <Match when={props.checkout.step === "done" && props.checkout}>
          {(done) => <p>Order {done().orderId} placed</p>}
        </Match>
      </Switch>
    </section>
  );
}
Result

An empty cart shows the fallback; adding a line inserts one <li> without touching the others; the payment area swaps between Pay now, Processing…, the error and the confirmation as checkout changes.

Context and error boundaries

Provide shared state once with a context and a hook that fails loudly without it; catch a failing subtree — a rejected resource included — with <ErrorBoundary> and let the user retry.

import { createContext, createResource, ErrorBoundary, useContext, type ParentProps } from "solid-js";
import { createStore } from "solid-js/store";
import { render } from "solid-js/web";

type Cart = { lines: { sku: string; qty: number }[] };
type CartApi = { cart: Cart; add(sku: string): void };

const CartContext = createContext<CartApi>();                // undefined outside a provider

export function CartProvider(props: ParentProps) {
  const [cart, setCart] = createStore<Cart>({ lines: [] });
  const add = (sku: string) => setCart("lines", (lines) => [...lines, { sku, qty: 1 }]);
  return <CartContext.Provider value={{ cart, add }}>{props.children}</CartContext.Provider>;
}

export function useCart(): CartApi {
  const api = useContext(CartContext);
  if (!api) throw new Error("useCart() needs a <CartProvider> above it");
  return api;
}

async function fetchProduct(sku: string): Promise<{ name: string }> {
  const response = await fetch(`/api/products/${encodeURIComponent(sku)}`);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.json();
}

function ProductCard(props: { sku: string }) {
  const { add } = useCart();                      // fine: `add` is a function, not reactive state
  const [product] = createResource(() => props.sku, fetchProduct);   // a rejection throws on read
  const addToCart = () => add(props.sku);
  return <article><h3>{product()?.name}</h3><button onClick={addToCart}>Add to cart</button></article>;
}

export function ProductPage(props: { sku: string }) {
  const failed = (error: unknown, retry: () => void) => (
    <p role="alert">Could not load the product ({String(error)}). <button onClick={retry}>Retry</button></p>
  );
  return <ErrorBoundary fallback={failed}><ProductCard sku={props.sku} /></ErrorBoundary>;
}

// Once, at the root: every page below shares one cart, and it survives navigation between them.
render(() => (
  <CartProvider>
    <ProductPage sku="kb-01" />
  </CartProvider>
), document.querySelector("#app")!);
Result

The card shows the product's name once it loads (add <Suspense> for a loading state); on an HTTP error the boundary replaces the card with the alert, and Retry re-creates the card, which fetches again.
