Recurring work that outlives the page

A page's timers die with the tab, so hand recurring work to the service worker in the browser and let the OS scheduler start a short-lived job in Node.

Browser — service worker
// Neither API is in TypeScript's lib.dom or lib.webworker yet: declare the parts used.
type PeriodicSync = { register(tag: string, options: { minInterval: number }): Promise<void> };
type OneOffSync = { register(tag: string): Promise<void> };
type SyncEvent = Event & { readonly tag: string; waitUntil(work: Promise<unknown>): void };

// page.ts (lib DOM) — feature-detect first: browsers that lack the API also reject the permission name.
const registration = await navigator.serviceWorker.ready;
let periodicSync: PeriodicSync | undefined;              // usable only when present AND granted
if ("periodicSync" in registration) {                    // Chromium only, and granted to installed apps
  const { state } = await navigator.permissions.query({ name: "periodic-background-sync" as PermissionName });
  if (state === "granted") periodicSync = registration.periodicSync as PeriodicSync;
}

if (periodicSync) {
  await periodicSync.register("refresh-deliveries", { minInterval: 12 * 3_600_000 });
} else if ("sync" in registration) {                     // a Chromium tab without it: once, when back online
  await (registration.sync as OneOffSync).register("refresh-deliveries");
} else {                                                 // Firefox, Safari: refresh whenever the page shows
  document.addEventListener("visibilitychange", () => {
    if (document.visibilityState === "visible") void fetch("/api/deliveries/active");
  });
}

// sw.ts (lib WebWorker) — runs with no page open
for (const type of ["periodicsync", "sync"]) {
  self.addEventListener(type, (event) => {
    const sync = event as SyncEvent;
    if (sync.tag === "refresh-deliveries") sync.waitUntil(refreshDeliveries());
  });
}

async function refreshDeliveries() {
  const response = await fetch("/api/deliveries/active");
  if (!response.ok) return;                              // never cache an error page over good data
  const cache = await caches.open("deliveries");
  await cache.put("/api/deliveries/active", response);   // the next page load paints from it
}
Node — a job the OS schedules
// crontab -e — every 15 minutes the job starts, works, and exits:
// */15 * * * * cd /srv/delivery && node jobs/refresh-eta.mts >> logs/refresh-eta.log 2>&1

// jobs/refresh-eta.mts
const deadline = AbortSignal.timeout(5 * 60_000);    // never overlap the next run
try {
  const response = await fetch("http://127.0.0.1:8080/internal/refresh-eta", {
    method: "POST",
    signal: deadline,
  });
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  console.log(new Date().toISOString(), "refreshed");
} catch (error) {
  console.error(new Date().toISOString(), "refresh failed:", error);
  process.exitCode = 1;                              // cron and systemd see the failure
}

// Inside a server that already runs all day, an in-process timer is enough —
// but it stops with the process and runs once per replica:
// setInterval(refreshEta, 15 * 60_000).unref();
Result

In Chromium the browser wakes the service worker roughly at the registered interval (or when connectivity returns) and refreshes the cache with no page open — an error response is skipped, never cached; cron starts the Node job every 15 minutes and logs one line per run.

Setup
  1. Browser: an installed web app (PWA) with a registered service worker, served over HTTPS. Periodic Background Sync and Background Sync are both Chromium-only (Chrome grants periodic sync only to an installed app, and spaces it by site engagement); elsewhere refresh on load and on visibilitychange
  2. The browser column is page.ts and sw.ts in one listing: type-check page.ts with lib: ["ESNext", "DOM"] and sw.ts with lib: ["ESNext", "WebWorker"]; both pass with the declared types, as they do here together under DOM
  3. Node: a host with cron (or a systemd timer, or a Kubernetes CronJob); save the job as jobs/refresh-eta.mts

Compiled with TypeScript 5.9.3 (lib DOM) on 2026-11-16; not run here — running it needs a service worker of an installed web app in a Chromium browser; a Node.js host with cron.

Sources: Web Periodic Background Synchronization API — MDN · Background Synchronization API — MDN

Which do I reach for — and what bites

  • One delay: await delay(ms, signal) (or node:timers/promises). A deadline: AbortSignal.timeout(ms), combined with the user's cancel through AbortSignal.any.
  • Something periodic that must keep time: a deadline loop. A UI clock that may skip a second: setInterval. Anything visual: requestAnimationFrame.
  • User input: debounce for search-as-you-type, throttle for scroll and resize. Already in an RxJS pipeline? Use its debounceTime / throttleTime.
  • N jobs: Promise.all for a handful, a worker pool with a limit for dozens, for…of when order or rate limits demand serial.
  • Inject the clock (or use mock.timers) — a test that really sleeps is slow and flaky in CI.
  • Store every timer id or AbortController you start, and clear or abort it when the screen, request or process ends.
  • setTimeout is a minimum, not a promise: hidden tabs run timers at most about once a second — and in Chromium, chained timers in a tab hidden for more than 5 minutes (and silent for 30 s) only once a minute. Never count ticks to measure time — read performance.now().
  • Date.now() differences are wall-clock: they jump with NTP and user edits. Use performance.now() for durations.
  • Promise.race with a timer leaves the timer armed (keeping Node alive) unless you clearTimeout it, and leaves the losing work running.
  • A floating setInterval in a component or module is a leak per mount: return its clearInterval from the effect, or tie it to an AbortSignal.

Timing Operators — RxJS vs Plain Async

debounce, throttle, audit, sample, delay, timeout, buffer: what each one drops, how to write it by hand, and how to test it without waiting.

  • browser

  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • rxjs >=7.8
  • Node.js or a browser

debounceTime(ms)emit after ms of silence; the last of a burst winsyes, most of a burstclearTimeout + setTimeout on every call

debounceTime — search when they stop typing

Cancel and restart, so the last value of a burst wins — and with distinctUntilChanged, the same query twice is one search.

RxJS
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo
import { debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, map, Subject } from "rxjs";

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

const query$ = new Subject<string>();
const subscription = query$
  .pipe(
    map((q) => q.trim()),
    debounceTime(300),               // the last value after 300 ms of silence
    distinctUntilChanged(),          // "lofi" again is not a new search
  )
  .subscribe((q) => log(`search "${q}"`));

for (const [at, text] of [[0, "lo"], [100, "lofi"], [600, "lofi "], [1000, "jazz"]] as const) {
  await advanceTo(at);
  query$.next(text);
}

await advanceTo(2000);
subscription.unsubscribe();          // a pending emission is cancelled with it
mock.timers.reset();
By hand
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

function debouncedSearch(search: (q: string) => void, waitMs: number) {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  let lastSearched: string | undefined;
  return {
    input(text: string) {
      clearTimeout(timer);                       // every keystroke restarts the wait
      timer = setTimeout(() => {
        const q = text.trim();
        if (q === lastSearched) return;          // the distinctUntilChanged part
        lastSearched = q;
        search(q);
      }, waitMs);
    },
    cancel: () => clearTimeout(timer),           // the unsubscribe part
  };
}

const box = debouncedSearch((q) => log(`search "${q}"`), 300);
for (const [at, text] of [[0, "lo"], [100, "lofi"], [600, "lofi "], [1000, "jazz"]] as const) {
  await advanceTo(at);
  box.input(text);
}

await advanceTo(2000);
box.cancel();
mock.timers.reset();
Result
400 ms   search "lofi"
1300 ms  search "jazz"

throttleTime — at most once per window, leading and trailing

Leading only drops the final position of a drag; add the trailing edge when the last value must land (seek previews, resize).

RxJS

const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

const seek$ = new Subject<number>();
const subscription = seek$
  .pipe(throttleTime(100, asyncScheduler, { leading: true, trailing: true }))   // default is leading only
  .subscribe((position) => log(`load preview at ${position}s`));

for (let at = 0; at <= 250; at += 50) {          // the user drags the seek bar: an event every 50 ms
  await advanceTo(at);

By hand
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

function throttle<A extends unknown[]>(fn: (...args: A) => void, intervalMs: number) {
  let last = -Infinity;
  let trailing: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  const fire = (args: A) => {
    last = Date.now();
    fn(...args);
  };
  const throttled = (...args: A) => {
    clearTimeout(trailing);                      // only the latest call waits for the trailing edge
    const wait = intervalMs - (Date.now() - last);
    if (wait <= 0) fire(args);                   // leading edge
    else trailing = setTimeout(() => fire(args), wait);   // trailing edge (drop this line for leading only)
  };
  return Object.assign(throttled, { cancel: () => clearTimeout(trailing) });
}

const onSeek = throttle((position: number) => log(`load preview at ${position}s`), 100);
for (let at = 0; at <= 250; at += 50) {          // the user drags the seek bar: an event every 50 ms
  await advanceTo(at);
  onSeek(at / 10);
}

await advanceTo(1000);
onSeek.cancel();
mock.timers.reset();
Result
0 ms     load preview at 0s
100 ms   load preview at 5s
200 ms   load preview at 15s
300 ms   load preview at 25s

delay and timeout

One shifts every value, the other gives up — here into a fallback rather than an error.

RxJS
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo
import { delay, map, of, Subject, timeout, timer } from "rxjs";

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

const loadSegment = (n: number, ms: number) => timer(ms).pipe(map(() => `segment ${n}`));   // a fetch
const lowBitrate = (n: number) => of(`segment ${n} (low bitrate)`);

// timeout: nothing within 200 ms -> switch to the fallback (without `with`, it errors with TimeoutError)
loadSegment(1, 120).pipe(timeout({ first: 200, with: () => lowBitrate(1) })).subscribe(log);
loadSegment(2, 500).pipe(timeout({ first: 200, with: () => lowBitrate(2) })).subscribe(log);

// delay: every value, later; nothing is dropped
const episodeEnded$ = new Subject<string>();
episodeEnded$.pipe(delay(300)).subscribe((next) => log(`show "Up next: ${next}"`));
episodeEnded$.next("Episode 2");

await advanceTo(1000);
mock.timers.reset();
By hand
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

const loadSegment = (n: number, ms: number) =>
  new Promise<string>((resolve) => setTimeout(() => resolve(`segment ${n}`), ms));   // a fetch taking `ms`
const lowBitrate = (n: number) => `segment ${n} (low bitrate)`;

// timeout: race the work against a timer, and always disarm the timer.
// With fetch, pass AbortSignal.timeout(200) instead, so the slow request is cancelled too.
async function withFallback<T>(work: Promise<T>, ms: number, fallback: () => T): Promise<T> {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  const deadline = new Promise<T>((resolve) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => resolve(fallback()), ms);
  });
  try {
    return await Promise.race([work, deadline]);
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

void withFallback(loadSegment(1, 120), 200, () => lowBitrate(1)).then(log);
void withFallback(loadSegment(2, 500), 200, () => lowBitrate(2)).then(log);

// delay: a timer per value
const onEpisodeEnded = (next: string) => setTimeout(() => log(`show "Up next: ${next}"`), 300);
onEpisodeEnded("Episode 2");

await advanceTo(1000);
mock.timers.reset();
Result
120 ms   segment 1
200 ms   segment 2 (low bitrate)
300 ms   show "Up next: Episode 2"

bufferTime — batching by time or size

Analytics and logs: one request per window, or sooner when the batch is full, and flush what is left on close.

RxJS
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two

import { bufferTime, filter, Subject } from "rxjs";

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });

analytics$
  .pipe(
    bufferTime(1000, null, 3),                   // every 1 s, or as soon as 3 are waiting
    filter((batch) => batch.length > 0),         // bufferTime also emits empty windows
  )
  .subscribe((batch) => log(`upload [${batch.join(", ")}]`));

const playerEvents: [number, string][] = [
  [100, "play"], [200, "seek"], [300, "seek"], [900, "pause"], [2600, "stop"],

By hand
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

function batcher<T>(upload: (batch: T[]) => void, windowMs: number, maxSize: number) {
  let items: T[] = [];
  let timer = setTimeout(flush, windowMs);       // windows run back to back, as bufferTime's do
  function flush(reopen = true) {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    if (items.length > 0) upload(items);
    items = [];
    if (reopen) timer = setTimeout(flush, windowMs);
  }
  return {
    add(item: T) {
      items.push(item);
      if (items.length >= maxSize) flush();     // full: send now, start a new window
    },
    close: () => flush(false),                  // send what is left, no new window
  };
}

const analytics = batcher<string>((batch) => log(`upload [${batch.join(", ")}]`), 1000, 3);
const playerEvents: [number, string][] = [
  [100, "play"], [200, "seek"], [300, "seek"], [900, "pause"], [2600, "stop"],
];
for (const [at, event] of playerEvents) {
  await advanceTo(at);
  analytics.add(event);
}

analytics.close();
mock.timers.reset();
Result
300 ms   upload [play, seek, seek]
1300 ms  upload [pause]
2600 ms  upload [stop]

sampleTime vs auditTime

Both emit the latest value; sampleTime on a fixed clock, auditTime once per burst — silent, and waking nothing, while the player is idle.

import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo
import { auditTime, sampleTime, Subject } from "rxjs";

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

const position$ = new Subject<number>();       // the player reports its position often and irregularly

// sampleTime: on a fixed 250 ms clock, the latest value — if a new one arrived since the last tick
position$.pipe(sampleTime(250)).subscribe((s) => log(`sample  progress bar -> ${s}s`));

// auditTime: the first value opens a 250 ms window; its end emits the latest. Silent while idle.
position$.pipe(auditTime(250)).subscribe((s) => log(`audit   save resume point ${s}s`));

for (const at of [0, 40, 80, 120, 160, 200, 240, 280, 320, 700, 740]) {
  await advanceTo(at);
  position$.next(at / 100);
}

await advanceTo(1500);
position$.complete();
mock.timers.reset();
Result

250 ms   audit   save resume point 2.4s
500 ms   sample  progress bar -> 3.2s

950 ms   audit   save resume point 7.4s

Repeating work on a schedule, without drift or overlap

interval(ms) keeps a fixed schedule, exhaustMap drops ticks that arrive while a refresh still runs, and catchError inside it keeps one failed refresh from ending the schedule; by hand, the same with try/catch and an absolute deadline.

RxJS
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo
import { catchError, defer, EMPTY, exhaustMap, interval } from "rxjs";

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

let calls = 0;
async function refreshNowPlaying() {
  const call = ++calls;
  log(`refresh #${call}`);
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, call === 3 ? 1500 : 40));   // one slow response
  if (call === 2) throw new Error("HTTP 503");                                   // one failed response
}

const subscription = interval(1000)                 // a fixed schedule: 1000, 2000, 3000…
  .pipe(exhaustMap(() =>                           // a tick while one is running is dropped
    defer(refreshNowPlaying).pipe(catchError((error: Error) => {
      log(`refresh failed: ${error.message}`);     // caught INSIDE: the schedule goes on
      return EMPTY;
    }))))
  .subscribe();

await advanceTo(5500);
subscription.unsubscribe();
mock.timers.reset();
By hand
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

let calls = 0;
async function refreshNowPlaying() {
  const call = ++calls;
  log(`refresh #${call}`);
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, call === 3 ? 1500 : 40));   // one slow response
  if (call === 2) throw new Error("HTTP 503");                                   // one failed response
}

function every(intervalMs: number, work: () => Promise<void>): () => void {
  let next = Date.now() + intervalMs;              // an absolute schedule: no drift
  let timer = setTimeout(run, intervalMs);
  let stopped = false;
  async function run() {
    // Awaited, so never two at once (like exhaustMap); caught, so one failure never ends the schedule.
    await work().catch((error: Error) => log(`refresh failed: ${error.message}`));
    if (stopped) return;                           // stopped while the work was running
    next += intervalMs;
    const late = Date.now() - next;
    if (late > 0) next += Math.ceil(late / intervalMs) * intervalMs;   // missed slots are skipped
    timer = setTimeout(run, next - Date.now());
  }
  return () => {
    stopped = true;
    clearTimeout(timer);
  };
}

const stop = every(1000, refreshNowPlaying);
await advanceTo(5500);
stop();
mock.timers.reset();
Result
1000 ms  refresh #1
2000 ms  refresh #2
2040 ms  refresh failed: HTTP 503
3000 ms  refresh #3
5000 ms  refresh #4

Make time injectable — and the tests instant

Inside TestScheduler.run every RxJS scheduler is virtual and marbles describe time; t.mock.timers does the same for plain setTimeout.

import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { test } from "node:test";
import { debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged, type Observable, type SchedulerLike } from "rxjs";
import { TestScheduler } from "rxjs/testing";

// Production code takes the scheduler as a parameter... or, inside TestScheduler.run, not at all:
const searchTerms = (keys$: Observable<string>, scheduler?: SchedulerLike) =>
  keys$.pipe(debounceTime(300, scheduler), distinctUntilChanged());

test("searchTerms keeps the last key of each burst (marbles)", () => {
  const scheduler = new TestScheduler((actual, expected) => assert.deepEqual(actual, expected));
  scheduler.run(({ cold, expectObservable }) => {
    // a at 0, b at 100, c at 200, c again at 700; complete at 701
    const keys$ = cold("a 99ms b 99ms c 499ms c|");
    expectObservable(searchTerms(keys$)).toBe("500ms c 200ms |");   // run() makes every scheduler virtual
  });
});

function debounce<A extends unknown[]>(fn: (...args: A) => void, waitMs: number) {
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  return (...args: A) => {
    clearTimeout(timer);
    timer = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), waitMs);
  };
}

test("debounce calls once, with the last arguments (mock timers)", (t) => {
  t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout"] });    // undone automatically when the test ends
  const search = t.mock.fn((_query: string) => {});
  const onInput = debounce(search, 300);

  onInput("a");
  t.mock.timers.tick(100);
  onInput("ab");
  t.mock.timers.tick(299);
  assert.equal(search.mock.callCount(), 0);          // still inside the quiet period
  t.mock.timers.tick(1);
  assert.deepEqual(search.mock.calls.map((call) => call.arguments), [["ab"]]);
});
Result

Both tests pass — ✔ searchTerms keeps the last key of each burst (marbles), ✔ debounce calls once, with the last arguments (mock timers), tests 2, pass 2 — in milliseconds, and the process exits 0 (the timings vary).

Setup

  2. npm i rxjs
  3. Save as search.test.mts and run node --test (or node search.test.mts)

Owning the timer safely

Most timing bugs are lifetime bugs: one stored handle, cancelled before every restart, tied to the screen so a forgotten stop() cannot leak — and nothing started on a screen that is already gone (without that check, the late start() below would tick for ever).

RxJS — one Subscription
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo
import { interval, type Subscription, takeUntil, fromEvent } from "rxjs";

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

class ResumePointSaver {
  #subscription: Subscription | undefined;       // the one handle this object owns

  start(position: () => number, screen: AbortSignal) {
    this.#subscription?.unsubscribe();           // idempotent: a second start never adds a timer
    if (screen.aborted) return;                  // fromEvent(screen, "abort") would never fire now
    this.#subscription = interval(1000)
      .pipe(takeUntil(fromEvent(screen, "abort")))   // ends with the screen, even if stop() is forgotten
      .subscribe(() => log(`save resume point ${position()}s`));
  }
  stop() {
    this.#subscription?.unsubscribe();
    this.#subscription = undefined;
  }
}

const screen = new AbortController();
const saver = new ResumePointSaver();
let position = 0;
saver.start(() => (position += 1), screen.signal);
saver.start(() => (position += 1), screen.signal);   // e.g. play pressed twice
await advanceTo(2500);
screen.abort();                                  // the user left the player…
saver.start(() => (position += 1), screen.signal);   // …and a late `await` calls start() afterwards
await advanceTo(5000);
log(`saves: ${position}`);
mock.timers.reset();
By hand — one AbortController
import { mock } from "node:test";                              // the test clock: these two
import { setImmediate as flush } from "node:timers/promises";  // imports and all down to advanceTo

mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "setInterval", "Date"] });
const log = (message: string) => console.log(`${Date.now()} ms`.padEnd(8), message);
const advanceTo = async (ms: number) => {
  while (Date.now() < ms) {
    mock.timers.tick(10);
    await flush();                                             // let promise callbacks run
  }
};

class ResumePointSaver {
  #stop: AbortController | undefined;            // the one handle this object owns

  start(position: () => number, screen: AbortSignal) {
    this.#stop?.abort();                         // idempotent: a second start never adds a timer
    if (screen.aborted) return;                  // an "abort" listener added now would never run
    this.#stop = new AbortController();
    const lifetime = AbortSignal.any([this.#stop.signal, screen]);   // ends with the screen, too
    const timer = setInterval(() => log(`save resume point ${position()}s`), 1000);
    lifetime.addEventListener("abort", () => clearInterval(timer), { once: true });
  }
  stop() {
    this.#stop?.abort();
    this.#stop = undefined;
  }
}

const screen = new AbortController();
const saver = new ResumePointSaver();
let position = 0;
saver.start(() => (position += 1), screen.signal);
saver.start(() => (position += 1), screen.signal);   // e.g. play pressed twice
await advanceTo(2500);
screen.abort();                                  // the user left the player…
saver.start(() => (position += 1), screen.signal);   // …and a late `await` calls start() afterwards
await advanceTo(5000);
log(`saves: ${position}`);
mock.timers.reset();
Result
1000 ms  save resume point 1s
2000 ms  save resume point 2s
5000 ms  saves: 2

Safety checklist for timing code

  • Store every Subscription, timer id or AbortController you start, and end it in stop(), an effect cleanup, or on the screen's AbortSignal.
  • Cancel before restarting (this.#subscription?.unsubscribe(), this.#stop?.abort()), or a second start() doubles the timers.
  • Periodic work: an absolute schedule (timer(0, ms), or a deadline loop) and no overlap (exhaustMap, or await the work before scheduling the next).
  • Inject time. TestScheduler.run for RxJS, t.mock.timers.enable({ apis: ["setTimeout", "Date"] }) for plain code — a test that really sleeps flakes in CI.
  • Know what each operator drops: debounceTime and auditTime keep the last, throttleTime the first unless trailing: true, sampleTime the latest per tick.
  • An abort listener added after the abort never runs, and fromEvent(signal, "abort") never fires: check signal.aborted before starting anything.
  • An error inside exhaustMap/switchMap on a timer ends the whole schedule; catch it inside, per tick (defer(work).pipe(catchError(...))), or in a try around the awaited work.
  • bufferTime emits empty arrays every window — filter((b) => b.length > 0) before uploading — and keeps a timer running even when idle.
  • timeout(ms) without with errors with TimeoutError and ends the stream; inside a switchMap, catch it there.
  • Promise.race with a timer neither cancels the loser nor disarms the timer by itself: clearTimeout in finally, and prefer AbortSignal.timeout wherever a signal can be passed.
  • Don't measure elapsed time with Date.now() differences in production — the wall clock jumps; use performance.now() (or the scheduler's now()).
  • Mock timers replace setTimeout, setInterval and Date, but not AbortSignal.timeout or named imports from node:timers/promises — code that must be tested on a virtual clock should take its timers or scheduler as a parameter.

Concurrency Models — Event Loop, Workers & Atomics

One thread per event loop; parallelism means another loop (a Worker) and messages, or — rarely — shared memory with Atomics.

  • browser
  • node
  • typescript >=5.5
  • node >=22.18
  • Node.js or a browser

Sources: Worker threads — Node.js · Using Web Workers — MDN · The Node.js event loop — Node.js

GCD, actors and tasks → JavaScript

The page, or a Node process, is one big @MainActor: nothing runs in parallel unless you start a worker.

NeedSwiftJavaScriptWhat changes
Main-thread work@MainActor, DispatchQueue.maineverything, by defaultno data races on ordinary objects — and no parallelism either

The event loop: microtasks before tasks

Inside a callback (and in CommonJS) it is sync, nextTick, promise microtasks, then the next phase, while at the top level of an ES module promise jobs run before nextTick.

import { readFile } from "node:fs";

// Inside an I/O callback the order below is fixed. (In CommonJS main-module code nextTick also
// runs before promises, but setTimeout(0) vs setImmediate has no fixed order there.)
readFile(new URL(import.meta.url), () => {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("6. setTimeout 0      — timers phase, next turn of the loop"), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log("5. setImmediate      — check phase, right after I/O"));
  Promise.resolve().then(() => {
    console.log("3. promise .then      — microtask");
    queueMicrotask(() => console.log("4. nested microtask  — still before any task"));
  });
  process.nextTick(() => console.log("2. process.nextTick  — before promise microtasks"));
  console.log("1. synchronous code — always runs to completion first");
});

// At the top level of an ES module (this file) evaluation is itself a promise job, so promise
// callbacks run BEFORE nextTick here, and setTimeout(0) vs setImmediate has no fixed order.
process.nextTick(() => console.log("d. top-level nextTick — after every promise job, in an ES module"));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("b. top-level promise — before nextTick, in an ES module"));

async function saveDraft() {
  console.log("a. before await — synchronous, in the caller's task");
  await null;
  console.log("c. after await  — a microtask, queued behind the promise above");
}

void saveDraft();
// A browser has no nextTick or setImmediate: sync → microtasks → (maybe a render) → the next task.
Result
a. before await — synchronous, in the caller's task
b. top-level promise — before nextTick, in an ES module
c. after await  — a microtask, queued behind the promise above
d. top-level nextTick — after every promise job, in an ES module
1. synchronous code — always runs to completion first
2. process.nextTick  — before promise microtasks
3. promise .then      — microtask
4. nested microtask  — still before any task
5. setImmediate      — check phase, right after I/O
6. setTimeout 0      — timers phase, next turn of the loop

The race JavaScript does have: state changing across an await

Between two awaits nothing else runs, but a read–modify–write that spans an await interleaves with another one, so serialise it with a promise mutex or share the request in flight.

import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

type Cart = { items: string[] };
let stored: Cart = { items: [] };                              // stands in for a server or IndexedDB

async function addToCart(sku: string) {                       // read, modify, write — across an await
  const cart = structuredClone(stored);                       // read
  await sleep(5);                                             // e.g. check stock with the server
  cart.items.push(sku);
  stored = cart;                                              // write: whatever happened meanwhile is lost
}

await Promise.all([addToCart("mug"), addToCart("teapot")]);   // two taps, close together
console.log("unguarded:", stored.items);                     // both read the empty cart: one is lost

class Mutex {                                                  // fix 1: one section at a time
  #tail: Promise<unknown> = Promise.resolve();

  run<T>(section: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
    const result = this.#tail.then(() => section());         // starts when the previous one settles
    this.#tail = result.catch(() => {});
    return result;
  }
}

const cartLock = new Mutex();
stored = { items: [] };
await Promise.all(["mug", "teapot"].map((sku) => cartLock.run(() => addToCart(sku))));
console.log("with a mutex:", stored.items);

let refreshes = 0;                                            // fix 2, single-flight: callers share
let inFlight: Promise<string> | undefined;                    // the one request already in flight

function refreshToken(): Promise<string> {
  inFlight ??= sleep(5)
    .then(() => `token-${++refreshes}`)
    .finally(() => {
      inFlight = undefined;                                   // the next 401 after this starts afresh
    });
  return inFlight;
}

const tokens = await Promise.all([refreshToken(), refreshToken(), refreshToken()]);   // three 401s at once
console.log("single-flight:", tokens, "refreshes:", refreshes);
Result
unguarded: [ 'teapot' ]
with a mutex: [ 'mug', 'teapot' ]
single-flight: [ 'token-1', 'token-1', 'token-1' ] refreshes: 1

Off the main thread in the browser: a Web Worker

A worker keeps the page responsive while a large upload is parsed, and a MessageChannel per request makes sure one file's reply can never settle another file's promise.

page.ts — the main thread
type ReportRequest = { csv: ArrayBuffer; reply: MessagePort };
type ReportResult = { rows: number; revenueByRegion: Record<string, number> };
type ReportReply = { ok: true; report: ReportResult } | { ok: false; error: string };

// Bundlers recognise this exact shape and emit the worker as its own file.
const worker = new Worker(new URL("./report-worker.ts", import.meta.url), { type: "module" });
const picker = document.querySelector<HTMLInputElement>("#csv-file")!;
const output = document.querySelector<HTMLOutputElement>("#report")!;

// One MessageChannel per request: its reply can only ever settle its own promise.
function buildReport(csv: ArrayBuffer): Promise<ReportResult> {
  const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel();
  const settled = new AbortController();
  return new Promise<ReportResult>((resolve, reject) => {
    port1.onmessage = ({ data }: MessageEvent<ReportReply>) =>
      data.ok ? resolve(data.report) : reject(new Error(data.error));
    // The script failed to load, or threw outside a request: no reply will ever come.
    const onError = (e: ErrorEvent) => reject(new Error(`report worker failed: ${e.message}`));
    worker.addEventListener("error", onError, { signal: settled.signal });
    worker.postMessage({ csv, reply: port2 } satisfies ReportRequest, [csv, port2]);   // both transferred
  }).finally(() => {
    port1.close();
    settled.abort();                                     // removes this request's error listener
  });
}

let latestPick = 0;
picker.addEventListener("change", async () => {
  const file = picker.files?.[0];
  if (!file) return;
  const pick = ++latestPick;
  output.textContent = "Building report…";             // still scrollable, still clickable
  try {
    const { rows, revenueByRegion } = await buildReport(await file.arrayBuffer());
    if (pick !== latestPick) return;                   // a newer file was picked meanwhile
    const totals = Object.entries(revenueByRegion).map(([region, c]) => `${region} $${(c / 100).toFixed(2)}`);
    output.textContent = `${rows} orders · ${totals.join(" · ")}`;
  } catch (error) {
    if (pick === latestPick) output.textContent = `Could not read ${file.name}: ${(error as Error).message}`;
  }
});
report-worker.ts — its own thread
// A dedicated worker: no DOM, its own event loop and heap.
// In a real project, type-check worker files with "lib": ["ESNext", "WebWorker"].
type ReportRequest = { csv: ArrayBuffer; reply: MessagePort };
type ReportResult = { rows: number; revenueByRegion: Record<string, number> };
type ReportReply = { ok: true; report: ReportResult } | { ok: false; error: string };

function buildReport(csv: ArrayBuffer): ReportResult {   // CPU-bound: fine here, fatal on the main thread
  const lines = new TextDecoder().decode(csv).trimEnd().split("\n");
  if (lines[0] !== "region,cents") throw new Error("not an orders export");
  const revenueByRegion: Record<string, number> = {};
  for (const line of lines.slice(1)) {
    const [region = "unknown", cents = "0"] = line.split(",");
    revenueByRegion[region] = (revenueByRegion[region] ?? 0) + Number(cents);
  }
  return { rows: lines.length - 1, revenueByRegion };
}

self.onmessage = ({ data: { csv, reply } }: MessageEvent<ReportRequest>) => {
  let message: ReportReply;
  try {
    message = { ok: true, report: buildReport(csv) };
  } catch (error) {
    message = { ok: false, error: (error as Error).message };   // a bad file fails its own request only
  }
  reply.postMessage(message);                            // answered on the caller's own channel
  reply.close();
};
Result

Choosing a CSV export shows Building report… while the page keeps scrolling, then a line such as 400000 orders · north $2498000.00 · south $2499000.00 · ….

Setup
  1. A page with <input type="file" id="csv-file"> and <output id="report"></output>, built with Vite or another bundler that understands new Worker(new URL(...), { type: "module" })

Off the main thread in Node: worker_threads

A file can start itself as a worker — new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url)) with an isMainThread branch — so the worker code stays typed and in one place.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { isMainThread, parentPort, Worker, workerData } from "node:worker_threads";

type Report = { rows: number; revenueByRegion: Record<string, number> };

function buildReport(csv: string): Report {                // CPU-bound: it blocks whichever thread runs it
  const revenueByRegion: Record<string, number> = {};
  const lines = csv.split("\n");
  for (let i = 1; i < lines.length; i++) {
    const [region = "", cents = "0"] = lines[i]!.split(",");
    revenueByRegion[region] = (revenueByRegion[region] ?? 0) + Number(cents);
  }
  return { rows: lines.length - 1, revenueByRegion };
}

function exportCsv(rows: number): string {                 // stand-in for a large export
  const regions = ["north", "south", "east", "west"];
  const lines = ["region,cents"];
  for (let i = 0; i < rows; i++) lines.push(`${regions[i % 4]},${(i * 37) % 5000}`);
  return lines.join("\n");
}

if (isMainThread) {
  // Meanwhile this thread keeps serving HTTP requests, timers and I/O.
  const worker = new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url), { workerData: exportCsv(400_000) });
  const [{ rows, revenueByRegion }] = (await once(worker, "message")) as [Report];
  const totals = Object.entries(revenueByRegion).map(([region, cents]) => `${region} $${cents / 100}`);
  console.log(`${rows} orders:`, totals.join(", "));
} else {
  parentPort!.postMessage(buildReport(workerData as string));   // then the worker has nothing left and exits
}
Result
400000 orders: north $2498000, south $2499000, east $2500000, west $2501000
Setup

  2. Save as main.mts and run node main.mts

Waiting for N parallel jobs

One worker per job and Promise.all — fail-fast — or Promise.allSettled when one bad month must not sink the others.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { isMainThread, parentPort, Worker, workerData } from "node:worker_threads";

type Job = { month: string; rows: number };
type Result = { month: string; cents: number };

function monthlyRevenue({ month, rows }: Job): Result {      // stand-in for parsing that month's export
  if (rows < 0) throw new RangeError(`${month}: corrupt export`);
  let cents = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < rows; i++) cents += (i * 37) % 5000;
  return { month, cents };
}

async function inWorker(job: Job): Promise<Result> {
  const worker = new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url), { workerData: job });
  const [result] = (await once(worker, "message")) as [Result];   // rejects if the worker throws
  return result;
}

if (isMainThread) {
  const months: Job[] = [
    { month: "Jan", rows: 3_000_000 }, { month: "Feb", rows: 2_800_000 }, { month: "Mar", rows: 3_100_000 },
  ];

  const all = await Promise.all(months.map(inWorker));    // in parallel, a core each; the first failure wins
  console.log(all.map((r) => `${r.month} $${r.cents / 100}`).join(", "));

  const settled = await Promise.allSettled([...months, { month: "Apr", rows: -1 }].map(inWorker));
  for (const outcome of settled) {
    if (outcome.status === "fulfilled") console.log(`${outcome.value.month} ok`);
    else console.log(`failed: ${(outcome.reason as Error).message}`);
  }
} else {
  parentPort!.postMessage(monthlyRevenue(workerData as Job));
}
Result
Jan $74985000, Feb $69986000, Mar $77484500
Jan ok
Feb ok
Mar ok
failed: Apr: corrupt export

A worker pool

A fixed number of lanes reuse one worker each and pull from a shared queue, and a job whose worker crashes or exits without replying fails only itself while the lane replaces the worker.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { isMainThread, parentPort, Worker } from "node:worker_threads";

type Job = { month: string; rows: number };

function noReply([code]: unknown[]): never {
  throw new Error(`worker exited (code ${code}) without replying`);
}

async function runOnPool(jobs: Job[], size: number, script: URL): Promise<PromiseSettledResult<number>[]> {
  const outcomes: PromiseSettledResult<number>[] = [];
  let next = 0;

  const lane = async () => {                                 // one per thread (long-lived pools: Piscina)
    let worker = new Worker(script);                         // reused for job after job…
    let exited = once(worker, "exit");                       // …with one "exit" listener for its whole life
    while (next < jobs.length) {
      const index = next++;                                  // claimed synchronously: one lane per job
      try {
        worker.postMessage(jobs[index]);
        const [cents] = await Promise.race([once(worker, "message"), exited.then(noReply)]);   // or "error"
        outcomes[index] = { status: "fulfilled", value: cents as number };
      } catch (reason) {
        outcomes[index] = { status: "rejected", reason };    // fail this job only, and go on
        worker = new Worker(script);                         // it crashed or exited: replace it
        exited = once(worker, "exit");
      }
    }

    await worker.terminate();                                // reached whatever the jobs did
  };

  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: size }, lane));
  return outcomes;
}

if (isMainThread) {
  const jobs: Job[] = Object.entries({ Feb: -1, Mar: 0, Apr: 4e5 }).map(([month, rows]) => ({ month, rows }));
  (await runOnPool(jobs, 2, new URL(import.meta.url))).forEach((o, i) =>   // 3 jobs on 2 threads
    console.log(jobs[i]!.month, o.status === "fulfilled" ? `$${o.value / 100}` : `${o.reason}`));
} else {
  parentPort!.on("message", ({ month, rows }: Job) => {      // long-lived: one message per job
    if (rows < 0) throw new RangeError(`${month}: corrupt export`);   // uncaught: this worker dies
    if (rows === 0) process.exit(0);                         // e.g. a library that exits: no reply at all
    parentPort!.postMessage(rows * 2_500);                   // stand-in: that month's revenue in cents
  });
}
Result
Feb RangeError: Feb: corrupt export
Mar Error: worker exited (code 0) without replying
Apr $10000000

Transferring vs copying

postMessage copies with the structured-clone algorithm unless a buffer is in the transfer list, in which case it moves and the sender's copy is detached.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { MessageChannel } from "node:worker_threads";

const { port1, port2 } = new MessageChannel();          // the channel a Worker uses underneath
const csv = new TextEncoder().encode("region,cents\nnorth,1200\nsouth,800\n").buffer;

// Copy (the default): Maps, Dates and typed arrays survive; both sides own their own copy.
port1.postMessage({ exportedAt: new Date(0), regions: new Map([["north", 1]]), csv });
const [copied] = await once(port2, "message");
console.log("copy:", copied.exportedAt instanceof Date, copied.regions.get("north"));
console.log("  sender still has", csv.byteLength, "bytes");

// Transfer: list the buffer and it moves. Zero-copy, and the sender's view is detached.
port1.postMessage({ csv }, [csv]);
const [moved] = await once(port2, "message");
console.log("transfer: receiver has", (moved.csv as ArrayBuffer).byteLength, "bytes");
console.log("  sender has", csv.byteLength, "bytes");

// structuredClone() is the same algorithm in one thread — and takes a transfer list too.
const draft = { totals: new Map([["east", 990]]), rows: new Uint8Array(16) };
const snapshot = structuredClone(draft, { transfer: [draft.rows.buffer] });
console.log("structuredClone:", snapshot.totals.get("east"), snapshot.rows.length);
console.log("  original rows:", draft.rows.length);
port1.close();
Result
copy: true 1
  sender still has 34 bytes
transfer: receiver has 34 bytes
  sender has 0 bytes
structuredClone: 990 16
  original rows: 0

What structured clone will not carry

Functions and symbols throw DataCloneError, while errors and class instances arrive stripped of their own class, name and fields, so send plain data and rebuild them on the other side.

// What structured clone (postMessage, workerData, structuredClone) does not carry across.
class HttpError extends Error {
  status: number;
  constructor(message: string, status: number) {
    super(message);
    this.name = "HttpError";
    this.status = status;
  }
}

const tryClone = (label: string, value: unknown) => {
  try {
    structuredClone(value);
    console.log(label, "→ cloned");
  } catch (e) {
    console.log(label, "→", (e as DOMException).name);
  }
};

tryClone("a function", { format: (cents: number) => `$${cents / 100}` });
tryClone("a Symbol", { id: Symbol("order") });

// An error clones as one of the seven standard types, picked by its `name` (else plain Error), with
// message, stack and cause; its own name, class and fields are lost. (Any class instance arrives as
// a plain object for the same reason.)
const lost = structuredClone(new HttpError("orders API down", 503)) as Partial<HttpError>;
console.log("HttpError arrives as", lost.constructor?.name, "| name:", lost.name, "| status:", lost.status);

const parse = structuredClone(new TypeError("parse failed", { cause: new Error("bad row 7") }));
console.log(parse.name, "keeps its cause:", (parse.cause as Error).message);

const batch = structuredClone(new AggregateError([new Error("Feb")], "1 month failed"));
const { errors } = batch as Partial<AggregateError>;
console.log("AggregateError arrives as", batch.constructor.name, "| errors:", errors);

// The fix: send plain data, and rebuild the error on the other side.
const wire = structuredClone({ name: "HttpError", message: "orders API down", status: 503 });
const rebuilt = new HttpError(wire.message, wire.status);
console.log("rebuilt:", rebuilt instanceof HttpError, rebuilt.name, rebuilt.status);
Result
a function → DataCloneError
a Symbol → DataCloneError
HttpError arrives as Error | name: Error | status: undefined
TypeError keeps its cause: bad row 7
AggregateError arrives as Error | errors: undefined
rebuilt: true HttpError 503

SharedArrayBuffer + Atomics for shared state

Shared memory is the one place real data races exist in JavaScript, so use Atomics for every read-modify-write and waitAsync/notify to signal without polling.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { isMainThread, Worker, workerData } from "node:worker_threads";

type Chunk = { shared: SharedArrayBuffer; rows: number };
const ROWS_DONE = 0;                                      // slot indexes in the shared Int32Array
const WORKERS_DONE = 1;

if (isMainThread) {
  const shared = new SharedArrayBuffer(2 * Int32Array.BYTES_PER_ELEMENT);   // shared, not copied
  const progress = new Int32Array(shared);
  const workers = Array.from({ length: 4 }, () =>
    new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url), { workerData: { shared, rows: 250_000 } satisfies Chunk }));
  const exited = workers.map((w) => once(w, "exit"));    // listen now: a fast worker may exit before we look

  let finished = 0;
  while (finished < 4) {                                // wait without blocking the main thread
    const { async, value } = Atomics.waitAsync(progress, WORKERS_DONE, finished);
    if (async) await value;
    finished = Atomics.load(progress, WORKERS_DONE);
  }
  console.log("rows parsed:", Atomics.load(progress, ROWS_DONE));   // exact; `+=` would lose updates
  await Promise.all(exited);
} else {
  const { shared, rows } = workerData as Chunk;
  const progress = new Int32Array(shared);
  for (let row = 1; row <= rows; row++) {
    // …parse the row…
    if (row % 10_000 === 0) Atomics.add(progress, ROWS_DONE, 10_000);   // progress, as an atomic add
  }
  Atomics.add(progress, WORKERS_DONE, 1);
  Atomics.notify(progress, WORKERS_DONE);               // wake whoever waits on that slot
}
Result
rows parsed: 1000000

Cancelling in-flight work

A busy worker never reads its messages, so check a shared flag in the loop, refuse an already-aborted signal up front, and keep terminate() for code that cannot cooperate.

import { once } from "node:events";
import { isMainThread, parentPort, Worker, workerData } from "node:worker_threads";

type Outcome = { status: "done" | "cancelled"; rowsParsed: number };
const TOTAL_ROWS = 200_000_000;

async function runReport(signal: AbortSignal): Promise<Outcome> {   // an ordinary AbortSignal API
  signal.throwIfAborted();                              // already cancelled: start nothing
  const cancelFlag = new Int32Array(new SharedArrayBuffer(4));
  const worker = new Worker(new URL(import.meta.url), { workerData: cancelFlag });
  const cancel = () => Atomics.store(cancelFlag, 0, 1);  // seen at once; a "cancel" message would wait
  signal.addEventListener("abort", cancel, { once: true });
  try {
    const [outcome] = await once(worker, "message");
    return outcome as Outcome;
  } finally {
    signal.removeEventListener("abort", cancel);        // the report is over: no listener left behind
  }
}

if (isMainThread) {
  const dialog = new AbortController();
  const report = runReport(dialog.signal);
  setTimeout(() => dialog.abort(), 20);                 // the user closes the report dialog
  const { status, rowsParsed } = await report;
  console.log(status, "| stopped early:", rowsParsed < TOTAL_ROWS);
  await runReport(dialog.signal).catch((e: Error) => console.log("closed dialog, new report:", e.name));

  const runaway = new Worker("for (;;) {}", { eval: true });   // inline code that never checks a flag
  await runaway.terminate();                            // the hard stop: no finally, no cleanup in it
  console.log("runaway worker terminated");
} else {
  const cancelFlag = workerData as Int32Array;
  let row = 0;
  for (; row < TOTAL_ROWS; row++) {
    if (row % 100_000 === 0 && Atomics.load(cancelFlag, 0) === 1) break;   // a cheap, regular check
    // …parse the row…
  }
  parentPort!.postMessage({ status: row < TOTAL_ROWS ? "cancelled" : "done", rowsParsed: row });
}
Result
cancelled | stopped early: true
closed dialog, new report: AbortError
runaway worker terminated

Talking points

Short answers that show depth.

  • JavaScript is single-threaded per event loop, not per process: every Worker is another loop with its own heap, and they talk by messages.
  • async/await is concurrency, not parallelism — it interleaves waiting. CPU-bound work still blocks the loop it runs on; only a worker runs it in parallel.
  • Microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) all run before the next task or render. A microtask that schedules another forever freezes the page as surely as a while (true).
  • No await means no interleaving: between two awaits your code is atomic. Races in JavaScript are about state changing across an await, which is why a single owner works like an actor.
  • Transfer large ArrayBuffers, ImageBitmaps and MessagePorts instead of copying them; copy small messages — and measure before optimising the rest.
  • Size pools from os.availableParallelism() (Node) or navigator.hardwareConcurrency (browser) minus one, and reuse workers: in Node, libraries such as Piscina do this for you.
  • SharedArrayBuffer in a browser needs cross-origin isolation (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp or credentialless); without it the constructor is not even defined. Atomics.waitAsync is in every engine since Firefox 145.
  • Atomics.wait blocks the thread: never on the browser's main thread (it throws there) — use Atomics.waitAsync.
  • Node's libuv thread pool already runs fs, crypto.pbkdf2, zlib and DNS lookups off the main thread: reach for worker_threads only for your own CPU-bound JavaScript.

Networking — REST with fetch

fetch as a typed client: status checks and validated decoding, timeouts, retry with jitter, token refresh, pagination, ETags and progress.

Sources: Using the Fetch API — MDN · AbortSignal — MDN · HTTP caching — MDN · Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) — MDN · Zod documentation · HTTP — Node.js documentation

What fetch does — and what you add

fetch is a transport, not a client: every row on the right is code you own once, in one wrapper.

Concernfetch on its ownWhat the wrapper adds
HTTP errorsResolves for every status; only a network failure or an abort rejectsCheck response.ok / response.status before reading the body
Decodingresponse.json() returns Promise<any> and throws SyntaxError on an HTML error pageParse unknown with a schema (zod) — as Order checks nothing
TimeoutNone — a stalled server hangs the call for minutessignal: AbortSignal.timeout(ms), combined with the caller's signal via AbortSignal.any
RetryNoneBackoff with jitter, idempotent requests only, honour Retry-After
AuthCookies by credentials; no token handlingAuthorization: Bearer, one shared refresh on 401
Cross-origin (browser)Blocked unless the API answers with CORS headers; an Authorization or JSON content-type header triggers an OPTIONS preflightServer: Access-Control-Allow-Origin (an exact origin, never * with credentials: "include"), -Allow-Headers, -Allow-Credentials
CachingBrowser: the HTTP cache obeys Cache-Control/ETag. Node: no cache at allcache: option in the browser; an ETag map in Node
Uploadsbody takes a string, Blob, FormData, URLSearchParams or a streamFormData for multipart file uploads — and no manual content-type, so the boundary is set for you
ProgressNo events; the body is a ReadableStreamCount bytes while reading response.body (download) or a stream body (upload)

A typed GET and POST

One function owns the status check and the decode, so a 404 or a renamed field fails loudly at the boundary instead of as undefined three screens later.

import { z } from "zod";

type Fetch = (url: URL, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>;

const ORDERS: Record<string, object> = {
  "/orders/o-1": { id: "o-1", total: 42.5, status: "paid" },
  "/orders/o-3": { id: "o-3", total: "42.50", status: "paid" },   // a backend regression
};

const shopApi: Fetch = async (url, init) => {        // the stand-in API, injected; omit it to use fetch
  if (init?.method === "POST") {
    const { total } = JSON.parse(String(init.body)) as { total: number };   // pick fields: never spread
    return Response.json({ id: "o-2", total, status: "open" }, { status: 201 });
  }
  const order = ORDERS[url.pathname];
  return order ? Response.json(order) : Response.json({ error: "not found" }, { status: 404 });
};

const Order = z.object({ id: z.string(), total: z.number(), status: z.enum(["open", "paid"]) });

class HttpError extends Error {
  status: number;

  constructor(status: number, body: string) {
    super(`HTTP ${status}: ${body}`);
    this.status = status;
  }
}

async function request<T>(schema: z.ZodType<T>, path: string, init: RequestInit = {}, send: Fetch = fetch) {
  const headers = new Headers(init.headers);
  headers.set("accept", "application/json");
  const response = await send(new URL(path, "https://api.shop.example"), { ...init, headers });
  if (!response.ok) throw new HttpError(response.status, await response.text());
  return schema.parse(await response.json());       // unknown in, Order out, or a ZodError naming the field
}

const order = await request(Order, "/orders/o-1", {}, shopApi);
const created = await request(Order, "/orders", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ total: 19.99 }),
}, shopApi);
console.log(order.status, order.total, "|", created.id, created.status, created.total);

for (const path of ["/orders/o-9", "/orders/o-3"]) {
  await request(Order, path, {}, shopApi).catch((e) =>
    console.log(e instanceof z.ZodError ? e.issues[0]?.path : `${e}`));
}
Result
paid 42.5 | o-2 open 19.99
Error: HTTP 404: {"error":"not found"}
[ 'total' ]

A small API client with errors as a union

Return a Result whose error is a discriminated union, keep the body read inside the guarded region, and inject fetch: callers must handle every failure kind — even a proxy's HTML page with status 200 — and tests need no server.

import { z } from "zod";

type ApiError =
  | { kind: "network"; message: string }
  | { kind: "timeout" }
  | { kind: "http"; status: number }
  | { kind: "decode"; detail: string };

type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: ApiError };

type Fetch = (url: URL, init?: RequestInit) => Promise<Response>;

const fail = (error: ApiError) => ({ ok: false as const, error });

async function call<T>(schema: z.ZodType<T>, url: URL, send: Fetch): Promise<Result<T>> {
  let body: unknown;
  try {
    const response = await send(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5_000) });
    if (!response.ok) {
      await response.body?.cancel();                 // release the connection
      return fail({ kind: "http", status: response.status });
    }
    body = await response.json();                    // inside the try: a cut-off or HTML body lands below
  } catch (e) {
    if (e instanceof SyntaxError) return fail({ kind: "decode", detail: "body is not JSON" });
    if (e instanceof DOMException && e.name === "TimeoutError") return fail({ kind: "timeout" });
    return fail({ kind: "network", message: String(e) });
  }

  const parsed = schema.safeParse(body);
  if (parsed.success) return { ok: true, value: parsed.data };
  return fail({ kind: "decode", detail: parsed.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path}: ${i.code}`).join(", ") });
}

const Order = z.object({ id: z.string(), total: z.number() });

const getOrder = (id: string, send: Fetch = fetch) =>
  call(Order, new URL(`/orders/${encodeURIComponent(id)}`, "https://api.shop.example"), send);

const fake: Fetch = async ({ pathname }) => {
  if (pathname === "/orders/o-1") return Response.json({ id: "o-1", total: 42.5 });
  if (pathname === "/orders/o-2") return Response.json({ id: "o-2", total: "42.50" });
  if (pathname === "/orders/o-3") return new Response("<html>Down for maintenance</html>");   // a proxy, 200
  if (pathname === "/orders/o-4") throw new TypeError("fetch failed");
  return new Response(null, { status: 404 });
};

for (const id of ["o-1", "o-2", "o-3", "o-4", "o-5"]) {
  console.log(id, JSON.stringify(await getOrder(id, fake)));   // the injected transport: no server needed
}
Result
o-1 {"ok":true,"value":{"id":"o-1","total":42.5}}
o-2 {"ok":false,"error":{"kind":"decode","detail":"total: invalid_type"}}
o-3 {"ok":false,"error":{"kind":"decode","detail":"body is not JSON"}}

Timeout and cancellation with AbortSignal

Give every request a deadline, and let the caller cancel too: AbortSignal.any combines both, and the error's name tells them apart.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { once } from "node:events";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";

const server = createServer((_req, res) => {
  const timer = setTimeout(() => res.end("report ready"), 200);   // a slow export endpoint
  res.on("close", () => clearTimeout(timer));                     // the client left: stop the work
}).listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await once(server, "listening");
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${(server.address() as AddressInfo).port}/reports/export`;

async function exportReport(timeoutMs: number, userSignal?: AbortSignal): Promise<string> {
  const deadline = AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs);
  const signal = userSignal ? AbortSignal.any([userSignal, deadline]) : deadline;
  const response = await fetch(url, { signal });
  return response.text();                       // the body read is covered by the same signal
}

async function attempt(label: string, timeoutMs: number, signal?: AbortSignal) {
  try {
    console.log(label, await exportReport(timeoutMs, signal));
  } catch (e) {
    const name = (e as DOMException).name;       // TimeoutError: retry later. AbortError: the user moved on.
    console.log(label, name);
  }
}

await attempt("50 ms deadline:", 50);
const leaveScreen = new AbortController();
setTimeout(() => leaveScreen.abort(), 20);
await attempt("user navigated away:", 5_000, leaveScreen.signal);
await attempt("2 s deadline:", 2_000);
server.close();
Result
50 ms deadline: TimeoutError
user navigated away: AbortError
2 s deadline: report ready

Retry with exponential backoff and jitter

Retry only what is safe to repeat (GET, PUT, DELETE, or a POST with an Idempotency-Key) and never what the caller cancelled, cap every delay including Retry-After, randomise it, and inject the randomness and the sleep so the test is instant.

type RetryOptions = {
  retries: number;
  baseMs: number;
  capMs: number;
  signal?: AbortSignal;
  random: () => number;                              // injected, like sleep, so tests run instantly
  sleep: (ms: number, signal?: AbortSignal) => Promise<void>;
};

const RETRYABLE = new Set([408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504]);

async function withRetry(send: (signal?: AbortSignal) => Promise<Response>, o: RetryOptions) {
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    let response: Response | undefined;
    try {
      response = await send(o.signal);
      if (!RETRYABLE.has(response.status) || attempt === o.retries) return response;
      await response.body?.cancel();                 // free the connection before waiting
    } catch (e) {
      if (o.signal?.aborted || attempt === o.retries) throw e;   // the caller gave up: never retry that
    }

    const jittered = Math.round(o.random() * Math.min(o.capMs, o.baseMs * 2 ** attempt));   // full jitter
    const retryAfter = Number(response?.headers.get("retry-after"));   // seconds; an HTTP date falls back
    await o.sleep(Math.min(o.capMs, retryAfter > 0 ? retryAfter * 1000 : jittered), o.signal);
  }
}

const options: RetryOptions = {
  retries: 4, baseMs: 100, capMs: 10_000,
  random: () => 0.5, sleep: async (ms) => console.log(`waited ${ms} ms`),
};

const replies = [
  () => Promise.reject(new TypeError("fetch failed")),
  () => new Response(null, { status: 429, headers: { "retry-after": "3600" } }),   // an hour: capped
  () => Response.json({ id: "o-1" }),
];
let calls = 0;
const response = await withRetry(async () => replies[calls++]!(), options);
console.log(response.status, "after", calls, "attempts");

const closedScreen = AbortSignal.abort();            // the user already left: fetch rejects at once
const getOrder = (signal?: AbortSignal) => fetch("https://api.shop.example/orders/o-1", { signal });
await withRetry(getOrder, { ...options, signal: closedScreen })   // no "waited" line follows: not retried
  .catch((e: DOMException) => console.log(e.name));
Result
waited 50 ms
waited 10000 ms
200 after 3 attempts
AbortError

Bearer auth with a single-flight refresh on 401

When five requests hit an expired token at once, exactly one refresh runs and the others wait for it, and a refused refresh becomes a typed sign-out instead of Bearer undefined (the cookie-authenticated refresh endpoint also needs the security sheet's CSRF check).

import { z } from "zod";

class SignedOutError extends Error {}

const BASE = "https://api.shop.example";

let refreshes = 0;
let sessionRevoked = false;

async function send(url: URL, init?: RequestInit): Promise<Response> {   // the stand-in API
  const valid = !sessionRevoked && new Headers(init?.headers).get("authorization") === "Bearer fresh";
  if (url.pathname !== "/token/refresh") return new Response(null, { status: valid ? 200 : 401 });
  refreshes++;
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 20));   // all five 401s arrive meanwhile
  return sessionRevoked ? new Response(null, { status: 401 }) : Response.json({ accessToken: "fresh" });
}

class AuthedClient {
  #token = "expired";                              // in a browser the refresh token is an HttpOnly cookie
  #refreshing: Promise<string> | null = null;
  #authorized = (path: string, token: string) =>
    send(new URL(path, BASE), { headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });

  async get(path: string): Promise<Response> {
    const used = this.#token;
    const response = await this.#authorized(path, used);
    if (response.status !== 401) return response;
    await response.body?.cancel();
    const token = this.#token !== used ? this.#token : await this.#refresh();   // already refreshed?
    return this.#authorized(path, token);            // retried once; a second 401 goes to the caller
  }

  #refresh(): Promise<string> {
    this.#refreshing ??= send(new URL("/token/refresh", BASE), { method: "POST", credentials: "include" })
      .then(async (r) => {
        if (!r.ok) throw new SignedOutError(`refresh refused (${r.status}): sign in again`);
        return (this.#token = z.object({ accessToken: z.string() }).parse(await r.json()).accessToken);
      })
      .finally(() => (this.#refreshing = null));
    return this.#refreshing;
  }
}

const client = new AuthedClient();
const orders = await Promise.all([1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map((n) => client.get(`/orders/o-${n}`)));   // all at once
console.log(orders.map((r) => r.status).join(" "), "| refreshes:", refreshes);

sessionRevoked = true;                               // signed out on another device; the old token expires
await client.get("/orders/o-6").catch((e) => console.log(e instanceof SignedOutError, e.message));
Result
200 200 200 200 200 | refreshes: 1
true refresh refused (401): sign in again

Cursor pagination as an async iterator

Callers write for await and never see cursors; pages are fetched only as they are consumed, so break stops the requests.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { once } from "node:events";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";
import { z } from "zod";

const ALL = Array.from({ length: 7 }, (_, i) => ({ id: `o-${i + 1}` }));
let requests = 0;
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  requests++;
  const params = new URL(req.url ?? "/", "http://localhost").searchParams;
  const start = Number(params.get("cursor") ?? 0);
  const end = start + Number(params.get("limit"));
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ items: ALL.slice(start, end), nextCursor: end < ALL.length ? `${end}` : null }));
}).listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await once(server, "listening");
const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${(server.address() as AddressInfo).port}`;

const Page = z.object({ items: z.array(z.object({ id: z.string() })), nextCursor: z.string().nullable() });

async function* orders(signal?: AbortSignal) {
  let cursor: string | null = null;
  do {
    const url = new URL("/orders?limit=3", base);
    if (cursor) url.searchParams.set("cursor", cursor);   // opaque: never compute it yourself
    const response = await fetch(url, { signal });
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    const page = Page.parse(await response.json());
    yield* page.items;
    cursor = page.nextCursor;
  } while (cursor);
}

const firstFour: string[] = [];
for await (const order of orders()) {
  firstFour.push(order.id);
  if (firstFour.length === 4) break;             // page 3 is never requested
}
console.log(firstFour.join(" "), "| requests:", requests);
console.log((await Array.fromAsync(orders())).length, "orders | requests:", requests);
server.close();
Result
o-1 o-2 o-3 o-4 | requests: 2
7 orders | requests: 5

Caching with ETag and If-None-Match

The server tags a representation and answers an empty 304 while the client's If-None-Match still matches, which browsers do for you per Cache-Control but Node's cacheless fetch leaves to you.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { once } from "node:events";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";

let catalog = { version: 1, products: ["mug", "tote"] };
const statuses: number[] = [];
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  const etag = `"catalog-v${catalog.version}"`;
  res.setHeader("etag", etag);
  res.setHeader("cache-control", "no-cache");     // may be stored, but must be revalidated every time
  res.statusCode = req.headers["if-none-match"] === etag ? 304 : 200;
  statuses.push(res.statusCode);
  res.end(res.statusCode === 304 ? undefined : JSON.stringify(catalog.products));
}).listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await once(server, "listening");
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${(server.address() as AddressInfo).port}/catalog`;

const cache = new Map<string, { etag: string; body: string[] }>();

async function getCatalog(): Promise<string[]> {
  const hit = cache.get(url);
  const response = await fetch(url, { headers: hit ? { "if-none-match": hit.etag } : {} });
  if (response.status === 304 && hit) return hit.body;   // no body was sent: reuse the stored one
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  const body = (await response.json()) as string[];
  const etag = response.headers.get("etag");
  if (etag) cache.set(url, { etag, body });
  return body;
}

console.log(await getCatalog());
console.log(await getCatalog());
catalog = { version: 2, products: ["mug", "tote", "cap"] };
console.log(await getCatalog());
console.log("server answered", statuses.join(", "));
server.close();
Result
[ 'mug', 'tote' ]
[ 'mug', 'tote' ]
[ 'mug', 'tote', 'cap' ]
server answered 200, 304, 200

Download with progress

Progress is bytes counted while the body streams, and Content-Length is a total only for an uncompressed response whose Content-Encoding the page can see (cross-origin that takes Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Content-Encoding), so clamp it and fall back to an indeterminate bar.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { once } from "node:events";
import { gzipSync } from "node:zlib";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";

const sprite = Buffer.alloc(300_000, 7);           // a thumbnail sprite for the video scrubber

const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  if (req.url === "/chunked") {
    res.write(sprite.subarray(0, 100_000));        // write() before end(): no Content-Length
    res.end(sprite.subarray(100_000));
  } else if (req.url === "/gzip") {
    res.setHeader("content-encoding", "gzip").end(gzipSync(sprite));   // Content-Length: the compressed size
  } else {
    res.end(sprite);                               // one end(): Node sends Content-Length
  }
}).listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await once(server, "listening");
const base = `http://127.0.0.1:${(server.address() as AddressInfo).port}`;

async function download(url: string, onProgress: (fraction?: number) => void) {
  const response = await fetch(url);
  if (!response.ok || !response.body) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);

  const length = Number(response.headers.get("content-length"));
  const total = !response.headers.has("content-encoding") && length > 0 ? length : undefined;

  const chunks: Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>[] = [];
  let loaded = 0;
  const reader = response.body.getReader();
  for (let read = await reader.read(); !read.done; read = await reader.read()) {
    chunks.push(read.value);
    loaded += read.value.length;
    onProgress(total ? Math.min(1, loaded / total) : undefined);   // undefined: an indeterminate bar
  }
  return new Uint8Array(await new Blob(chunks).arrayBuffer());
}

for (const route of ["/plain", "/chunked", "/gzip"]) {
  const fractions: (number | undefined)[] = [];
  const file = await download(base + route, (fraction) => fractions.push(fraction));
  const last = fractions.at(-1);
  const progress = last === undefined ? "indeterminate bar" : `${last * 100}%`;
  console.log(`${route}: ${file.length} bytes, progress ${progress}`);
}
server.close();
Result
/plain: 300000 bytes, progress 100%
/chunked: 300000 bytes, progress indeterminate bar
/gzip: 300000 bytes, progress indeterminate bar

Upload with progress

A stream body is pulled only as fast as the socket drains, so counting pulled bytes is upload progress in Node and in Chromium over HTTP/2, while XMLHttpRequest.upload.onprogress remains the portable choice in browsers.

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { once } from "node:events";
import type { AddressInfo } from "node:net";

const server = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  let received = 0;
  for await (const chunk of req) received += (chunk as Buffer).length;
  res.end(String(received));
}).listen(0, "127.0.0.1");
await once(server, "listening");
const url = `http://127.0.0.1:${(server.address() as AddressInfo).port}/media/upload`;

async function upload(data: Uint8Array, onProgress: (fraction: number) => void): Promise<string> {
  let sent = 0;
  const body = new ReadableStream<Uint8Array>({
    pull(controller) {
      if (sent === data.length) return controller.close();
      const chunk = data.subarray(sent, sent + 64 * 1024);
      controller.enqueue(chunk);
      sent += chunk.length;
      onProgress(sent / data.length);
    },
  });
  // `duplex: "half"` is required for a stream body; lib.dom does not declare it yet
  const init: RequestInit & { duplex: "half" } = { method: "PUT", body, duplex: "half" };
  const response = await fetch(url, init);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
  return response.text();
}

const seen: number[] = [];
const received = await upload(new Uint8Array(1_000_000), (f) => seen.push(f));
console.log(`server received ${received} bytes; progress ended at ${seen.at(-1)} after ${seen.length} steps`);
server.close();
Result
server received 1000000 bytes; progress ended at 1 after 16 steps

Rules worth saying out loud

The bugs that reach production because fetch looked simple.

  • await res.json() as Order — a type assertion, not a check. Parse unknown with a schema at the boundary.
  • Assuming fetch throws on 404/500. It resolves; branch on response.ok before reading the body.
  • Every request gets a deadline (AbortSignal.timeout) and accepts the caller's signal — a screen that closes cancels its requests, and a cancelled request is never retried.
  • Retry idempotent requests only, with capped, jittered backoff; a retry storm without jitter is a self-inflicted outage.
  • One refresh in flight per session: share the promise, retry the original request once, sign out on a refused refresh or a second 401.
  • A body can be read once — response.clone() before reading if two consumers need it; body.cancel() a response you discard.
  • Building query strings by concatenation. new URL() + searchParams.set encodes for you; encodeURIComponent for path segments.
  • In real apps a query cache (TanStack Query, RTK Query) owns dedupe, staleness and refetching; these cards are what it does underneath.

Networking — SOAP, gRPC & GraphQL

SOAP envelopes and faults, GraphQL over plain fetch with errors beside data, gRPC from generated stubs with deadlines — and when to pick which.
